2a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna case: two claim a found garment, each says all is theirs; each swears less than half is not theirs; they divide.
Second case: one claims all, the other claims half; oaths yield three-quarters and one-quarter respectively.
Animal case: two riders, or a rider and a leader, each claim all; both swear less than half, then divide.
Exception: if the parties admit each other's claims or have witnesses, they divide without any oath.
Why does the tanna need to teach two separate pairs of claims?
Restates the mishna's two pairs of claims as the basis for the question.
The mishna teaches one combined claim per party: each says found it and all of it is mine.
Why not teach only the found-it claim, since the all-mine claim is evidently implied?
Teaching only found-it could mean mere sight; so all-mine is taught to show sight alone does not acquire.
Challenge: can found-it really mean saw it, given Rabbenai's understanding of the term?
Cites Rabbenai's reading of Deuteronomy 22:3: finding means the item came into the finder's hand.
Reply: the tanna used colloquial speech, where seeing an item is also called finding it.
Upholds the view: sight alone does not acquire, which is why the tanna adds the all-mine claim.
Why not teach only the all-mine claim without the found-it claim?
If only all-mine were taught, found-it might be read as sight; the mishna's extra clause shows sight does not acquire.
Challenge: the mishna is not one case, since it lists this one and that one as separate claims.
Quotes the mishna's wording, with each party's claim introduced by this one says, as evidence.
Resolution attributed to Rav Pappa and variants: first clause concerns a found item, second a sale; both cases are needed.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If only found items were taught, one would think oaths apply there alone, since the other party loses nothing; sales would need none.
If only sales were taught, one would think oaths apply there, since each could justify taking the item; found items would need none.
Asks how the mishna can refer to a sale, since the buyer should be whoever paid the seller.
No: it concerns a seller who took money from both parties, one willingly and one unwillingly, so an oath settles it.
Suggests the mishna is not like Ben Nannas, who would bar oaths where one party is surely lying.
Cites the Shevuot mishna in which Ben Nannas objects that oaths in such cases are sworn in vain.
Even on Ben Nannas, here no oath is in vain: both may have lifted the item together, so both swear truthfully.
Suggests the mishna is not like Sumakhos, who would divide disputed property without any oath.
Asks what the mishna follows if not Sumakhos, since the Rabbis require the claimant to bear the burden of proof.
The Rabbis distinguish: where neither party holds the item the claimant bears the burden; where both hold it, they divide under oath.
If Sumakhos divides without oath where neither holds the item, then where both hold it, a fortiori no oath is needed.
No a fortiori: Sumakhos speaks only of uncertain claims on both sides, not of certain claims on both sides.
Rabba bar Rav Huna holds Sumakhos divides even with certain claims on both sides; what then can establish the mishna as Sumakhos?
Sumakhos speaks where the parties have a financial association with the item beyond their claims; without it, an oath is required.
Asks whether this is not an a fortiori inference: if there both parties have a financial stake, here too the same should follow.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects: if both claims are possible, then with no financial stake Sumakhos should a fortiori not divide without oath.
Even on Sumakhos, the mishna's oath is rabbinic, so the a fortiori does not apply.
Cites Rabbi Yohanan: the oath is a Sages' ordinance so no one seizes another's garment and claims it.
Suggests the mishna is not like Rabbi Yosei, who would leave disputed money unclaimed until Elijah, leaving fraud undeterred.
Asks what the mishna follows instead, namely the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Yosei.
Argues that since the Rabbis hold the remainder should wait, this garment is similar to the uncertain remainder.
Distinguishes: in the deposit one of the claimants is certainly right, while here both may be right, so they divide under oath.
If the mishna follows Rabbi Yosei, a fortiori the disputed garment should wait, since one claim may be fraudulent.
Even on Rabbi Yosei, a swindler is certain in the deposit case but not here; both may have lifted the garment together.
Alternative: Rabbi Yosei punishes the swindler by confiscating a deposit, but a swindler over a garment would lose nothing.
The alternative works for found items but not sales, where both parties paid, so it cannot explain the sale case.
The distinction is as first stated: in the mishna there is no certainty that one party lies, for both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei.
Cites the mishna on a storekeeper relying on his ledger, where each party takes an oath and collects payment.
Asks why the money is not set aside until Elijah, since a swindler certainly exists between storekeeper and laborer.
The storekeeper acted as the employer's agent and cannot be bound by the laborer's oath; the employer trusted the laborer without witnesses.
The laborer likewise answers that he worked for the employer, not the storekeeper, so both swear and collect from the employer.
Rabbi Hiyya's baraita: a debtor who admits part of a claim pays that part and swears about the rest.
Derives the baraita a fortiori: an admission should not outweigh witness testimony, so witnessed partial debt requires an oath on the rest.
Cites the mishna of two people holding a garment, each claiming to have found it, as a parallel halakha.
Each holding part of the garment is like witnesses confirming partial title, so the mishna requires each to swear.
Asks why the a fortiori is needed, since the comparison to partial admission seems self-evident.
It is needed so one does not think the oath applies only to admission by one's own mouth.
Rabba's explanation: the Torah imposes an oath on partial admission because a person would not lie to his creditor to his face.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rationale: a debtor who admits only part evades full payment, so an oath forces full admission; witnesses are different, so the a fortiori is needed.
Spells out the a fortiori: if a self-admission that carries no money liability still requires an oath, witnesses should require one too.
Asks whether a litigant's admission does not create monetary liability, since it counts as equal to a hundred witnesses.
The admission does not create liability for a fine (kenas); with fines the same a fortiori structure applies to witnesses.
Refutes: admission matters for an offering, and witnesses do not obligate an offering, so the comparison fails.
Not difficult: Rabbi Hiyya follows Rabbi Meir, who holds witnesses obligate an offering by a fortiori reasoning.
Cites the Karetot mishna: Rabbi Meir holds a witnessed transgressor must bring an offering, while the Rabbis exempt him.
Rabbi Meir's a fortiori: if witnesses can impose death, they can impose the lighter offering.
The Rabbis object: a defendant could say he sinned intentionally, which is exempt, so witnesses cannot establish unwitting sin.
Admission also obligates a guilt-offering or one-fifth payment for robbery, while witnesses do not, so the comparison fails again.
Not difficult: Rabbi Hiyya follows Rabbi Meir, so witnesses also obligate guilt-offerings and one-fifth by a fortiori reasoning.
Admission cannot be contradicted or refuted as conspiring witnesses can, so the same rules for witnesses cannot be assumed.
Rabbi Hiyya's inference may instead come from one witness: if one witness requires an oath, two witnesses should too.
Rejects that inference: one witness requires an oath only on the matter he testifies to, not on other claims.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Would the same rule apply to two witnesses, so the defendant swears only about the claim he denies, not the debt they testify to?
Rav Pappa's reformulation: Rabbi Hiyya's a fortiori derives from the extension of an oath that one witness imposes.
What is notable about that extension? One oath leads to another; would the same hold for witnesses establishing money liability?
Admission can show that something beyond the oath can obligate a further oath; one witness shows testimony open to contradiction still obligates an oath.
Rejects the one-witness inference: that extension applies only to the matter the witness testifies about.
Admission shows this distinction is irrelevant, since a defendant may swear even about a claim he denies.
The derivation is restated: the shared feature is a claim and denial before the court, which obligates an oath, including Rabbi Hiyya's case.
The common feature may not hold: a defendant contradicted by witnesses loses trust, unlike a non-contradicted one; Rav Hisda's rule is cited against this.
Refute differently: these cases escape conspiring-witness rules, which witnesses' testimony would face.
Not difficult: Rabbi Hiyya does not refute based on conspiring-witness rules, which do apply to a single witness.
Is the mishna's case comparable? The creditor has witnesses and the debtor none, unlike the garment where both holders are equally placed.
The comparison was actually to another ruling by Rabbi Hiyya.
Rabbi Hiyya's ruling: if one claims one hundred and the other admits only fifty, and hands it over, he must swear about the remainder.
Reason: handing over money while admitting part counts as admitting part, so the defendant still swears like any partial admitter.
Cites the mishna of two people holding a garment as a similar halakha.
Here each holds part, so what each holds is his, as if the other handed it over; hence each swears.
Rav Sheshet: one who says here you are and denies the rest is exempt, since the admitted money is treated as already in the creditor's hands.
For Rav Sheshet the mishna is difficult, since it requires an oath in a seemingly comparable case.
Rav Sheshet can answer that the mishna's oath is a rabbinic ordinance, and that a debtor who hands over money is generally exempt.
Rabbi Hiyya: the rabbinic oath must have a Torah counterpart, so Torah law must impose an oath on one who says here you are.
Raises an objection against Rabbi Hiyya's view from a baraita.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: on a note for an unspecified sum, if the creditor claims five and the debtor admits three, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar requires an oath; Rabbi Akiva exempts him.
Infers from the baraita that the oath turns on admitting three, since admitting only two would exempt him as a Here-you-are case.
Rejects the inference: the baraita's three-dinar wording excludes Rabbi Akiva's view, so admitting two still obligates an oath.
If admitting two also requires an oath, the baraita should have said so explicitly rather than phrasing it around the admission of part.
Admitting two is exempt; the Here-you-are rule still obliges an oath, but here the note supports the debtor, or the note creates a land lien.
Objection to Rav Sheshet from the baraita's latter clause: Rabbi Akiva's exemption implies admitting two would require an oath.
Rejects that: admitting two is also exempt, and the dispute with three excludes Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view.
Logical argument: if admitting two obligated an oath, Rabbi Akiva could not exempt the three-dinar admission, so the debtor must be exempt at two.
The alternative explanation seems to contradict Rabbi Hiyya, since here Here-you-are is exempt despite his view.
Rabbi Hiyya's case differs: the note supports the claim, or the lien on land means no oath is taken for denying a land-secured debt.
Mar Zutra objects to Rav Sheshet from a mishna about claims for vessels and land.
The Shevuot mishna: partial admissions of vessels or land, and the oath rules for each, are set out.
Infers from the mishna that a claim for two sets of vessels should obligate an oath, which would make Here-you-are obligate an oath.
No: even two sets of vessels are exempt; the mishna's point is that admitting some vessels binds the denied land too.
What does this teach? If so, an oath on one claim binds an additional land claim, which seems to be a known rule.
The Kiddushin mishna already states that an oath on movables binds the land guarantee, so the rule is repeated here.
The Shevuot mishna is the primary source for this rule, while the Kiddushin mishna mentions it only incidentally.

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the verse is needed to exclude land from the oath if admitting land always amounts to returning it.
The verse applies where the defendant dug pits, ditches or caves in the land, so returning it is not simply here you are.
Alternative case: admitting vessels but denying land still leaves no oath for the land, as the verse teaches.
A baraita lists four bailees who owe an oath only on partial admission combined with partial denial.
Asks whether the baraita's case is one where the bailee admitted some items, which would support Rabbi Hiyya.
No, the case is three cows, one lost by accident and one by negligence, so the admission is not a literal return.
A baraita challenges Rabbi Hiyya: witnesses prove part of the claim, and the verse imposes an oath only for admission by mouth.
The challenge fails because Rabbi Hiyya is himself a tanna who may dispute a baraita.
Objects that the tanna himself cites a verse, which seems to bear on the dispute.
Reply: according to Rabbi Hiyya, that verse teaches that partial admission obligates an oath.
Alternative reply from the father of Rabbi Aptoriki: the repeated words this and it each teach one halakha.
Asks how Rabbi Hiyya reads the double qualification: one word for partial admission, one for same-type admission.
The other Sage rejects the same-type requirement and follows Rabban Gamliel, who obligates an oath when the admission differs in kind.
A shepherd received animals without witnesses, denied it, and witnesses later showed he ate two of them.
Rabbi Zeira infers that by Rabbi Hiyya's first halakha the shepherd must swear about the rest or pay.
Abaye objects: the shepherd cannot swear, since he is a robber whom witnesses proved ate some animals.
Rabbi Zeira replies that he meant the opposing party swears and collects, not the shepherd.
Even if Rabbi Hiyya is rejected, the court should still obligate the shepherd to swear under Rav Nahman's ordinance.
A mishna: if the defendant completely denies the claim, he is exempt from an oath.
Rav Nahman holds that the judges still administer an oath of inducement even to a full denier.
The Gemara explains that Rav Nahman's halakha is a rabbinic ordinance, not an oath required by Torah law.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An ordinance cannot be built upon another ordinance, so no further oath is administered here.
Objection: why not derive disqualification from the shepherd status itself, since an ordinary shepherd is disqualified?
Distinguish a shepherd herding his own animals, presumed a robber, from one herding others' animals; giving animals to shepherds is otherwise forbidden.
Mishna: each litigant swears he lacks less than half of the garment, and they divide it.
Asks whether the oath concerns the part he holds or the part he lacks, since the latter wording is problematic.
Rav Huna's formulation: swear that he claims the item and that he lacks less than half of it.
Asks why he should not simply swear that all of it is his, as that is his claim.
Would the court give him the whole garment on such an oath? No, so he cannot swear it is all his.
Asks why he should not swear that half is his, making Rav Huna's complex formulation unnecessary.
Such an oath compromises his original claim to the entire garment.
Challenge: even under Rav Huna's formulation, he compromises his initial claim to the whole.
Reply: he says all of it is his, and the oath merely reflects the opponent's position.
Asks why the oath is required at all, since each litigant ends up with what he holds.
Rabbi Yochanan: it is a rabbinic ordinance so that no one seizes another's garment and claims it as his own.
Asks whether suspicion of financial dishonesty makes him also suspect for taking an oath.
Suspicion about money does not imply suspicion about oaths, since even a thief considers a false oath more severe.
Reductio: if that were not so, the partial-admission oath of the verse would also be disallowed on the same reasoning.
Rejection: the debtor only temporarily evades the creditor, intending to repay, which differs from theft.
Rav Hisda's ruling: a denier of a loan may testify, while a denier of a deposit may not, since deposits are not used.
Objection from the baraita of four bailees: a bailee does not need to buy time, so he too should be suspect of oath.
The bailee may be evading while intending to recover a stolen or lost deposit, so he is not a robber.
Asks why a deposit-denier is disqualified as a witness if he could equally be buying time.
Disqualification applies only where the deposit was in his house or in his hand when he denied it.
Objection: Rav Huna's oath on a deposit is difficult if suspicion of dishonesty bars oaths.
The bailee is not a robber, since he may rationalize that he paid for the item.
Rav Aha objects: paying for the deposit still violates the prohibition against coveting another's property.
Most people understand coveting as taking without payment, so the bailee may not know he acts criminally.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: Rav Nahman's oath of inducement for a full denier is hard, since a suspected thief should not be allowed to swear.
Further objection: Rabbi Hiyya's baraita letting both storekeeper and laborer swear and take pay is also hard on this principle.
Further objection: Rav Sheshet's three oaths for a suspected bailee are hard if suspicion of dishonesty bars oaths.
Conclusion: suspicion of financial dishonesty does not by itself make one suspect regarding oaths.
Abaye: the oaths arise because he may hold an old loan from the plaintiff and withholds the item as repayment, not theft.
Objection: if so, he should take the item without an oath, since the oath would not establish the truth.
Abaye refined: he may be uncertain whether the plaintiff owes him, so he withholds the item just in case.
Objection: if he can seize property on an uncertain debt, why not also swear falsely on the same uncertainty?
Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi: people hesitate to swear falsely but will seize property, since property can be returned and an oath cannot be retracted.
Rabbi Zeira's dilemma: if two hold a garment and one seizes all of it before the court, what is the halakha?
Asks the circumstances: does silence signal admission, and what more should the shouting party have done?
The dilemma concerns one who was silent first and shouted later: did he admit ownership, or was silence due to the court witnessing it?
Rav Nahman's proof from a baraita: both swear only when both hold the garment, otherwise the holder keeps it unless the claimant proves ownership.
Rejects the proof: the baraita may describe a case where both came to court, divided, and one later held the garment alone.
Alternative: the baraita may describe one holding the garment while the other grasps its edge, which Sumakhos concedes is worthless.
Restates the consecration dilemma: if seizure before the court removes the garment, a consecration of the whole is invalid.
Sides of the dilemma: is a verbal consecration to God like a transfer to a layman, making the consecrator like one who seized it?
Scriptural proof: from 'when a man shall sanctify his house', only what is in his possession may be consecrated, excluding this garment.
Begins a proof from a reported incident; the Gemara continues on the next daf.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates two litigants over a bathhouse; one consecrated it, and the Sages abstained from bathing there, uncertain whether the consecration took effect.
Rav Oshaya asks Rabba to put the question to Rav Hisda when he reaches Kafrei.
Rav Hamnuna cites a mishna and baraita on uncertain firstborns, arguing the bathhouse consecration parallels a priest's seizure.
Rabba rejects the proof: firstborn sanctity arises intrinsically at birth, not through consecration, so the cases are not comparable.
Rav Hananya cites a baraita where uncertain firstborns enter the tithing pen, supporting that the court removes them from a priest.
Objection: if the court did not remove it from the priest, why would the owner's animals enter the pen? It would exempt his property with the priest's.
Abaye rejects Rav Hananya's support: the baraita does not establish his point.
Abaye's resolution: the baraita concerns an owner with nine animals plus one uncertain firstborn, so the owner is exempt either way.
Abaye retracts, citing a mishna: if one counted animal rejoins the uncounted pen, all of them are exempt from tithing.
Argument from both horns: whether or not the uncertain animal is tithable, the owner's tally is valid.
Rava's principle: a tally fit to reach ten exempts those counted, so the remaining animals are exempt from tithing.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: why is the whole flock exempt when a counted animal rejoins the pen, given the verse on a certain tenth?
Rav Aha asks which uncertain animals the mishna means; if uncertain firstborns, they are already sacred and cannot be tithed.
Rather, the mishna concerns uncertain redemption of a firstborn donkey, which is redeemed by a lamb.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh: an Israelite with ten uncertain donkey firstborns separates ten lambs and tithes them, keeping all.
Asks what halakhic conclusion was reached about the bathhouse case.
Proof: Rav Huna resolved an analogous case by Rav Naḥman's rule that property not recoverable by legal process cannot be consecrated validly.
Objection: by inference, consecrating recoverable property would be valid, yet Rabbi Yoḥanan holds neither robber nor owner can consecrate property not in possession.
Answer: the bathhouse is an excavated, immovable bath already in the owner's possession and recoverable by legal process.
Rav Taḥalifa's baraita: two grasping a garment each take up to where the hand reaches, and the rest is divided equally, with an oath.
Asks how the mishna applies, since it says they divide without the hand-reach rule.
Rav Pappa: the mishna concerns litigants holding only the fringes, so each swears and they divide the garment.
Rav Mesharshiyya: grasping three by three fingerbreadths effects acquisition, following the verse about the shoe in Ruth 4:7.
Asks how this differs from Rav Hisda's ruling about a divorce bill still held by a string.
Divorce requires complete severance, while a cloth transaction requires only a valid act of giving part of the cloth.
Rava: even a garment with gold thread is divided between them.
Challenge: this is obvious, since they simply divide the remainder.
Answer: the case is where the gold is closer to one party, so Rava teaches an equal division, lest one dictate the cut line.
Baraita: creditor and debtor grip a promissory note; the note must be ratified through its signatories, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: creditor and debtor divide the debt attested in the note.
A note that fell into a judge's possession stays there until proof is provided, and the litigants cannot remove it.
Rabbi Yosei: the note keeps its presumptive validity, and the litigants proceed according to its contents.
Objection: does ratification mean the creditor collects in full? Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would then divide it like the garment mishna.
Rava, citing Rav Naḥman: where ratified, all agree they divide; they dispute only where it is not ratified.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requires ratification even if the debtor admits writing the note, otherwise the creditor receives nothing.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's position.
The unratified note is merely a shard; only the debtor's corroboration makes it valid, and he claims repayment, so ratification is needed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: ratification is not required when the debtor admits writing the note, so they divide it even if unratified.
Baraita: a note that fell into a judge's hands may not be removed until proof is provided.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what distinguishes a note that fell into a judge's possession, which the creditor cannot retrieve to collect.
Rava: the baraita concerns a ratified note found by a third party, which is not returned, since repayment may have occurred.
The ruling about ratified notes is needed because repayment may have happened and the debtor lost the note.
Rabbi Yosei holds the note keeps its presumptive status, since a debtor who had repaid would have destroyed it immediately.
Objection: a baraita on a found marriage contract, which is not returned when payment is claimed, conflicts with the note ruling.
Rabbi Yosei's distinction: a still-married wife gets the found contract back, but a widow or divorcee does not, since she may have been paid.
Reversing the baraita's order: the note may never be removed, per Rabbi Yosei, while the Rabbis say it keeps presumptive status.
Asks why the Rabbis disagree across the two baraitot, since here they ignore repayment but there they consider it.
Resolution: the marriage-contract baraita follows Rabbi Yosei entirely and is incomplete, so the contradiction disappears.
Rav Pappa: do not reverse the baraita; Rabbi Yosei speaks to the Rabbis on their own terms, considering possible repayment.
Rav Pappa's reading: Rabbi Yosei argues that a still-married wife should receive the contract, since payment is not yet due.
Objection: the husband may have paid money in exchange for the contract, so returning it would let her collect twice.
Ravina: the Rabbis suspect two marriage contracts were written, while Rabbi Yosei considers that rare, resolving the contradiction.
Rabbi Elazar: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel divides a note by the part each grasps; Rabbi Yochanan says always divide equally.
Asks whether Rabbi Yochanan holds equal division even when one grasps the standard part and the other the essential part.
Objection: the baraita on the garment says each takes up to his hand's reach, so the same should apply here.
Answer: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling concerns the essential part lying in the middle, not one grasping each part.
Asks what the equal-division ruling adds, since division seems obvious.
It is needed where the essential part is closer to one party, so the other may demand an equal division.
Objection: if each takes a standard or essential part, why would half a note matter, like half a note covering a flask?
Ravina: the division concerns monetary value, since the date on the essential part raises the note's worth to the creditor.
Objection: if the item itself were divided, as with a garment, it would be ruined, so division must be of monetary value.
Not difficult: the garment may indeed be cut in two.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the division: each party receives an item of monetary value that could still be made into a children's garment.
Gemara asks: if a gold-threaded garment is divided, does the garment itself get split, which would ruin it?
Not a difficulty: the divided garment remains usable as a garment for royal children, so it is not ruined.
Gemara asks the same about the mishna of two riders on an animal: must the animal be divided, destroying it?
Restates the challenge: if dividing the animal ruins it, how can the mishna direct that division?
Granted, a kosher animal stays fit for slaughter and division for its meat, so division is not destructive.
But if the animal is non-kosher, dividing it would ruin it, so the same objection arises.
Rather, the division is of monetary value; here too, the found item is divided by its value.
Rami bar Hama infers from the mishna that one who lifts a found item for another makes the other the acquirer.
His proof: otherwise neither litigant would acquire, each half would lie as if on the ground, so the other must acquire it.
Rava rejects the proof: lifting solely for another does not make the other acquire; the mishna works through each litigant's own acquisition.
Rava's support: a principal is exempt for an agent's theft, but co-thieves are liable, so acquiring for oneself extends to partners.
Rava derives a new halakha: a deaf-mute and a competent person lifting a found item together each acquire their share.
Gemara asks: the deaf-mute acquires because the competent person lifts for him, but how does the competent person acquire his own share?
Answer: the deaf-mute acquires while the competent person does not, deriving from two deaf-mutes who acquire together.
Gemara objects: if the competent person acquires nothing for himself, how can the derivation hold, since he lifted only for himself?
Rather, neither acquires: since the competent person acquires nothing, the deaf-mute does not acquire either.
Asks what distinguishes this case from two deaf-mutes, who both acquire the item.
Sages ordained joint acquisition for two deaf-mutes to avoid quarrels; here, the deaf-mute has no such ordinance and cannot acquire.
Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi the source of Rami's inference, since the first clause describes two claimants each saying all is theirs.
Rami proves from the mishna's superfluous case: a third party has no claim, so the lifter acquires for the other.
Objection: the clause is not superfluous, since the first clause concerns found items and the latter concerns buying and selling.
Rami derives it from the latter clause, where one claims all and the other claims half, which would otherwise be superfluous.
Asks whether the clause concerns a found item or buying and selling, and if the latter, what new ruling it teaches.
Answer: the one claiming half is not like one returning a lost item, since he may be maneuvering to avoid an oath.
Rami again derives from the two-riders clause, which would otherwise be superfluous, that the lifter acquires for the other.
Objection: perhaps the mishna teaches that one who merely sits on an animal acquires it, without moving it.
Derivation from the last clause: when claimants admit or have witnesses, they divide without oath, which must concern a found item.
Asks whether this refers to buying and selling, and if so why it needs stating.
Answer: it must refer to a found item, so one who lifts for another acquires for him.
Rava offers his own principle: one who acquires for himself also acquires part for another.
Quotes the mishna: two people sitting on an animal, or one sitting while the other leads it.
Rav Yosef introduces a transmission from Rav Yehuda; the statement continues beyond this daf.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda reports hearing two halakhot from Shmuel about riding and leading, but cannot recall which applies to which.
Asks what the case is: if it concerns riding alone and leading alone, leading surely acquires, so why the uncertainty?
Rather, the dilemma concerns riding while another leads: does the rider take precedence by gripping, or the leader, since the animal moves because of him?
Rav Yosef reports that Rav Yehuda told him he would analyze the matter from a mishna, though he does not recall Shmuel's view.
Mishna on the wagon: Rabbi Meir exempts the rider; Shmuel's reversed wording implies riders do not acquire, a fortiori when another leads.
Abaye objects: Rav Yosef often told us to analyze it ourselves, never attributing it to Rav Yehuda, so the attribution seems mistaken.
Rav Yosef replies that he remembers Rav Yehuda's proof and his own response to it.
Rav Yosef asks how one can resolve the rider case from the wagon, since a wagon passenger does not hold reins while a rider does.
Rav Yehuda replied that Rav and Shmuel hold that holding reins of an ownerless animal does not effect acquisition.
Abaye poses the same objection in another version, to Rav Yosef, regarding the distinction in holding reins.

Objection from a mishna on two riders: if it follows Rabbi Meir, even a wagon passenger acquires; so the Rabbis must hold riding acquires.

ranges.en: The baraita says they acquired in that manner; Rabbi Yehuda holds one acquires a camel only by pulling and a donkey only by driving.

ranges.en: Lists cases where riding acquires: on a public road, for an important man, for a woman, and for a contemptible person.

Mishnah: a rider asks a pedestrian to lift a found item; the lifter acquires it, but a later claim of prior acquisition counts for nothing.
Cites the pe'a mishna: Rabbi Eliezer says one gleaning for a named poor man acquires for him, while the Rabbis disagree.
Ulla, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the dispute concerns a rich person gleaning pe'a on behalf of a poor person.
Explains the reasoning: Rabbi Eliezer applies miggo, while the Rabbis apply it only once; poor-to-poor acquisition is agreed by all.

ranges.en: Asks whose view the mishna follows; if the dispute concerns only rich versus poor, it fits neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Eliezer.

Rav Nachman: a laborer is different, since his hand is like the employer's while he works as his agent.

Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba cites Rabbi Yochanan: the lifter acquires for another; the mishna's case is a request to give, not to acquire.
Mishnah: one who falls upon a found item without a formal mode of acquisition loses it to a second person who seizes it properly.
Reish Lakish: a person's four cubits acquire ownerless items for him everywhere, an ordinance instituted to prevent quarrels.
Abaye and Rava raise objections from pe'a and Nezikin mishnas, challenging whether one's four cubits acquire property everywhere.
Quotes Pe'a: a poor person who throws gleaned pe'a onto the rest, falls upon it, or spreads a garment over it does not acquire it.

Asks: if the ordinance applies even without stated intent, why would he not acquire the produce?

ranges.en: Rav Pappa's alternative: the four-cubit ordinance applies only on public land, not in an owner's field, and pe'a rights do not include it.

Rav Sheshet: the ordinance applies in an alleyway where crowds do not gather, not in the public domain where they do.
Asks: Reish Lakish's wording says everywhere, which seems to include the public domain.
Everywhere is not literal; it includes the sides adjacent to the public domain, where crowds do not gather.

Asks what the Sages' dispute is about.

Ravina: no agency for transgression applies where the agent is liable himself; when the agent is not liable, as with a courtyard, the sender is.

Rav Samma: no agency for transgression applies where the agent may freely choose; a courtyard receives items without consent, so the sender is liable.
Asks the practical difference between the two answers, citing a priest sending an agent to betroth a divorcee, and a man rounding a minor boy's hair corners.
Under each formulation, the sender's liability follows whether the agent could freely choose, or whether the agent is subject to liability.

Everyone agrees a courtyard acts as her hand for a divorce bill; they disagree only over acquiring a found item in her courtyard.

ranges.en: Abba Kohen Bardela derives the found-item halakha from divorce; another Sage rejects deriving found items from a divorce bill.

Mishnah: if one sees a crippled deer or unfledged pigeons chased and says his field acquires them, he acquires; otherwise he acquires nothing.

Challenges the baraita: its wording suggests a sheaf is forgotten, while its derivation seems to exclude the town case.

Challenges: 'go back' is still needed for the mishna that a sheaf ahead of the harvester is not forgotten, but one behind is.

ranges.en: A ruling that a rented field serves as the place where tithe is acquired for the recipient.

ranges.en: A courtyard acquires for a person as his hand, so a gift can be acquired in his absence but a bill of divorce cannot be delivered to an absent wife.

The mishna rules that the found items of a minor child, a Canaanite slave, or a wife belong to the husband or father.

The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yosei really holds that a minor can acquire by Torah law.

Rava gives an alternative explanation.

ranges.en: The Sages made a sharecropper's son who cannot acquire treated as one who can, so the poor can glean after their own sons.

Why does the mishna specify a divorced wife's found item, since if he divorced her the item is obviously hers?
The case is one of uncertain divorce, where the husband still supports her and so might retain her finds.
This is rejected: the rule that a wife's finds go to her husband exists to prevent enmity, and here enmity is useful for finalizing the divorce.
The mishna rules that a finder of promissory notes should return them only if they lack a property guarantee, per Rabbi Meir, while the Sages forbid returning them in either case.
If the debtor admits the debt, why should the finder not return the note with a guarantee, and if not, why return it without one?
The mishna concerns a debtor who admits the debt, and the finder must not return the note for fear the date was falsified and sold land is wrongly seized.

No: the credibility of notes in general stands because they stay with the creditor, and these notes were compromised by being lost.
A mishna is cited that one may write a promissory note for a borrower even without the lender present.
How can that note be written ab initio, given the concern that the borrower misdated it and sold land unlawfully?
Rav Asi begins a reply to this question.

ranges.en: The mishna is clarified to concern deeds of transfer, which create a lien by themselves from the date they are written.

That rule applies only when the document actually reached the creditor, not when it was never delivered.

If Shmuel rejects those concerns, how can the mishna be explained under either Rav Asi's or Abaye's approach?

Rabbi Natan bar Oshaya says the creditor can use the note to plug the opening of his flask.
If the note is only worth its paper, why not return it to the debtor for that use instead?

ranges.en: The claim that the loan never happened and the note is forged, so the finder has no claim to the paper.

Rabbi Yohanan says the dispute concerns a debtor who admits the debt, and that a denying debtor's note must not be returned.
A baraita agrees with Rabbi Yohanan and refutes one element of Rabbi Elazar's view and two elements of Shmuel's.
The baraita's ruling on notes with and without guarantees is cited, including Rabbi Meir's view and the Rabbis' view on collecting from liened property.
This refutes Rabbi Elazar's claim that no collusion is suspected under either Rabbi Meir or the Rabbis.
A second baraita on notes without guarantees is cited, distinguishing collection from liened and unsold property.

Why was only one element of Rabbi Elazar's view said to be refuted, when the baraita refutes two?

ranges.en: The two elements of Rabbi Elazar's view are actually one, since both rest on his reading of Rabbi Meir as limiting collection even from unsold property.

Rava bar Ittai challenges that reading, citing Shmuel's own ruling that a scribe must consult the seller about a guarantee in a sale.
Could the statement attributed to Shmuel be a dispute among the transmitters of his teachings?

An incident is cited where Avuh bar Ihi bought a loft, lost it to a creditor, and Shmuel rules that the distinction between loans and sales holds.

ranges.en: Once a buyer takes possession he cannot withdraw, since he bought without a guarantee; some add that even with a guarantee he must first see the authorization to repossess.
Rav holds that a buyer of a field that turns out not to belong to the seller gets back the price and the enhancement, while Shmuel allows only the price.
The students ask Rav Huna whether Shmuel's reason is the absence of a stipulation about enhancement or the appearance of interest when the seller holds no land.
Rav Huna replies yes and no, leaving the matter unresolved for him.

The Gemara asks whether the enhancement clause refers to a robber's sale or a creditor's repossession, and who collects the produce.

The Gemara proposes that the whole mishna is obviously about a robber and a robbery victim, which leaves Rava's objection standing.
The Gemara rejects the parallel: the produce clause concerns robbery while the enhancement clause concerns a creditor.

Who would the robber collect from, unless the case is a robber who sold the field and the buyer enhanced it?
Shmuel could have answered that the baraita adds a sale to a third party, so it can be read as a creditor case that fits his view.
A second baraita is cited on collecting produce from unsold property, which seems to challenge Shmuel's view.

Rabba bar Rav Huna offers an alternative case explaining the same baraita.

ranges.en: Restates the baraita's case: thugs seized the field from a robber, so the principal comes from liened property and produce from unsold property.

If so, why not collect produce from liened property too, and why is the rule stated without qualification?
Does Shmuel hold that a buyer from a robber has no right to enhancement, given his other rulings?
Shmuel is said to have instructed a scribe to write the seller's commitment covering enhancement and produce, which supports his view.
Is this a creditor case, or a robber case that contradicts Shmuel's ruling that a buyer from a robber gets no enhancement?
Rav Yosef says the robber owns land and can repay in land, so the payment looks like a sale rather than interest.

Rav Huna reads that baraita as referring to a buyer from a robber, so it does not support Shmuel.

If Shmuel explains the baraita as a robber case or a creditor case, both clauses seem to conflict with his ruling.

Alternatively it is a creditor case, and it is not a difficulty for Shmuel because the baraita speaks of enhancement.

ranges.en: Explains that nearly ripened produce counts as independent of the land, so the creditor must pay for it; Shmuel's ruling covers only unripe enhancement.
Objection: Shmuel regularly collected debts from buyers without compensation even for enhancement that had reached the shoulders.
Resolution: Shmuel's cases involved debts covering both land and improvements, while the baraita concerns a debt covering only the land.
Premise: the resolution is acceptable on the view that a buyer cannot dismiss a creditor by paying land value even when he has cash.
Objection: if the buyer could pay the land's value, he should be able to ask for a seah of land equal to his improvements.
Resolution: the debtor had designated the land as security for the debt, so the buyer cannot claim any part of it, even for improvements.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether a buyer who knowingly bought stolen land can recover the price paid and the value of improvements.
Question: what is the basis of the disagreement between Rav and Shmuel?
Rav's position: a buyer who knows the sale is invalid gives the money to the seller as a deposit.

Because gathering is too burdensome, the owner gives up the kernels, and the finder may keep them.
When scattered more densely, the owner exerts himself to gather them, so he does not renounce them.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma: what is the halakha for half a kav scattered in an area of two by four cubits?
Is renunciation due to burdensome gathering, which would not apply to half a kav in two by four cubits?
Or perhaps renunciation is because kernels lack value, which would apply even to the half-kav case.
Second dilemma: two kav in an area of eight by four cubits, compared with one kav in four by four cubits.
Is renunciation due to burdensome gathering, which would apply all the more to two kav in eight by four cubits?
Or perhaps renunciation is because kernels lack value, and two kav in eight by four cubits are valuable, so no renunciation.
Sesame seeds: what is the halakha for one kav of sesame in an area of four by four cubits?
If renunciation is because kernels lack value, sesame is valuable, so no renunciation.
Or perhaps renunciation is due to burdensome gathering, which applies all the more to sesame.
Dates and pomegranates: what is the halakha for one kav of each in an area of four by four cubits?
If renunciation is because the fruits lack value, dates and pomegranates fall under that same reasoning.
Or perhaps renunciation is due to burdensome gathering, which does not apply to dates and pomegranates.
The Gemara concludes that all these dilemmas remain unresolved, and a new statement is introduced.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Introduces the topic: despair from an unconscious state, when the owner is unaware that his item was lost.
Abaye: unconscious despair is not despair, so the owner keeps his claim and the finder may not keep the item.
Rava: unconscious despair counts as despair, so the finder may keep the item.
Everyone agrees that for an item bearing a mark, unconscious despair does not count, even if the owner later despairs.
Such an item came to the finder improperly, since the owner would think he will show the mark and retrieve the item.
An item swept away by the sea or a river is permitted to the finder even when it bears a mark, as the Torah allows.
The dispute concerns only items without a distinguishing mark.
Abaye: there is no despair, since the owner did not know the item had fallen from him.
Rava: the owner despairs as soon as he discovers the loss, so the despair is dated from when the item fell.
Mnemonic letters encode the proofs cited for and against each side.
Come and hear: scattered produce belongs to the finder, though the owner seemingly did not know it had fallen.
Rejects the proof: Rav Ukva's case is kernels deliberately left on the threshing floor, so the despair is conscious.
Scattered coins belong to the finder.
Why does the finder keep them if the owner did not know they had fallen?
Rejects the proof: a person constantly feels his money pouch, so the owner soon learns of the loss and despairs.
Round fig cakes and baker's loaves belong to the finder.
Why do they belong to the finder if the owner did not know they had fallen?
Rejects the proof: these items are heavy, so the owner soon notices the loss and despairs.
Strips of purple wool belong to the finder.
Why do they belong to the finder if the owner did not know they had fallen?
Rejects the proof: valuable strips are felt for constantly, so the owner soon learns of the loss, following Rabbi Yitzhak.
Coins found in synagogues, study halls, and crowded places belong to the finder, because owners despair of them.
Why do the coins belong to the finder if the owner did not know they had fallen?
Rabbi Yitzhak: a person constantly feels his money pouch, so the owner soon becomes aware of the loss.
Come and hear: anyone may glean once the nemushot have passed through the field.
Nemushot: elderly people walking slowly, per Rabbi Yohanan; or the second wave of gleaners, per Resh Lakish.
Why may anyone glean, if poor people elsewhere do not despair of the gleanings?
Since poor people gather here, distant poor despair from the outset, assuming those here will take the gleanings.
Come and hear: dried figs on a path, or under a branch hanging over a path, are permitted to the finder.
The mishna: such figs are exempt from tithes, while olives and carobs on the ground may not be taken.
For Abaye the first clause is not difficult: figs are valuable, so the owner feels for them and despairs soon after they fall.
The latter clause is difficult for Rava, since olives and carobs are forbidden, implying unconscious despair does not count.
Rabbi Abbahu: olives differ, since their appearance identifies the owner's tree, so the owner does not despair.
If so, the first clause should also prohibit fallen figs.
Rav Pappa: a fig becomes disgusting once it falls, so the owner renounces it.
Come and hear a baraita: a thief who took an item from one person and gave it to another, and likewise a robber.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a river such as the Jordan that takes an item from one person and gives it to another; the recipient need not return it.
Why does a thief's taking produce despair, when a thief acts surreptitiously, unlike a robber or river that the owner sees?
Rav Pappa: the thief refers to armed bandits, whom the owner sees, so the owner despairs; both types are robbers.
Come and hear: beams, wood, or stones swept by a river onto another's field belong to the field's owner, since the owners despaired.
Rejects the inference: the case is one where the owners could rescue the items, so not rescuing shows clear despair.
The latter clause says the finder must return the items if the owners pursued them, raising the question of why pursuit matters.
If owners can rescue the items, why mention pursuit at all, since they keep ownership even without pursuing?
Owners who can rescue only with difficulty: pursuing shows no despair, while not pursuing shows despair.
Come and hear: teruma separated without the owner's consent is valid only if the owner is not concerned it was robbery.
Baraita: if the owner rebukes the separator for not taking better produce, and better produce is found, the teruma is valid.
If the owners gather and add to the teruma, it is valid regardless of the produce found.
Why is the teruma valid from the start, when the separator did not then know the owner would agree?
Rava, following Abaye: the owner designated the separator as an agent, so the teruma is valid.
Reasoning: if the owner did not designate an agent, the teruma would not be valid, so an agent must be appointed.
Numbers 18:28, 'also you', includes an agent, so an agent's separation must be done with the owner's knowledge.
Rather, the owner designated him as agent and said to separate teruma without naming crops, so he separates from intermediate produce.
If the agent separated from better produce, the owner's later rebuke and the discovery of better produce decide the teruma's validity.
Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi visit Mari bar Isak's orchard; the sharecropper serves dates and pomegranates, and Mar Zutra refuses to eat.
Mari bar Isak finds them eating and rebukes his sharecropper for not bringing better fruit.
Ameimar and Rav Ashi ask Mar Zutra why he is not eating now.
A baraita: if better produce is found, the teruma is valid, showing the owner's consent.
Mar Zutra cites Rava: consent to better produce applies only to teruma, a mitzva; here the rebuke reflects shame, not real consent.
Come and hear another proof from Leviticus 11: dew that moistened produce while the owner was pleased makes it susceptible to impurity.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The produce does not fall under the verse's 'when water is placed' that makes it susceptible to impurity.
What is the reason that dried produce does not become susceptible, even though the owner is glad about the dew?
We do not say that once it is revealed the owner is pleased with the moisture now, he was pleased from the outset.
Rejects the analogy: there the verse reads 'ki yitten', indicating that the owner himself must place the water.
If so, the first clause should also not apply, since the owner did not place the dew.
Rav Pappa raised a contradiction between the written and read forms of the verse's word yuttan, and how to reconcile them.
Rav Pappa's resolution: yuttan requires the owner's knowledge, just as yitten does, so this proves nothing about despair.
Come and hear: Deuteronomy 22:3 requires returning only lost items available to others, so an item swept away by a river may be kept.
The prohibition parallels the permission: with or without a mark, the finder may not keep it until despair is shown, refuting Rava.
The halakha follows Abaye in the disputes listed by the mnemonic.
Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi how dates blown off a tree may be eaten if unconscious despair does not count.
Rav Ashi: repugnant creatures eat fallen dates, so the owner despairs from the outset and the finder may keep them.
Rav Aha: perhaps the trees belonged to orphans, who cannot relinquish property and so cannot despair.
Rav Ashi: a valley is not presumed to be orphans' land, so this concern does not apply.
If the trees were presumed to belong to orphans, or were fenced against creatures, what is the halakha?
Rav Ashi: the dates are forbidden in those cases.
Mishna: bundles of grain found in a public area belong to the finder.
Rabba: this applies even to an item with a mark, since a mark prone to being trampled is not a mark.
Rava: the ruling applies only without a mark; with a mark the finder must proclaim, since a trampled-prone mark counts.
Rabba and Rava independently dispute whether a mark prone to being trampled counts as a mark.
Mishna: bundles in a public area belong to the finder.
In a secluded area, if there is no mark, what does the finder proclaim?
The mishna's public-area ruling implies a trampled-prone mark is not a mark, which refutes Rava.
Rava can answer that the bundles have no mark, so the finder proclaims that the owner must describe the location.
The finder proclaims that the owner should name the location; Rabba holds a location is not a mark, while Rava holds it is.
The amoraim dispute whether a location counts as a distinguishing mark: Rabba denies it, Rava affirms it.
Come and hear: bundles in a public area belong to the finder, while bundles in a secluded area are taken and proclaimed, and sheaves are proclaimed in either area.
How does Rabba reconcile this baraita, and how does Rava?
Rabba explains the baraita by a mark, and Rava by location, each following his own line of reasoning.
Baraita: bundles in a public area belong to the finder, which Rabba explains as referring to bundles with a mark.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bundles found in a secluded area are not trampled, so a mark survives; sheaves are not trampled anywhere because they stand high.
Rava: the location is the mark; in public areas bundles get kicked and roll, while heavy sheaves do not roll.
Come and hear: baker's loaves that are found belong to the finder.
By inference, a homeowner's loaves found must be proclaimed by the finder rather than kept.
What is the reason a homeowner's loaves must be proclaimed?
Each person shapes loaves uniquely, so the loaves carry a mark; the finder proclaims them regardless of location.
Loaves must be proclaimed in both public and secluded areas, showing a trampled-prone mark counts, which refutes Rabba.
Rabba replies: loaves of a homeowner in a public area are returned because people do not pass food without picking it up.
Objections: gentiles may not handle food carefully and beasts trample loaves; answers: gentiles fear sorcery, and beasts are absent there.
Suggestion: this dispute parallels a tannaitic dispute, where Rabbi Yehuda requires proclaiming items with an alteration.
Rabbi Yehuda's example: a fig cake with a shard, or a loaf with coins, must be proclaimed, implying the first tanna says the finder keeps them.
The dispute concerns a mark prone to being trampled: the first tanna denies it counts, and Rabbi Yehuda affirms it.
Rav Zevid, in Rava's name: if the first tanna denies trampled-prone marks, why does a homeowner's loaf in a public area get proclaimed?
Rav Zevid's resolution: all agree trampled-prone marks count, and the dispute concerns marks that arise on their own.
Rabba's reply: all agree trampled-prone marks do not count and food is not passed, so the dispute concerns spontaneous marks.
Another version: all agree spontaneous marks count and trampled-prone marks do not, so the dispute must be about passing food.
The dispute concerns whether one passes food without picking it up: the first tanna says one passes, Rabbi Yehuda says not.
Rav Zevid again, in Rava's name: if the first tanna denies trampled-prone marks and holds one passes food, why proclaim a homeowner's loaves?
Rav Zevid's second resolution, in Rava's name: all agree trampled-prone marks count, and the dispute concerns spontaneous marks.
Rabba's reply in this version: all agree trampled-prone marks do not count and food is not passed, so the dispute concerns spontaneous marks.
Rav Zevid, in Rava's name: an owner who says woe for my monetary loss has thereby despaired of recovery.
Rav Zevid, in Rava's name, states the halakha on this matter.
Halakha: bundles in a public area belong to the finder; in a secluded area they belong to him if they fell, but he proclaims if they were placed.
For items without a mark, the rules above apply; for items with a mark, the finder must proclaim in every case.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna teaches that strings of fish may be kept as found items.
Why should the knot tying the fish not serve as a distinguishing mark?
Every fisherman ties fish with the same knot, so the knot is not distinctive.
Why should the number of fish on a string not serve as a distinguishing mark?
The number is the same on all strings in the area, so it is not distinctive.
The Sages posed a dilemma to Rav Sheshet about whether number counts as a distinguishing mark.
When no other mark exists, is the number of items a distinguishing mark or not?
Rav Sheshet replies by citing a baraita on the matter.
Baraita: finder of metal vessels need not return them without a mark, weight, measure, or count, which all serve as marks.
Mishna teaches that cuts of meat may be kept as found items.
Why should the weight of the cut not serve as a distinguishing mark?
The mishna refers to cuts that all weigh the same, so weight is not distinctive.
Why should the cut itself, or a mark made by cutting or stamping, not serve as a distinguishing mark?
Baraita: finder of fish cuts or a bitten fish must proclaim them, while barrels of wine, oil, grain, figs, or olives belong to the finder.
With what case are we dealing in this baraita?
The baraita refers to a cut with a distinctive shape, like a triangular cut, and not to the place it was cut from.
Quoting the baraita again: barrels of wine, oil, grain, figs, and olives belong to the finder.
A mishna teaches that jugs of wine or oil must be proclaimed, which seems to contradict the baraita.
Rabbi Zeira, citing Rav, explains the mishna refers to sealed jugs, whose seals are distinguishing marks.
By inference the baraita must refer to open barrels, which would be a deliberate loss.
Rav Hoshaya says the baraita refers to barrels covered by a lid but not sealed.
Abaye says both the mishna and the baraita refer to sealed jugs, so there is no contradiction.
The mishna applies to jugs found before the storehouses opened, and the baraita to barrels found after, when seals no longer identify owners.
Example: Rav Yaakov bar Abba found a barrel after storehouses opened, and Abaye told him to keep it.
Rav Beivai asked Rav Nachman whether the location where an item was found is a distinguishing mark.
Rav Nachman answers by citing the baraita listing barrels of wine, oil, grain, figs, and olives as belonging to the finder.
If location were a distinguishing mark, the finder could proclaim the find and point to its location.
Rav Zevid says the baraita refers to a barrel found on a riverbank, where many people's goods are loaded, so location is not distinctive there.
Rav Mari asks: what is the reason the Sages said a riverbank location is not a distinguishing mark?
The Sages ruled that a riverbank location is not a distinguishing mark.
The claimant can be told that others also lost items at that same place, so location proves nothing.
Some report a variant: Rav Mari asks why location in general is not a distinguishing mark.
The Sages said that location is not a distinguishing mark.
The claimant can be told that another person also placed an item at that same spot.
A man found pitch near a winepress and brought the matter before Rav.
Rav told him to take the pitch for himself.
Rav saw the man hesitating and told him to share the pitch with his son Hiyya.
Does Rav hold that location is not a distinguishing mark, which would explain why he allowed the finder to keep it?
Rabbi Abba says the reason is the owner's despair, since grass grew through the pitch, showing it had lain there long.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says a finder of anpurya vessels need not proclaim them.
What are anpurya vessels?
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says they are new vessels that their buyer has not yet looked at closely enough to recognize.
If the vessels have a distinguishing mark, what difference does it make whether the buyer has looked at them closely?
If the vessels have no distinguishing mark, what difference does it make whether the buyer has looked at them closely?
Actually the vessels have no distinguishing mark, and the difference concerns the case of a scholar's description.
A scholar who has looked closely is certain of the vessel, so it is returned to him by description; if not, it is not returned.
Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: in three matters alone the Sages deviate from the truth, including a tractate and a bed, to avoid shame.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the practical difference that follows from the claim that a scholar may lie about a host?
Mar Zutra says the difference concerns returning lost items by visual recognition: only a scholar who deviates in those three matters alone gets his item back.
A silver goblet was stolen from the host of Mar Zutra Hasida.
Mar Zutra saw a student wiping his hands on another man's cloak.
Mar Zutra judged that the student did not care about others' property, bound him, and he confessed to the theft.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar concedes that new vessels seen clearly must be proclaimed; needles and axes need not be, unless the finder found them in pairs.
What does the term badei mean, and why is it called that?
Badei means branches, since an item hangs from another item the way a leaf hangs from a branch.
A mishna in Sukkah uses the same usage: one leaf on one branch.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says rescuers from beasts or floods, and finders in crowded places, keep the item because the owner despairs of recovering it.
Did Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar mean only places with a majority of gentiles, or even places with a majority of Jews?
If he meant even majority-Jewish places, do the Rabbis disagree with him or not?
If the Rabbis disagree in majority-Jewish places, do they also disagree in majority-gentile places?
If the Rabbis disagree even in majority-gentile places, is the halakha like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar or not?
If the halakha follows him, does it apply only in majority-gentile places or also in majority-Jewish ones?
Baraita: coins found in synagogues, study halls, or crowded places belong to the finder, so Rabbi Shimon seems to hold even Jewish-majority places count.
The baraita may refer to scattered coins, but then why restrict it to places where crowds gather?
Rather, the baraita concerns coins that are bound together.
With what case are we dealing, if synagogues and study halls are Jewish places?
The case is gentile assembly houses, study halls with gentile guards, and our synagogues where gentiles sit.
Mishna in Makhshirin: in a mixed city the finder must proclaim if Jews are the majority, but not if gentiles are, which seems to follow Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
That mishna follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Shimon, so it cannot prove his view.
Resolve from it that the Rabbis concede to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in majority-gentile places.
Rather, the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds the rule even in majority-Jewish places.
With what case are we dealing: a concealed item? If it is concealed, why would the item be left with the finder?
Mishna: a vessel found concealed in a garbage heap may not be touched, but if exposed the finder takes it and proclaims it.
Rav Pappa explains: the heap was not meant for clearing, but the owner later decided to clear it, so the same logic applies here and depends on the city's majority.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alternatively, the mishna may be read as following the Rabbis, so the earlier proof is not decisive.
The mishna does not say the found items belong to the finder; it says he is not obligated to proclaim them.
The finder should leave the items in place, and a Jew will come, give a distinguishing mark, and take them.
Rav Asi: a barrel of wine found in a gentile-majority city is permitted to drink once a Jew supplies a mark, yet it still belongs to the finder.
In accordance with whose view is Rav Asi's ruling? Conclude that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view applies only in gentile-majority places.
Rather, Rabbi Shimon holds even in Jewish-majority places, and Rav Asi follows him in one case but disagrees in the other.
Once the wine is forbidden for benefit, what practical difference does the finding ruling make?
Rav Ashi: it matters for deriving benefit from the container, which is permitted.
A man found four dinars tied in a cloth that had been thrown into the Biran River and went to Rav Yehuda for guidance.
Rav Yehuda told him to go proclaim the find.
But is the Biran River not like the tide of the sea, where the finder may keep what he finds?
The Biran River is different, because its obstacles mean the owner does not despair of recovering the coins.
But the population there is mostly gentile, so the halakha must not follow Rabbi Shimon even in gentile-majority places.
The Biran is different: Jews dammed and dredge it, so the coins fell from a Jew and the owner still hopes to recover them.
Rav Yehuda walked behind Shmuel in the market where grain was pounded, and asked him a question about a purse.
If one found a purse here, what is the halakha?
Shmuel: the halakha is as the mishna states, and the purse belongs to the finder.
If a Jew came and supplied a distinguishing mark to describe it, what is the halakha?
Shmuel: the finder must return it.
Rav Yehuda objects that these two rulings contradict each other.
By strict law the purse belongs to the finder; returning it is beyond the letter of the law, like Shmuel's father returning donkeys after twelve months.
Rava walked behind Rav Naḥman in the tanners' market, or some say in the market frequented by the Sages, and asked about a purse.
If one found a purse here, what is the halakha?
Rav Naḥman: the purse belongs to the finder, as the mishna states.
If a Jew came and supplied a distinguishing mark, what is the halakha?
Rav Naḥman: in that case too the purse belongs to the finder.
But the owner is standing and screaming, so he clearly still wants his purse back.
His screaming is futile, like one who cries out over a collapsed house or a ship sunk at sea.
A kite carried meat from the market and dropped it among palm trees; the finder came before Abaye to ask what to do.
Abaye told him to take the meat for himself.
But the marketplace of kosher meat is a Jewish-majority place, where the owner should be able to recover the meat.
Conclude that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even in Jewish-majority places.
A kite is different: what it takes is like an item swept away by the tide of the sea.
But Rav said that meat that was hidden from sight and unsupervised is forbidden.
Here the finder stood and watched the meat from the moment the kite took it until it was dropped.
Rabbi Ḥanina found a slaughtered young goat between Tiberias and Tzippori, and the Sages permitted it to him.
Rabbi Ami explains the permission: it follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on found items and Rabbi Ḥananya son of Rabbi Yosei HaGlili on slaughter.
Baraita: if a man's kids and roosters were lost and found slaughtered, Rabbi Yehuda forbids the meat and Rabbi Ḥananya permits it.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reconciles the views: Rabbi Yehuda speaks of a garbage heap, and Rabbi Ḥananya of a house.
Since the meat was permitted for slaughter, the place is Jewish-majority, so the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar even in Jewish-majority places.
Rava: the place is gentile-majority, but most of the slaughterers are Jews.
Rabbi Ami found slaughtered fledglings between Tiberias and Tzippori and asked various sages, who all told him to take them.
Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa found a skein of thread woven into a net and asked Rabbi Yoḥanan, who told him to take it for himself.
Mishna: for these found items one must proclaim: produce in a vessel or a vessel itself, coins in a pouch or a pouch, and piles of produce or coins.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna lists found items like stacked coins, piles of produce, loaves, wool, wine, and oil, which must be proclaimed.
The Gemara infers from the mishna that produce inside a vessel or coins inside a pouch is what requires proclaiming, and cites a baraita stating this explicitly.
Baraita: produce lying before a vessel, or coins before a pouch, belong to the finder.
Baraita: if produce is partly in a vessel and partly on the ground, or coins partly in a pouch, the finder must proclaim.
Another baraita seems to contradict this: an unmarked item next to a marked item must be proclaimed, yet the finder keeps the unmarked one if the owner takes only his own.
Rav Zevid: the proclaiming baraita concerns a container with flax, whose fibers cling together, so flax falling out does not prove it was never inside.
Rav Pappa: both rulings concern a basket of produce; the baraita applies when some produce remains in the basket, the mishna when none does.
Alternatively, the baraita applies when the basket's mouth faces the produce, showing it fell out, and the mishna when it does not.
Alternatively, the mishna applies to a basket with a rim that blocks spilling, and the baraita to a basket with no rim.
Mishna: piles of produce and piles of coins must be proclaimed.
The Gemara tries to infer from this that number, or location, is a distinguishing mark, and rejects each inference as based on an uncertain text.
Mishna: three coins stacked one atop another must be proclaimed.
Rabbi Yitzḥak of Migdal: the finder must proclaim coins arranged in well-ordered towers.
Baraita: scattered coins belong to the finder, but coins arranged in well-ordered towers must be proclaimed.
The mishna's example of three coins stacked one atop another illustrates such towers.
The baraita seems to contradict itself: if scattered coins belong to the finder, then overlapping coins would not be proclaimed, yet the later clause implies they would be.
The later clause of the baraita: coins not arranged in towers, partly overlapping, belong to the finder.
The tanna calls any pile not arranged in well-ordered towers scattered, which resolves the apparent contradiction.
Rabbi Ḥanina: one must proclaim only coins minted by three different kings; coins of one king need not be proclaimed.
What are the circumstances? Towered coins of one king would still need proclaiming, and untowered coins of three kings would not.
Rather, Rabbi Ḥanina's ruling is about coins of one king of varying sizes that resemble coins of three kings.
Towered coins are coins where the bottom is broadest and the others stack on it, so they were placed deliberately and are not lost.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: even coins minted by one king must be proclaimed.
What does one proclaim to make the owner describe the item, and why does the mishna specify three coins?
Ravina: the finder proclaims coins in the plural, so two coins would not be a distinguishing description; hence the mishna specifies three.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks: what is the halakha for coins arranged in a round bracelet, a straight line, a triangle, or a ladder?
Resolve one dilemma from Rabba bar Avuh's criterion: coins that one can lift all at once with a wood chip must be proclaimed, which suggests the ladder arrangement qualifies.
Rav Ashi raises a further dilemma.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the coins are arranged like the stones of a Mercury temple, what is the halakha?
Baraita: scattered coins belong to the finder, but coins arranged like the stones of a Mercury temple must be proclaimed, with one coin on each side and one on top.
Baraita: a finder of a sela coin cannot be overruled by a claimant who names a mark that does not identify the coin, since the coin could have passed through other hands.
Mishna: bound fledglings in a fence or field path are not touched; a concealed vessel in a garbage dump is left, while an exposed one is taken and proclaimed.
What is the reason one may not touch the fledglings?
Someone concealed the birds, and a finder who took them would leave the owner with no mark to reclaim them, so the birds should stay until the owner comes.
Why does the knot binding the birds not serve as a distinguishing mark?
Rav: the birds were bound by their wings, and everyone binds them that way, so the knot is not distinctive.
Why does the location not serve as a distinguishing mark?
Rav Ukva bar Ḥama: the birds hop and do not stay in place, so location is not distinctive.
If the birds hop, they may have come from elsewhere, and then the finder may keep them.
The birds may have come from elsewhere or been concealed, so it is uncertain; Rav holds one may not take such an item initially, but if taken one need not return it.
Mishna: a concealed vessel in a garbage dump is not touched, while an exposed one is taken and proclaimed.
A baraita says the finder of a concealed vessel in a garbage dump takes it and proclaims it, since garbage dumps are routinely cleared, so the item was probably lost.
Rav Zevid: the mishna concerns large containers and cups, while the baraita concerns small knives and forks that could easily have fallen.
Rav Pappa: both concern containers and cups; the baraita applies to a dump meant for clearing, and the mishna to one not meant for clearing.
How could one proclaim a vessel found in a dump designed for clearing, since a deliberate concealment is an abandonment?
Rather, the baraita concerns a dump not designed for clearing, where the landowner reconsidered and decided to clear it.
Granted, Rav Pappa's reading explains why the baraita says the dump is routinely cleared; but on Rav Zevid's reading, what is the relevance of that phrase?
On Rav Zevid's reading it means small utensils are routinely discarded into a dump by accident.

Mishna: items found in a rubble heap or an old wall belong to the finder; in a new wall, the outer half belongs to the finder and the inner half to the homeowner, unless the house is regularly rented out.
Baraita: the finder keeps items in rubble or old walls because the owner can be told they belong to the Amorites who lived there earlier.
Does that mean Amorites concealed items but Jews do not? Perhaps the homeowner himself placed the item in the wall.
The baraita is needed only for the specific case of a claimant, so the answer stands.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An item that is very rusted shows it has lain there a long time.
Mishna: if lost items are found in a new wall from its midpoint outward they belong to the finder; from midpoint inward they belong to the homeowner.
Rav Ashi: ownership of a knife or pouch found in a wall follows the handle or laces, and whichever way they face decides it.
If so, what is the mishna's ruling for, since one could simply check which way the handle or straps face?
The mishna concerns rags or metal strips, which have no handle to show direction.
Baraita: if the hollow in the wall was filled with lost items, the homeowner and the finder divide them.
Isn't that obvious?
No, it is needed only where the hollow slants to one side, lest one think the items slid down and filled it all.
Mishna: if the homeowner regularly rents the house to a steady turnover of residents, lost items found inside belong to the finder.
Why should the items belong to the finder rather than to the last renter?
Mishna in Shekalim: money found among animal merchants in Jerusalem is presumed second-tithe money, and on the Temple Mount it is considered non-sacred.
The mishna continues: money found elsewhere in Jerusalem is non-sacred on ordinary days, but during a festival it is presumed second-tithe.
Rav Shemaya bar Ze'eira explains: the markets are cleaned daily, so money found there must have been left after the earlier people left; the same logic applies to rented houses.
Reish Lakish, citing bar Kappara: the mishna applies when the homeowner made the house an inn for three Jews, so the owner despairs of recovery.
Conclude from it that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's ruling applies even in Jewish-majority places.
Rav Menashya bar Ya'akov: the mishna applies when the house was made an inn for three gentiles, so Rabbi Shimon's ruling may be limited to gentile-majority places.
Rav Naḥman citing Rabba bar Avuh: even if the inn was for three Jews, one cannot conclude Rabbi Shimon's ruling holds in Jewish-majority places.
What is the reason the item belongs to the finder?
The owner despairs of recovery: he told the innkeepers several times to return it and they did not, so they evidently intend to keep it.
Rav Naḥman follows his usual reasoning, as he says: if one saw a sela coin fall, the owner would despair of recovering it.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a coin fell from one of two people, the finder must return it.
What is the reason?
The loser does not despair: he assumes the only other person present took it and will simply be accused of the theft.
If the coin fell from one of three people, the finder is not obligated to return it.
What is the reason?
The loser despairs, since any of the two others could deny taking it, so he cannot make a definite claim.
Rava: the three-person exemption applies only when the coin is worth less than a peruta per person; if each would receive a peruta, the finder must return it.
What is the reason?
Perhaps the three are partners, so none despairs, each assuming another holds the coin for all of them.
Some report that Rava said: even if the coin is worth only two perutot, the finder must return it.
What is the reason for this version?
Perhaps they are partners and one relinquishes his share, leaving two partners each with a peruta share.
Rava: one who takes a coin seen falling, intending to steal it before the owner despairs, violates the prohibitions on robbery and on disregarding a lost item.
The prohibitions are grounded in the verses: you shall not rob, you shall return it to your brother, and you may not disregard it.
Even if the finder later returns it as a gift after the owner despairs, the earlier transgression remains.
