If he took it intending to return it, but later after despair decided to steal it, he violates only the positive commandment to return lost items.
If he waited until the owner despaired before taking it, he violates only the prohibition against disregarding a lost item.
Rava: if one saw a dinar fall into sand, took it, and the owner had already despaired, the finder need not return it.
What is the reason?
The owner despairs, since even if he sifts the sand, he may think a coin lost from him will be offset by one he finds elsewhere.
Mishna: items found without a mark in a store belong to the finder; those found between the counter and the storekeeper, or coins before a money changer, follow the same logic.
Mishna: for one who buys produce, or receives it as a gift, coins found mixed in belong to him; if the coins are bundled, he must proclaim them.
Rabbi Elazar: even coins placed on the table itself belong to the finder.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Elazar from the mishna's two clauses, which give opposite inferences, so no conclusion can be drawn from it.
From where does Rabbi Elazar derive his ruling, if not from the mishna?
Rava: the mishna is precise because money changers keep their money in a drawer, so even coins on the table belong to the changer only if they are found there.
Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai: the Sages taught this only in the case of produce bought from another.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: coins found in produce bought from a merchant belong to the buyer, but produce bought from the owner himself requires returning the coins.
Rav Naḥman asks: does the owner thresh his grain himself, or do his workers, who might own the coins, do it?
Explain the baraita as referring to grain threshed by the owner's Canaanite slaves, so any coins belong to the owner.
Mishna: the garment is included among lost items to be returned, drawing an analogy to items with marks and claimants that must be proclaimed.
In which generalization is the garment included?
Rava: it is included in the phrase about every lost item of your brother in Deuteronomy 22:3.
Why does the Torah list ox, donkey, sheep, and garment separately if one would suffice?
Each is needed for a distinct halakha: without the donkey, one might think a donkey is returned only if witnesses describe its saddle or marks, not the animal itself.
Why are ox and sheep specifically listed?
Rava's answer fails: if the Torah wrote only ox, the sheared tail wool would be included, and a fortiori the sheared wool of a sheep.
Rather, Rava says the donkey refers to the damage-of-the-pit case per Rabbi Yehuda, and the sheep to lost items per all, and neither has a clear reason to be stated.
Perhaps the sheep is written to teach the return of dung?
Dung is not returned, because its owner renounced ownership of it.
Perhaps the sheep teaches that items can be identified by marks; is that a Torah or rabbinic law?
The Torah writes sheep to teach that items are returned even by marks, which resolves the dilemma in favor of Torah law.
The Gemara rejects this: the tanna teaches marks together with garment, which shows marks are a separate matter, so sheep does not teach marks.
Baraita: the verse excludes lost items worth less than a peruta; the Rabbis derive this from which shall be lost, and Rabbi Yehuda from and you have found it.
What is the practical difference between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda?
Abaye: there is no practical difference; they differ only in which phrase of the verse yields the exclusion.
If the Rabbis derive the exclusion from which shall be lost, what do they do with and you have found it?
According to the Rabbis, that phrase teaches Rabbenai's rule that an item becomes a found item only when it enters the finder's possession.
If Rabbi Yehuda derives the exclusion from and you have found it, what does he do with which has been lost from him?
That phrase teaches Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: an item swept away by a river that is not available to be found by anyone may be kept.
From where does Rabbi Yehuda derive Rabbenai's rule, given that he uses and you have found it for the exclusion?
From where does the first tanna derive Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule, given that he uses which shall be lost from him for the exclusion?
Rava: the practical difference is an item worth a peruta when lost but less when found; the verse's reading of value at loss or at finding decides the case.
But even on the view that the phrase requires value at finding, the item is not worth a peruta then, so why return it?
Rather, the difference is an item worth less than a peruta when lost that appreciated to a peruta when found.
On one view, the item must be returned because the verse refers to its value at finding; on the other, no return because it refers to its value at loss.
But even on the view derived from and you have found it, we require the value of a peruta at the time of loss, so the item would not be returned.
Rather, the difference concerns an item worth a peruta at loss, devalued, then appreciated again, so the valuation time governs the outcome.
Is the sheep-marks halakha of Torah or rabbinic law, and what practical difference does that make?

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara answers that the practical difference concerns returning a lost get based on identifying marks, depending on whether that is Torah or rabbinic law.
Gemara brings a Mishna whose inclusion of garments suggests that identifying items by marks is by Torah law.
Rejects that proof: the tanna mentioned marks needlessly, since claimants alone were the relevant criterion.
Brings a baraita on the donkey: returning it by its saddle marks suggests identification by marks is Torah law.
Emends the baraita: the donkey is returned only on witnesses, not on distinguishing marks.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:2 about the finder holding the item until the owner claims it, as a source for returning by marks.
Would it enter your mind that the finder returns the item before the owner claims it, when he cannot know who the owner is?
Rather, derosh refers to the finder scrutinizing whether the claimant is a swindler, not to the owner's claim.
Asks whether a claimant shown not to be a swindler by his marks means identification by marks is Torah law.
No: swindler status is determined by scrutinizing witnesses, not by distinguishing marks.
Brings a mishna: testimony about a dead man requires seeing his face and nose, even though marks on body and garments exist.
Concludes from that mishna that identification by distinguishing marks is not by Torah law.
Sages reply: bodily marks were nonspecific, like height, and garment marks are unreliable because of possible loans.
If we fear a loan, how do we return a donkey on the basis of the saddle's marks?
Sages reply: people do not borrow saddles, since a saddle not fitted to the donkey would chafe it.
Alternatively, the garment marks were nonspecific, such as the garment being white or red.
Brings a baraita: a found get tied to a pouch, purse, ring, or garments is valid even if found long after it was lost.
If loans are feared, why is a get found tied in a pouch valid? Let us fear the pouch belongs to someone else.
Sages reply: people do not lend pouches, purses or signet rings, for the stated reasons.
Suggests a dispute among tannaim, citing a baraita in which Elazar ben Mahavai permits testimony based on a mole.
Asks whether the tannaim's dispute is really about whether identification by marks is Torah or rabbinic law.
Rava: everyone holds identification by marks is Torah law; the dispute is whether a mole is common among one's contemporaries.
Alternatively, everyone agrees a mole is not common; the dispute is whether marks are apt to change after death.
Alternatively, everyone agrees marks are not apt to change after death, and identification by marks is rabbinic law.
Alternatively, the dispute is whether a mole is a clear-cut distinguishing mark.
Rava says: suppose identification by marks is not by Torah law.
Asks how a lost item can be returned on the basis of marks if that is not Torah law.
Rava answers: the finder returns the item by marks because he benefits from the same practice when he loses something himself.
Rav Safra objects: can a person perform an act benefiting himself with property that is not his?
Rava's reply: the owner prefers to describe marks and take possession, and each owner tacitly agrees to this practice.
Cites the mishna of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on three promissory notes, to test the tacit-agreement explanation.
If return by marks rests on tacit agreement, is it satisfactory to the debtor for the notes to go to the creditor?
Rava replies that there the return is based on logical reasoning, not on marks.
Notes found with one debtor are typically kept by the debtor, so they go back to him; this shows the reasoning is about where documents are typically found.
Notes of several debtors with one creditor are typically kept by the creditor, so they go back to the creditor.

28a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks: if return by marks rests on tacit agreement, is it satisfactory to the debtor for a bundle of notes to go to the creditor?
Rava states that identification of an item by distinguishing marks is by Torah law.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:2, that the finder keeps the item until the owner claims it, as the source.
Would it enter your mind that the finder hands the item over before the owner claims it?
Rather, derosh means the finder scrutinizes whether the claimant is a swindler or not.
Asks: is it not that the claimant proves he is not a swindler by his distinguishing marks?
Concludes from this that identification by distinguishing marks is by Torah law.
Rava begins: if identification by marks is by Torah law, then the following cases follow.
The Gemara interjects: did Rava not already conclude that marks are by Torah law, making the conditional odd?
Rava phrased it conditionally because one could still reject his conclusion as explained on 27b.
If two claimants each describe marks, the finder keeps the item and gives it to neither.
If one claimant has marks and the other has two witnesses, the item goes to the claimant with witnesses.
If each claimant has marks but one has a single witness, that witness counts as absent and the finder keeps it.
Garment case: witnesses that it was woven for one claimant versus witnesses that it fell from the other; it goes to the falling witnesses.
Reason: perhaps the weaver sold the garment and it later fell from another person who is the current owner.
If one claimant gives the length and the other the width, the item goes to the claimant who gave the length.
Reason: width can be estimated when the owner dons the garment and stands, but length cannot, so length is clearer.
If one gives length and width separately and the other gives only their combined gamma, the item goes to the separate-measures claimant.
If one gives length and width and the other gives weight, the item goes to the weight claimant, as weight is harder to estimate.
Bill of divorce case: husband says he did not yet give it; wife says she received it and gives marks; it goes to the wife.
With what marks did she describe it? Measurements of height and width are not clear-cut, since she could have seen it in his hand.
Rather, she describes a perforation next to a specific letter, which she could know only if the get had been in her hand.
String case: husband describes the marks of the string binding the get, and the wife describes them too; it goes to the wife.
With what string marks did she describe it? Color is not sufficient proof, since she could have seen the string in his hand.
Rather, she stated the length of the string as wrapped around the document, which she could know only by holding the get.
Storage case: husband says the get was kept in a case; wife says the same; it goes to the husband.
Reason: storage in a case does not prove her ownership, since he keeps every valuable item in his case.
Mishna: a finder must proclaim his find until the neighbors know of it, per Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Yehuda sets three festivals plus seven days.
A tanna taught that the finder proclaims until the neighbors of the lost item know of its existence.
What are the neighbors of the lost item? If the owner's neighbors are meant, the finder should simply return it, so this cannot be right.
Rather, the neighbors are those of the place where the lost item was found.
Restates Rabbi Yehuda's position in the mishna: three festivals, plus seven days for the owner to travel and return.
Raises a contradiction from the mishna in Taanit: Rabban Gamliel needs fifteen days for pilgrims to return home, not three.
Rav Yosef: not difficult; the Taanit case refers to the First Temple journey of fifteen days, and this case to the Second Temple journey of three days.
First Temple: the people were so numerous, as in I Kings 4:20, that the distance to the far reaches needed fifteen days.
Second Temple: the people were fewer, as in Ezra 2:64, so the journey took less time.
Abaye objects: Ezra 2:70 shows the people settled all their cities, so the distance was no shorter in the Second Temple.
Abaye continues: the opposite is reasonable; the numerous First Temple nation had caravans traveling day and night, so three days sufficed.
In the Second Temple, with fewer people and no organized caravans traveling day and night, fifteen days were required.
Rava says there is no difference between the First and Second Temple periods; the journey always required fifteen days.
Rabbi Yehuda used three days because the Sages did not wish to trouble the finder with an excessively long wait.
Ravina says: from Rabbi Yehuda's calculation, learn that the finder specifies the nature of the item, e.g., a cloak.
Reason: otherwise the owner would need an extra day to check all his vessels, which would extend the period further.
Rather, learn that the finder specifies the nature of the item, such as a cloak; the Gemara affirms this.
Rava says: even if the finder need not specify the nature, Rabbi Yehuda would not extend the period, to avoid troubling the finder.
Baraita: on each festival the finder proclaims his find, stating the festival's number, except that on the third he gives no number.
Asks: why does he not state that it is the third festival, as he did for the second?

28b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Replies that confusing the second festival with the first is no problem, since the finder can still proclaim on the third.
Baraita: originally the finder proclaimed for three festivals and seven days, giving the owner time to travel and return.
After the Temple's destruction, finders proclaim in synagogues and study halls, and during oppression they inform neighbors and acquaintances.
Asks what is meant by the time the oppressors proliferated.
The period is when people said a lost item belongs to the king, so public proclamation risked confiscation.
Anecdote: Rabbi Ami found a purse of dinars, and a Roman told him to keep it, since Romans do not say lost items belong to the king.
Baraita: a Claimant's Stone in Jerusalem, where the finder proclaimed and the owner stated marks and took the item.
Mishna: a claimant who names the item but not its marks does not receive it, and a swindler does not receive it even with marks.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:2, where derosh is read as the finder's scrutiny of whether the claimant is a swindler.
Dispute: Rav Yehuda says the finder proclaims a lost item without naming it, while Rav Nachman says he names it, such as a cloak.
Rav Yehuda holds that the finder proclaims only that he found a lost item.
If the finder named a cloak, we would fear a swindler who learned the marks and claims the item.
Rav Nachman holds that the finder proclaims a cloak, and we are not concerned about a swindler claiming it.
If we feared swindlers in every such case, the matter would have no end, since a swindler could guess the item's nature.
Brings the mishna: a claimant who names the item but not its marks does not receive it, as a proof.
Granted, if the finder names no item, the mishna teaches that unmarked claims fail; but if he names it, that would be obvious.
If the finder names a cloak and the claimant names a cloak, is it necessary to say he gets nothing without marks?
Rav Safra: the mishna refers to a case where the claimant gave marks that are not exclusive to the item, so he does not prove ownership.
Mishna continues: a swindler does not receive the item even if he states its marks.
Baraita: originally owners received items by stating marks; when swindlers proliferated, they had to bring witnesses attesting they are not swindlers.
Story: the father of Rav Pappa lost a donkey, came to Rabba bar Rav Huna, and was told to bring witnesses.
Rabba bar Rav Huna tells him to bring witnesses that he is not a swindler, and then he may take the donkey.
The father of Rav Pappa brings witnesses as instructed.
Rabba asks the witnesses whether they know that he is a swindler.
The witnesses answer yes, that they know he is a swindler.
Incredulous, the father asks whether he is called a swindler.
The witnesses clarify they were saying he is not a swindler, and had understood the question the other way.
Rabba bar Rav Huna reasons that the witnesses meant to support him, since no person brings condemnation upon himself.
Mishna: an animal that does not work and eats must be sold, since the finder must return it as the verse requires.
Asks what shall be done with the money received from the sale of the animal.
Rabbi Tarfon says the finder may use the money and bears liability; Rabbi Akiva says he may not use it and is not liable.
Asks whether the finder must care for the animal forever, and relays that Rav Nachman says Shmuel said otherwise.
Shmuel rules the finder tends a working animal for twelve months, and a baraita agrees, after which it is sold and money set aside.
Baraita: calves and foals are tended for three months, and geese and roosters for thirty days, before sale.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: a chicken is like a large domesticated animal, since its eggs cover its food, so it is tended for twelve months.
Baraita: chickens and large animals are tended for twelve months, calves and foals for thirty days, and geese and roosters for three days if costly.
Asks why the baraitot contradict each other on calves and foals, and on geese and roosters.
Calves and foals grazing need three months, while those needing fattening are tended for thirty days, requiring more exertion.
Large geese and roosters need thirty days, while small ones need three days because they require more exertion.
Mishna: an animal that does not work but eats must be sold.
Baraita: the finder may not feed the sale proceeds of one animal to the animals he tends, or the owner would receive nothing.
Asks what shall be done with the money from the sale of the animal.
Rabbi Tarfon says the finder may use the money; the dispute is then recounted.
The Gemara notes the tannaim agree up to this point and then analyzes where their actual disagreement lies.

29a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Only if the finder used the money is he liable; if he did not use it and it is lost, everyone agrees he is exempt.
Suggests that this mishna refutes Rav Yosef's view on the status of a bailee for a lost item.
Rabba holds the finder is an unpaid bailee, liable only for negligence; Rav Yosef holds he is a paid bailee, liable even for theft or loss.
Rav Yosef could reply that everyone agrees a paid bailee is liable for theft or loss; the dispute concerns damage beyond control.
The tannaim disagree only about damage beyond control, the obligation of a borrower, in the case of the finder's use.
Rabbi Tarfon holds the Sages permitted the finder to use the money, so he is a borrower and liable even for circumstances beyond control.
Rabbi Akiva holds the Sages did not permit the finder to use the money, so he is not a borrower.
Because he may not use the money, Rabbi Akiva's finder does not count as a borrower.
If so, why does Rabbi Akiva need to state that the finder is not liable if the money is lost?
If the dispute concerns theft and loss, Rabbi Akiva's explanation is what the mishna teaches, since he holds the finder is exempt.
If the finder were a paid bailee as Rav Yosef holds, he would be liable for theft and loss; the mishna teaches otherwise.
Since he may not use the money, he is not a paid bailee and is not liable for theft or loss.
If everyone agrees on theft and loss, why does Rabbi Akiva's statement state that he is not liable, when it could be taught more directly?
The mishna should have taught only that Rabbi Akiva says he may not use the money, which implies he is not a borrower and bears no liability.
Why does Rabbi Akiva's statement add that the finder is not liable if the money is lost?
The addition parallels Rabbi Tarfon's formulation, which states that the finder is liable if the money is lost.
Why does Rabbi Tarfon's statement need to add that the finder is liable if the money is lost?
Since the Sages permitted him to use the money, he is treated as one who actually used it and is therefore liable.
How can Rav Yosef explain the dispute as concerning damage beyond control, when the mishna says that if the money is lost he is not liable?

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara resolves the mishna's wording by linking it to Rabba's distinction between stolen and lost items.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Tarfon on permitting the finder to use the money.
Background story: orphans' dinars held by Raḥava, who brings the case to Rav Yosef.
Raḥava asks whether he may make use of the dinars.
Rav Yosef reports Rav Yehuda's citation of Shmuel, that the halakha follows Rabbi Tarfon.
Abaye objects that Rav Huna's ruling on the matter was already stated and conflicts with this reading.
Rav Huna limits the leniency to proceeds of a lost item, where the finder exerted effort, not to lost coins.
Rav Yosef accepts the objection and tells Raḥava he cannot permit the use of the dinars.
Mishna: a finder of scrolls may read one in thirty days to air it, but may not study new passages or read with others.
Mishna: a finder of a garment shakes it once in thirty days, but may not use it for personal display.
Mishna: silver and copper vessels may be used to prevent tarnish, gold and glass vessels are left until Elijah comes.
Mishna: a finder of an undignified item such as a sack need not take it up.
Shmuel rules that a finder of phylacteries in the marketplace assesses their value and sets the money aside at once.
Ravina objects from the mishna's scroll rule, inferring that rolling is allowed but assessing and setting money aside is not.
Abaye distinguishes phylacteries, which are commonly produced, from scrolls, which are hard to obtain.
Baraita: a borrower of a Torah scroll may not lend it on, may open and read it, but may not study new passages or read with others.
Baraita: a depositee rolls a scroll every twelve months and may read it; Sumakhos and R Eliezer ben Yaakov give other intervals.
The Gemara quotes the baraita's rule that a borrowed Torah scroll may not be lent to a third party.
Why does the tanna single out a Torah scroll, when the rule seems to apply to any item?
Resh Lakish cites a mishna in Gittin stating that borrowers and renters may not lend or sublet, showing the rule is general.
The Torah scroll is singled out so no one assumes an owner would welcome a mitzva done with his property.
If reading is obvious, why did the tanna state it, and what was the purpose of that clause?
The clause is needed to teach that he may not study new passages at first.
The Gemara repeats the baraita on a depositee rolling a scroll every twelve months and reading it.
What is the depositee doing with the scroll, and does reading for his own use conflict with the earlier permission?
The tanna means reading while rolling is permitted, but opening it for one's own purposes is prohibited.
Sumakhos and R Eliezer ben Yaakov give differing scroll intervals in the baraita.
Is R Eliezer ben Yaakov's view identical to the first tanna's, making his statement redundant?
Emend the text: R Eliezer ben Yaakov says both new and old scrolls are rolled every thirty days.
Conclusion of the baraita: no first-time study and no reading with another person.
A baraita seems to permit two people to read one scroll together, contradicting the mishna.
Abaye reconciles the sources: two may read together only when following the same matter.
The mishna's garment rule is quoted again: shake it once in thirty days.
Does shaking a garment truly benefit it, since shaking is generally harmful?
R Yoḥanan says a daily shaker of garments is harmed, and only one with a weaver at home may shake daily; this conflicts with the mishna.
Reconcile: the mishna refers to one person shaking, while R Yoḥanan refers to two shaking together.
Reconcile: the mishna refers to shaking by hand, while R Yoḥanan refers to shaking with a stick.
Reconcile: the mishna refers to wool, while R Yoḥanan refers to linen.
R Yoḥanan advises drinking from a witches' cup over lukewarm water, with qualifications on metal, earthenware, boiling and flavorings.
R Yoḥanan advises one who wants to squander a large inheritance to wear linen, use glass, and hire laborers without supervising them.
The Gemara explains the advice by specifying Roman linen and expensive white glass, and the hands-off supervision.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the earlier case concerns laborers working with oxen, whose unsupervised work could trample crops.
Mishna: one may spread a found garment for its own sake, but not for his own prestige.
Raised as a dilemma: what is the halakha if one spreads it both for his own sake and for its sake?
Suggested proof from the mishna that spreading for its sake alone is permitted.
The proof is rejected: the latter clause only forbids spreading for prestige, so no inference follows either way.
Suggested proof from a baraita: a found garment may not be spread for his sake before guests, nor for its sake.
Distinguishes that case: spreading before guests invites the evil eye or theft.
Suggested proof from a baraita on a calf in a yoke, which is unfit when its owner intends it to thresh.
Distinguishes that case, since the verse about the heifer disqualifies any labor it performed.
If any labor disqualifies the calf, why is the first clause not also unfit?
Compares it to a mishna on a bird resting on a red heifer, which remains fit, while mounting disqualifies.
What is the reason for the difference between the two cases?
Rav Pappa explains by the spelling of the verse: the written and vocalized forms show the owner must be amenable to the labor.
Because the verse uses the active form, the owner's amenability to the act is required, so mating disqualifies while resting does not.
Mishna: one may use found silver or copper vessels, and the same applies to other vessels.
Baraita: specific guidance on using wooden, copper, silver, tool and gold or glass vessels, extended by analogy to deposits.
What is the bailee doing with a deposit, given the owner should tend to his own property?
The case is a deposit whose owner has traveled overseas, so the bailee must look after it until his return.
Mishna: one who finds a sack, basket or undignified item need not take it up.
From where are these halakhot derived?
Baraita derives the rule from the verse about returning a lost item and disregarding it at times.
Explains the occasions: a priest facing a graveyard, an elderly person for whom it is undignified, or a finder whose wages exceed the item's value.
For which case was the verse needed to teach that a lost item may be disregarded?
Rejects the priest-graveyard case as obvious, since a positive mitzva does not override a prohibition, and ritual law yields to monetary matters.
Suggests the verse teaches exemption where the finder's labor is worth more than the item.
Rejects that reading: the rule comes from a teaching of Rav Yehuda citing Rav, derived from a verse on the release of debts.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse of no needy among you is read as a command that one's own needs come before others', so one may keep his own assets.
The verse teaches exemption from returning a lost item when the finder is elderly and tending it is beneath his dignity.
Rabba rules that one who has struck a straying animal to guide it is liable to return it.
Abaye throws a clod at Rabba's goats and is told he has become liable to return them, so he must do so.
A dilemma: if one returns items in the field but not in town, is he obligated to return them in town as well?
Rava rules that whatever one must recover for his own property he must recover for others, and likewise for unloading and loading.
R Yishmael ben R Yosei pays a porter half a dinar to avoid lifting the wood, declares it ownerless, and repeats this with the same man.
He declares the wood ownerless to everyone but that man, excluding him from reacquiring it.
Is property truly rendered ownerless in such a case?
A mishna in Peah: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether a declaration of ownerless property is valid, and Beit Hillel requires it to be for all.
R Yishmael declared the wood ownerless to everyone, and his personal statement only barred the man from reacquiring it.
R Yishmael was elderly and the lifting beneath his dignity, so why did he bother making the wood ownerless?
He acted beyond the strict letter of the law, when he could have simply refused the request.
A baraita on Exodus 18:20 parses the verse to show that one must act beyond the strict letter of the law.
The Master taught the parsing of the verse, beginning with visiting the sick.
Visiting the sick falls under acts of kindness, so why is it listed separately?
It is needed for a contemporary of the sick person, who takes a sixtieth of the illness, so even so one must visit.
The baraita continues with the word wherein, which refers to burial.
Burial also falls under acts of kindness, so why is it listed separately?
It is needed for an elderly person for whom burial is beneath his dignity, teaching that he must still take part.
The baraita's final clause, that they must perform, refers to acting beyond the letter of the law.
R Yohanan says Jerusalem was destroyed because its courts ruled strictly by Torah law in the city.
What else should the courts have done, if not rule by arbitrary decisions?
The courts should have grounded their rulings in Torah law but not gone beyond the letter of the law.
Mishna opens: which item is considered lost property?
Mishna: a donkey or cow grazing on the path is not lost, but a donkey with overturned gear or a cow running into vineyards is lost.
Mishna: one must return the lost animal even if it flees and is returned four or five times.
The obligation derives from the verse about returning a brother's wandering ox or sheep.
Mishna: a finder who lost income may not demand a sela, only a laborer's wage, and may stipulate terms before a court.
Are all those cases in the chapter not considered lost property?
Rav Yehuda explains that the tanna is defining the principle of which lost items one must return.
Restating the mishna's principle: grazing animals are not lost, but overturned gear or a runaway in vineyards makes them lost.
Is a grazing animal still not lost even if left untended indefinitely? Rav Yehuda cites Rav that three days is the threshold, but what are the circumstances?
If one who finds at night obligates after even an hour, while by day even much time does not, the three-day rule seems inconsistent.
The three-day rule applies only when the animal was seen both early morning and at nightfall; after three days it is certainly lost.
A baraita teaches the same rule, beginning with a found cloak or axe.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna continues: a cow in the vineyards is lost property, a cloak or ax by a fence is not, and water threatening a field must be barred.
Rava derives from the verse about every lost item of your brother that the obligation extends to protecting land.
Rav Hananya brings a baraita about water flooding a field, which he says supports Rava's view.
Rava rejects that support: the baraita might be about something else, so do not use it to back my ruling.
The baraita concerns a field that has sheaves of grain lying on the land.
If the baraita concerns sheaves, why state it at all, since the obligation seems obvious?
It is needed where the sheaves require the land to dry, lest one think they share the land's status and need not be returned.
Mishna restated: a found donkey or cow grazing on the path is not lost property.
The two clauses of the mishna seem to contradict each other about which animals in which positions count as lost.
Abaye explains the tanna pairs each case with its counterpart: grazing on the path and running among vineyards are contrasted.
Rava objects that if the tanna uses the counterpart style, he should have taught the stringent case and the lenient case directly.
Rava resolves it by direction: an animal facing the field is lost, and the rule about land-damage explains the grazing case.
The grazing-among-vineyards case concerns damage to the land, while running among vineyards concerns the animal's own loss from wounds.
Why not also derive the lost-item rule for grazing among vineyards from damage to the land?
The case concerns land belonging to gentiles, which one need not return or guard.
Why not derive it instead from loss of the animal itself, since gentiles might kill it?
The case is one where gentiles first warn the owner and only then kill the animal.
Perhaps they already warned the owner about this particular animal?
If the owner was warned and ignored it, the loss is deliberate, so there is no obligation to return it.
Concluding: such a loss is then a deliberate one, not a lost item the finder must return.
Mishna: one returns a fleeing animal repeatedly, four or five times, citing the verse on returning a brother's wandering ox.
A sage objects that the compound verb allows only two returns, one for hashev and one for teshivem.
Rava replies: hashev means unlimited returns, and teshivem extends the mitzva to returning to garden or ruined house.
What are the circumstances: if the place is protected it is obvious, and if not, why is it a return?
The place is protected; the owner's knowledge is not required, per R Elazar, since the Torah broadened the lost-item return.
The mitzva of sending away the mother bird is cited from Deuteronomy 22:7.
A sage proposes that the compound form of sending away allows only two dispatches.
Rava replies that sending away applies even a hundred times, and teshallah extends it to cases involving a mitzva.
Another sage applies the same objection to the compound form in the verse on rebuking a neighbor.
Rava replies that rebuke applies even a hundred times, and tokhiah extends the obligation to a student rebuking a teacher.
A verse on helping an animal of one's enemy yields the same rule: help even when the owner is not present.
A verse on raising an animal fallen under its burden is cited to derive that the obligation extends beyond the owner's presence.
Why does the Torah write both unloading and loading, if one mitzva would suffice?
Unloading alone might be limited by cruelty to animals and financial loss, so loading is written to teach its independent obligation.
If only loading were stated, one might limit it to paid work, so unloading is written to cover unpaid help as well.
If R Shimon holds that loading is also free, why are both verses needed?
Why is the word for lost item written separately as well?
The two verses are needed for cases where the owner's pain and the helper's pain differ, while lost items carry no such distinction.
Concluding: if lost items were stated alone, one might think the owner is not present, so the rule is taught for that case too.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concluding the prior point: unloading and loading are both written because a helper might otherwise be excused when the owner is present.
From the verse on a murderer put to death, the Gemara derives that any means of execution is valid when the prescribed one is unavailable.
From the verse on striking the idolatrous city by sword, the same derivation applies: any available manner of execution is valid.
From the verse on returning a poor man's pledge at sunset, the Gemara derives the duty to return it even when taken without court sanction.
From the compound verb on returning a neighbor's garment before sunset, the same extension to pledges taken without court sanction is derived.
Why are two verses needed to teach the same halakha about returning a garment needed by the debtor?
One verse covers a garment worn by day and the other a garment worn by night.
From the verse on opening one's hand to the poor, the duty to give charity is extended to poor people of other cities.
From the verse on giving to the poor, the duty is extended to small gifts as well as large ones.
From the verse on furnishing a released Hebrew slave, the duty is extended to cases where the house is not blessed through him.
If R Elazar ben Azarya limits the gift to cases of blessing, why is the compound verb needed at all?
The Torah speaks in ordinary human idiom, so the compound verb carries no special derivation.
From the verse on lending to the needy, the duty to lend is extended to a person who has resources but does not want to use them.
Per R Shimon, the lending duty does not apply in that case, so why is the doubled verb needed?
Again the Torah speaks in human idiom, so nothing may be derived from the doubled verb.
Mishna and baraita: a finder who lost wages is paid as an idle laborer, not given a sela.
What does the phrase as an idle laborer mean?
Abaye explains it is the wage a person would accept to leave his usual work for returning the lost item.
Mishna: if three men can form a court, the finder may stipulate his compensation before them.
Story: Issur and Rav Safra dissolve a joint venture, and Rav Safra brings the matter to Rabba bar Rav Huna.
Rabba bar Rav Huna tells Rav Safra to bring the three witnesses before whom the partnership was dissolved.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alternative proposal: have two of the three court members, or two witnesses, testify that the partnership was dissolved before a court of three.
Rav Safra asks where Rabba bar Rav Huna derives that dissolution must be before a court.
Rabba cites the mishna: a finder may stipulate his terms only before a court, so one settles another's property only before a court.
Rav Safra objects: the mishna case removes property from one person to another, unlike self-disclosure of his own share, which two witnesses can establish.
Rav Safra cites the mishna on a widow selling estate property without a court, showing a court is not needed to reclaim one's own property.
Abaye objects that this mishna was already discussed and that the widow's case requires a court, undermining Rav Safra's comparison.
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi, citing Rav Naḥman, holds that a widow's court need only be lay judges, not experts, supporting the need for a court.
Mishna: an animal found in its owner's stable need not be returned, one found in a public area must be, and a priest may not defile himself to return one in a graveyard.
Mishna: one must keep unloading and loading an overburdened animal even four or five times, citing the verse on helping an enemy's donkey.
Mishna: a passerby is exempt if the owner is able to unload, but an old or infirm owner obligates the passerby; unloading is a mitzva, loading is not.
Mishna: R Shimon holds loading is also a mitzva, and R Yosei HaGelili limits the duty to a burden the animal can bear.
Rava explains that the stable in the mishna neither encourages straying nor secures the animal.
The Gemara supports Rava by showing the mishna's wording would be redundant if the stable secured the animal.
Restating the mishna: an animal found in a stable is not one whose return one must undertake.
R Yitzchak limits the stable ruling to animals standing within the city limits, and by inference the public-area ruling applies everywhere.
Some teach the latter clause differently, so that a public-area find is obligatory, and R Yitzchak applies that beyond the city limits.
R Yitzchak clarifies that the stable exemption holds even outside the city limits, based on the mishna's reading.
Mishna: a priest may not defile himself to return an animal lost in a graveyard.
From where is it derived that a parent's command to become impure or to refrain from returning a lost item should not be obeyed?
A baraita derives it from Leviticus 19:3: the phrase I am the Lord shows that parents and children alike are bound by honor of God.
Without this verse one might think the child must obey, so the Torah's wording teaches that the mitzva of Shabbat overrides.
Why would a positive mitzva to honor a parent not override a prohibition and a positive mitzva of the priest?
The derivation is needed because honoring parents is equated with honoring God, so one might think a priest must obey; the Torah teaches otherwise.
Restating the principle: unloading is a Torah mitzva, loading is not.
What does not loading mean, if loading is written in the verse on helping a fallen donkey?
Unloading is a mitzva done for free, while loading is done for pay; R Shimon holds both are free.
What is the reasoning of the Rabbis who distinguish unloading from loading in pay?
If the verse covered only loading, one might argue unloading is more obligatory, so the Torah wrote unloading to show it is free and loading is paid.
What is R Shimon's reasoning for holding that loading is also free?
The verses are not clearly defined as to which refers to loading and which to unloading.
Why do the Rabbis not say the verses are unclear too?
The phrase collapsed under its burden clearly refers to unloading, while fallen by the way can mean animals lying with loads, so the verses are ambiguous.
Rava begins a new statement on the topic.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Both tanna'im show the prevention of animal suffering is Torah law; even R Shimon disputes only because the verses are unclear.
Is the a fortiori inference drawn from the suffering of animals, which applies to unloading but not loading?
Rejecting that, the inference may rest on monetary loss, which unloading has and loading lacks, so animal suffering is not the basis.
But loading also risks monetary loss, since the owner may miss the market or thieves may come, so monetary loss cannot ground the inference.
The Gemara argues from R Yosei HaGelili's limit on overloading, which implies the Rabbis require unloading only for what is a Torah-level concern for animals.
Perhaps the dispute is over the meaning of under its burden, not over Torah-level suffering, so the proof fails.
The Gemara argues from the mishna's exemption of a passerby, since if suffering were Torah law the owner's presence should make no difference.
Actually suffering is Torah law: the exemption means free only, and the passerby still must unload for pay, as the verse indicates.
A mnemonic list of the cases examined: the animal of a Jew, of a gentile, a friend, an enemy, and a collapsed animal.
A baraita about a gentile's animal collapsed under its burden is cited as support, arguing that suffering alone explains the duty to unload it.
There the duty arises from enmity that would result if gentiles saw Jews neglecting their own, not from suffering.
Another baraita is cited: a Jew does not tend a gentile's animal loaded with libation wine, which supports reading the case as Torah-level suffering.
If suffering is not Torah law, the refusal makes sense, but if it is, why does the Jew not tend the animal and cause it suffering?
The baraita means that loading the animal with libation wine is forbidden, so he need not tend it, and refusal causes no enmity.
A baraita: if a gentile's animal is collapsed under a Jew's burden, one may refuse to unload it.
If suffering is Torah law, why does the verse allow forgoing rather than simply requiring release?
Suffering is Torah law, and the baraita concerns loading, where animal suffering is not the factor.
If the baraita concerns loading, why does it state release for the Jew's animal, and why not apply the same to the first clause?
Release is required there because the Jewish owner suffers delay while waiting for the animal to be loaded.
If that is so, then the same halakha should hold even in the first clause, without a duty for the Jewish partner.
The first clause concerns a gentile driver with the Jewish owner absent, the latter clause a Jewish driver.
On what basis is it asserted that a Jew's animal is driven by a Jew and a gentile's by a gentile?
The typical case is that a person follows his own donkey, so the presumption holds.
But unloading is the case in which the verses on forgoing and releasing are written.
The baraita follows R Yosei HaGelili, who holds suffering is not Torah law, a minority view against the Rabbis.
A baraita: for a friend's collapsed animal versus an enemy's animal needing loading, the enemy's animal is preferred to subdue the evil inclination, even if suffering is Torah law.
A baraita about a Jewish enemy rather than a gentile enemy: if suffering is Torah law, why would the nationality of the enemy matter?
The enemy in the verse differs from the enemy in the earlier baraita, where loading an enemy's animal is preferred to unloading a friend's.
The Gemara brings another baraita as proof.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita on Exodus 23:5: the duty to unload applies to a collapsed animal under a burden it can bear, not to a habitual collapser or standing one.
If suffering were Torah law, collapsed, habitual, and standing animals would all require unloading, so the baraita must reflect a narrower view.
The baraita follows R Yosei HaGelili, who holds that the duty to prevent animal suffering is rabbinic, not Torah law.
The baraita's reading of under its burden as a load the animal can bear fits R Yosei HaGelili, so it is his view.
But the latter clause excludes unloading, which seems to conflict with R Yosei HaGelili's view and align with the Rabbis.
Actually the baraita is R Yosei HaGelili's, and in the matter of loading he agrees with the Rabbis.
Baraita: the verse on seeing an enemy's collapsed donkey covers sight, measured as a ris, and one walks the animal a parasang and may take pay for it.
Mishna: if one finds his own lost item and his father's, his own takes precedence, and likewise with his teacher's.
Mishna: for a father's and a teacher's lost items, the teacher's takes precedence, unless the father is a Torah scholar.
Mishna: for burdens and captivity, the teacher is helped first, unless the father is a Torah scholar.
From where are these precedence rules derived?
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: the verse that there shall be no needy among you is read as a command that one's own property comes first.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: one who scrupulously follows this principle at others' expense ends up impoverished.
Restating the mishna on carrying a father's and teacher's burdens, with the teacher first.
Baraita: the teacher whose burden takes precedence is one who taught wisdom of Talmud, per R Meir, while R Yehuda and R Yosei widen the category.
Rava illustrates with his teacher Rav Seḥora, and Shmuel tears his garment over a teacher who taught him a mishna's details.
Ulla says Babylonian scholars rise and rend garments for one another, but for returning a lost item the preeminent teacher alone takes precedence.
Rav Ḥisda asks Rav Huna whether a student needed as a study partner takes precedence over his teacher's lost item.
Rav Huna rebukes Rav Ḥisda, saying he will need him for forty years, and they stop speaking to each other.
Each sage fasts forty days: Rav Ḥisda out of regret, and Rav Huna because he suspected an offense.
Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef cites R Yoḥanan for R Yehuda's view, and Rav Aḥa bar Rav Huna cites Rav Sheshet for R Yosei's view.
Did R Yoḥanan really rule that way, given his rule that the halakha follows an unattributed mishna, which here is R Meir's view?
Wisdom here means the majority of his wisdom, so the teacher is the one who taught most of it.
Baraita: Bible study is a virtue, Mishna study is rewarded, and Talmud study is the greatest virtue, though one should favor Mishna over Talmud.
The baraita seems self-contradictory, calling Talmud study the greatest virtue and also urging Mishna study over Talmud.
R Yoḥanan begins his resolution of the apparent contradiction.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening baraita asserting that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught students to prioritize Mishna study over Talmud study.
The Gemara asks which homiletic exposition underlies the baraita's claim that Talmud study is the greatest virtue.
Isaiah 58:1 cited as the verse that Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Elai interpreted homiletically.
Explains the verse: Torah scholars' unwitting sins count as deliberate, while ignoramuses' deliberate sins count as unwitting.
Cites the Avot mishna that unwitting error in Talmud study counts as deliberate sin, supporting the explanation.
The Gemara asks what homiletic reading Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Elai applied to a second verse.
Isaiah 66:5 quoted as the verse under homiletic interpretation.
Glosses each phrase of Isaiah 66:5, identifying the groups and resolving the worry that the Jewish people will be shamed.
Chapter-closing formula, then the mishna on who receives the thief's double or fourfold payment when an unpaid bailee compensated the owner.
Gemara asks why the mishna needs to list both animals and vessels, since a general rule about any deposit would suffice.
Both cases are needed, since teaching either alone would wrongly imply the transfer of double-payment rights applies only to that kind of item.
Rami bar Hama objects: a person cannot transfer ownership of what does not yet exist, and even Rabbi Meir's exception covers only date-palm fruit.
Reply distinguishing this case: here the transfer is built into the original deposit agreement, so it takes effect when the item is deposited.

34a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection to the premise: who can say the deposit will be stolen, the thief caught, and that he will pay rather than confess.
Rava replies that the owner effectively transferred the cow to the bailee in advance, conditioned on theft and payment, so profits are his.
Rabbi Zeira objects that the same logic would give the bailee the fleece and offspring, and cites a baraita excluding them.
Rabbi Zeira's reply: the transfer covers everything except the fleece and offspring, which the owner keeps.
The Gemara asks why the mishna states the rule without qualification, if owners do not necessarily intend such transfers.
Typically a person transfers gains that come from outside the animal, like thief's payments, which are hard to foresee, but not its own produce.
Alternative formulation of Rava's view: ownership transfers immediately before the theft rather than at the time of deposit.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two formulations of Rava's response.
Two differences: the fleece and offspring problem disappears on the second version, and an animal standing in a marsh could not be acquired.
Rabbi Yochanan explains the mishna's 'if the bailee paid' to mean he merely declared he would pay, acquiring the double payment.
Objection from the mishna: it implies only a bailee who actually paid gets the double payment, which conflicts with Rabbi Yochanan.
Reply: the latter clause shows the inference is unreliable, so the mishna supports no conclusion about actual payment.
A baraita about a renter who declared he would pay accords with Rabbi Yochanan, showing the double payment goes to him.
Rav Pappa's view: unpaid and paid bailees acquire the double payment by admitting negligence or theft, while a borrower's bare declaration does not.
The Gemara asks with what claim a borrower could exempt himself from liability.
Only by claiming the animal died from ordinary labor, an uncommon event that is accepted only with corroborating proof.
Some attribute to Rav Pappa the view that a borrower's declaration transfers the double payment, since he can claim ordinary labor.
Rav Zevid counters Rav Pappa, citing Abaye's position on borrowers.
Abaye's ruling: a borrower gets the double payment only upon actually paying the owner, not by declaration.
The reason: the borrower enjoys all the benefit of the animal without paying, so a bare declaration does not transfer the double payment.
A baraita about a borrower who went ahead and paid shows the double payment goes to him, supporting Rav Zevid.
Dilemma: the baraita does not refute Rav Pappa's first version, but under his second version may it refute him?
Rav Pappa could answer that the mishna was read as a declaration of intent to pay, so the baraita is read the same way.
The Gemara questions the analogy: the mishna lacks the word went ahead, which the baraita contains, implying actual payment.
Went ahead means he went ahead and declared intent to pay, without yet paying.
The Gemara asks whether the different wording for renter and borrower implies the borrower's baraita specifically requires actual payment.
Rejects the inference: the two baraitot may be unrelated, so differing wording proves nothing.
Sages testify that the baraitot of two academies were taught together as one long baraita, so wording discrepancies can be used.
The Gemara calls it obvious that a bailee who first refused but later declared intent to pay acquires the double payment.
Raises a dilemma about the case where the bailee first declared intent to pay, which remains unresolved in this span.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dilemma: if the bailee retracts his declared intent to pay, does he lose the double payment, or is he merely postponing payment?
Dilemma: if the bailee declared intent to pay, died, and his sons refused, do they retract or merely postpone payment?
Dilemma: if the bailee died before declaring intent and his sons paid, may the owner deny transferring the double payment to them?
Dilemma: if the owner died and the bailee paid his sons, can the sons deny the transfer, or does the bailee still receive the double payment?
Series of dilemmas about partial payment, multiple borrowed items, and partners or spouses paying, all left unresolved.
Rav Huna rules that even a bailee who declares intent to pay must swear that the item is not in his possession.
The Gemara asks the reason for requiring that oath.
We fear the bailee may have set his eyes on the item, so the oath guards against that covetous motive.
Objection from a mishna on a creditor and debtor disputing the value of lost collateral, showing when an oath is required.
The Gemara asks which case the halakha about who swears refers to, since the latter clause needs no such explanation.
Shmuel says it refers to the first clause of the mishna, not the latter one.
The Gemara asks what Shmuel means by the first clause.
The debtor must swear in the three-dinar case, but the Sages made the creditor swear to prevent a false oath by the debtor.
Begins a new conditional question linking this mishna to Rav Huna's statement.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection to Rav Huna: if the creditor must swear the collateral is not in his possession, how can he later produce it?
Rava answers that the mishna concerns collateral proven burned by witnesses, so the creditor need not swear he lacks it.
The Gemara asks where the creditor could produce collateral that was burned or stolen, and why the oath shifts to him at all.
Creditors can locate a thief since they know who enters their house, but debtors have no such inkling, so the debtor cannot produce it.
Abaye holds the oath shifts to the creditor by decree; Rav Ashi holds both swear on different points, with the creditor first.
Rav Huna bar Tahlifa, in Rava's name: the mishna's latter clause refutes Rav Huna, since the creditor could also swear on value.
Rav Ashi reports Rav Kahana's answer: the debtor trusts the creditor about the collateral's location, but the creditor does not trust the debtor on value.
The Gemara asks why each party trusts the other on one matter but not on the other.
Proverbs 11:3 explains it: the debtor sees the creditor as upright and blessed, while the creditor sees the debtor as faithless and ruined.
Narrative of a bailee who lost jewels: Rav Nachman rules that not knowing where they were placed is negligence and orders his palace sold.
Rava objects that this resembles the mishna where a paying bailee gets the double payment, implying he should profit from the increase.
Rav Nachman did not answer because the cases differ: the paying bailee acted voluntarily, while here the bailee forced the owner to go to court.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Nachman holds that repossessed appraised property returns when the debtor repays.
Rejects that reading: appraisal is usually final, but the jewel case was an erroneous appraisal since the bailee always had the items.
Neharde'a Sages limit return of appraised property to twelve months; Ameimar, from Neharde'a himself, holds return is always allowed.
Ruling that appraisal repossession always returns, grounded in Deuteronomy 6:18 that one should do what is right and good.
Debtor may reclaim appraised property from a creditor's creditor, but not from buyers, heirs, donees, or a husband holding his wife's property.
Cites Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina's Usha enactment: a husband repossesses property his wife sold in usufruct from buyers after her death.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Aha and Ravina dispute whether, when the debtor himself authorized repossession, paying the debt reverses the repossession.
Explains the dispute: one view treats the authorized repossession as a full sale that cannot be retracted, the other as no full sale.
The Gemara asks from when a creditor who repossessed land may consume its produce.
Three views: from receipt of the authorization document (Rabba), from its witnesses' signatures (Abaye), or after the proclamation period ends (Rava).
Mishna on a renter who lends a cow that dies naturally with the borrower: the renter swears and the borrower pays; Rabbi Yosei disagrees.
Rav Idi bar Avin asks Abaye how the renter acquires the cow, implying acquisition through the oath.
Objection: then the owner could tell the renter to drop his oath and sue the borrower directly for the cow.
Abaye replies: the renter acquires the cow from the moment of death, and the oath only eases the owner's suspicions rather than being legally required.
Rabbi Zeira's example: alternating rentals and loans leave the owner owing several cows, two for borrowings and two for rentals.
Rav Aha of Difti objects to Ravina: it is one cow moving between statuses, so how can the owner owe multiple cows for it?
Ravina replies: the cow cannot be returned intact, so the borrower owes what he committed to return, which is two cows.
Mar bar Rav Ashi's third view: the renter is owed two cows, one for the loan and one for the rental, each acquired or used accordingly.
Rabbi Yirmeya: sometimes both renter and borrower swear falsely and are both liable for a sin-offering.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Summarizes the four combinations of which offering the renter and borrower owe, depending on the death, theft, and claim involved.
The Gemara asks how such combinations arise at all.
A false oath denying a monetary claim brings a guilt-offering; a false oath of mere utterance brings a sin-offering.
Works through renter and borrower offering combinations, depending on whether the cow died naturally, was stolen, or died by labor.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yirmeya's systematic presentation adds, since these are merely applications of known principles.
It rejects Rabbi Ami's view that a judge-administered oath creates no sin-offering liability; liability applies even when others administer it.
Dispute: a bailee who passes the deposit to another bailee is exempt per Rav, but liable even for unavoidable damage per Rabbi Yochanan.
Abaye explains both sides: a competent second bailee justifies exemption under Rav, while under Rabbi Yochanan the owner's stated objection makes the transfer liable.
Rav Hisda: Rav's ruling was not stated explicitly but inferred from another case.
Story: gardeners routinely left spades with an old woman; one left them with a colleague, who redeposited them with her, and they were stolen.
Rav exempted the gardener, but the ruling rests on the gardeners' own routine of depositing with her, not a general rule on bailees.
Rabbi Ami sat and stated the halakha about a bailee who passes a deposit to another.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects from the renter-lends-cow mishna: if Rabbi Yochanan is right, the owner should make the renter liable for the loan.
Rabbi Ami replies the case is where the owner authorized the renter to lend the deposit onward.
The Gemara asks: then the borrower should pay the owner, since the owner sanctioned the lending.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel answers: the owner told the renter to lend it at his discretion, so it is not as if the owner lent it.
Rami bar Hama objects from a mishna on coins given to minors, asking why the owner's stated objection does not make adults liable too.
Rava replies that no proof can be drawn from that mishna, since the case of anyone depositing with another is different.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A bailee deposits items with awareness that his wife and children may safeguard them, since he cannot always be present.
Neharde'an sages infer from the Mishna's precise wording that the minor-versus-adult distinction applies only to one's own children.
Rava rules that a bailee who passes a deposit to another bailee is liable, including the case of an unpaid bailee passing to a paid one.
Why should the first bailee be liable in the case of an unpaid bailee passing to a paid one?
The owner can say he trusts the first bailee's oath but not the second's, so the first bailee is liable.
An amoraic dispute is stated about a negligent bailee whose animal went to a marsh and died naturally.
Abaye, citing Rabba, rules that the bailee is liable in that case.
Rava, citing Rabba, rules that the bailee is exempt in that case.
Abaye repeats in Rabba's name that the bailee is liable.
Abaye's ruling holds even on the view that a case beginning in negligence and ending in accident is exempt, so the bailee is liable.
What is the reason the bailee is liable?
Because the air of the marsh killed the animal, and the negligence led to the death.
Rava, citing Rabba, rules that the bailee is exempt, even on the view that initial negligence with accidental ending is liable.
What is the reason the bailee is exempt?
The Angel of Death causes death regardless of location, so it makes no difference where the animal was.
Abaye concedes that the bailee is exempt if the animal returned home and died there.
What is the reason for that exemption?
The animal returned, so one cannot claim the air of the marsh killed it.
Rava concedes that if the animal was stolen to the marsh and died in the thief's house, the bailee is liable.
What is the reason the bailee is liable in the thief's house case?
Even if the Angel of Death spared it, it would still be standing in the thief's house because of the bailee's negligence.
Abaye challenges Rava: by his Angel of Death reasoning, how is the exchange of Rabbi Abba bar Memel and Rabbi Ami explained?
Abaye cites the earlier objection that Rabbi Abba bar Memel raised against Rabbi Ami.
Rabbi Ami replied that the owner had given the renter permission to lend the deposit.
Abaye argues that Rabbi Ami could have invoked the Angel of Death reasoning, so the answer is unnecessary.
Rava replies that his own view has no such objection, because the owner's claim about trust is not raised under Abaye's reasoning.
Rami bar Hama objects from a mishna: bringing the animal to a cliff edge makes the bailee liable, implying the death in its usual manner is exempt.
Why should the owner not say the air of the mountain or exhaustion from climbing killed the animal?
The case is one where the bailee took the animal to a good pasture, which is not negligent.
If so, the bailee should be exempt even when the animal fell.
He is liable because he was able to subdue the animal and did not subdue it.
If so, the first clause should say the fall is an accident, since he should have subdued the animal.
The first clause refers to a case where the animal overpowered him, ascended, and then descended.
The mishna teaches that Rabbi Yosei permits the other party to do business with the cow.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda objects that Rav Yehuda himself reported Shmuel saying Rabbi Yosei disagreed.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Is the halakha like Rabbi Yosei even in the first mishna, or not?
Rav Yehuda replies that Rabbi Yosei disagreed even in the first mishna, and the halakha follows him there too.
Amoraim of Eretz Yisrael disagreed; Rabbi Elazar holds Rabbi Yosei disagreed and the halakha follows him even in the first mishna.
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds Rabbi Yosei concedes in the first mishna because the bailee already paid and acquired the animal.
The formulation is problematic: if he paid the thief pays him, but if not, the thief does not pay?
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yoḥanan's own statement, which seems to contradict the formulation just given.
The quoted Rabbi Yoḥanan view: the mishna means the bailee's declaration of choosing to pay suffices even before actual payment.
The text should be emended: Rabbi Yosei concedes because the bailee already said he hereby chooses to pay.
Mishna: one who tells two people he robbed one of them, or that one's father deposited with him, without knowing which, pays both.
Mishna: two depositors each claim the full amount, one deposited 100 and the other 200; he pays 100 to each and the rest waits for Elijah.
Rabbi Yosei objects: then the swindler loses nothing, so the whole deposit should wait for Elijah.
Mishna: a deposit of two vessels with conflicting claims is divided, with the rest awaiting Elijah.
Rabbi Yosei again objects that the swindler loses nothing, so the whole deposit should wait for Elijah.
From the mishna's rule of paying both claimants, we infer that in cases of doubt property is given out rather than left with its holder.
The Gemara cites the mishna's second clause, where the disputed sum waits for Elijah, as contradicting that inference.
The Sages reply that a deposit and a robbery differ: the robber sinned and is penalized, while the depositor did not sin.
The Gemara finds further contradictions between deposit cases, and between robbery cases, in the mishna's clauses.
Rava resolves the contradiction: separate bundles imply negligence and payment to both, while a joint deposit requires only proven shares.
The Gemara notes a further contradiction between two robbery cases, and points to the mishna's wording as the source.
The mishna's robbery case is restated: one who says he robbed one of two, or that one's father deposited, pays both claimants.
A mishna in Yevamot has a robber of one of five victims place the goods between them, which seems to contradict the mishna's rule.
Perhaps the present mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, who makes the robber pay each victim, so there is no contradiction? How is it known otherwise?
The cases differ: a claimant who demands payment needs proof, while a robber seeking atonement pays both, so the mishna's wording supports this.
The Master explains that the earlier case concerns claimants who demand payment from the one holding the money.
What does the other party, the thief, claim in response?
Rav Yehuda says Rav holds the other party is silent, since he does not know whom he owes; Rav Mattana gives a different account of Rav's view.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One opinion holds that the robber's screaming denying the claims is not an admission, whereas silence counts as admission.
The opposing opinion holds that silence here is not an admission, since the robber may be silent out of uncertainty about who the victim is.
The Master rules that the robber places the stolen item between the claimants and withdraws from them.
If all of them take it and leave, the victim may lose his property, which conflicts with Rav's rule that one may not take or return uncertain property.
Rav Safra explains the baraita: the robber should keep the item in his own possession or before the court.
Abaye asks Rava whether Rabbi Akiva said something in the dispute over one who robbed one of five people.
Rabbi Akiva's view: this is not the way to remove a transgression until one pays the value of the stolen item to each victim.
From Rabbi Akiva's view, we infer that in uncertain cases property is given out to claimants rather than left with its holder.
A Bava Batra mishna about a house collapsing on a son and his mother seems to show Rabbi Akiva leaving property in its holders' possession.
Rava distinguishes: the house case involves two uncertain claims, while the robbery case involves a certain claim from the victims.
But the mishna's case of two people, each claiming an uncertain amount, is also an uncertain-versus-uncertain case, yet it divides the money.
How do we know that the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva rather than Rabbi Tarfon?
A baraita shows Rabbi Tarfon concedes to the two-claimant case, and that concession is against his usual disputant Rabbi Akiva.
How do we know it is a case of uncertain claims on both sides, rather than victims who are certain they were robbed?
This is unlikely: the mishna does not say the victims demand payment, and a baraita shows both parties claim not to know.
The contradiction is resolved as before, since the mishna is about a robber who comes to fulfill his obligation to Heaven.
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi: Rava said deposits in separate bundles imply the bailee should discern, yet all agree a shepherd divides shared animals.
Rav Ashi replies that the shepherd case concerns animals placed in his flock without his knowledge, so no discernment is expected.
The mishna teaches the case of two vessels, one worth 100 dinars and one worth 1000, with the same division and the rest awaiting Elijah.
Both the money case and the vessel case must be taught, since the vessel case involves loss, so the Rabbis may differ from Rabbi Yosei in each.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does Rabbi Yosei hold the fraud-loss reason, so that the second case is not implied by the first?
Both cases are needed for the Rabbis, and the tanna teaches not only this but also that, moving from an obvious case to a novel one.
Mishna: a bailee of deposited produce may not touch it even if it spoils; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he sells it before the court.
What is the reason the first tanna says the bailee may not touch the produce?
Rav Kahana: a person prefers one kav of his own produce to nine kav of another's, so the owner would not want it touched.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: we fear the depositor may have already rendered the produce teruma and tithe elsewhere.
A baraita says the owner may render the produce teruma elsewhere because the bailee may not touch it, which fits Rav Kahana's reason but not Rav Nachman's.
But on Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view, what does the word therefore mean?
The owner's ability to tithe is the reason the bailee may not sell, since the owner can rely on the produce being still in the bailee's possession.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana says Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the dispute concerns standard deterioration, while above-standard deterioration is sold before the court by all.
Rabbi Yoḥanan certainly disagrees with Rav Nachman, since the teruma concern applies regardless of the rate of deterioration.
Shall we say Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees with Rav Kahana?
Rav Kahana's preference applies only to standard deterioration; with accelerated deterioration he would agree the bailee sells.
But did Rav Kahana not say one prefers a kav of his own to nine kav of another, implying the preference holds even with accelerated loss?
That expression is merely an exaggeration, and the preference holds only when deterioration is at the standard rate.
A baraita objects: the owner should fear the produce deteriorated above the standard rate, was sold, and he is eating untithed produce.
Deterioration above the standard rate is uncommon, and the Sages do not issue decrees for uncommon cases.
If more produce is missing than standard, what should be done, given the concern that the owner already tithed it elsewhere?
Even when the produce is sold, it is sold to priests at the teruma price, so any teruma concern is covered.
On Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's view as well, why not sell the produce to priests at the teruma price?
Rabba bar bar Ḥana holds above-standard deterioration is uncommon, so the bailee sells to priests at the teruma price once the loss is seen.
Rav Nachman holds above-standard deterioration is common and may have happened early, so selling risks the owner eating untithed produce.
A baraita objects: Rabbi Meir says the bailee may not touch spoiled wine, oil or honey, while the Rabbis say he should sell them in court, to others only.
A parallel baraita on charity collectors who sell only to others and not to themselves supports the rule against self-sale to avoid suspicion.
It is taught that produce that rotted, without qualification, is not touched by the bailee.
Does this not refer even to rotting above the standard rate of deterioration?
No, it refers to standard deterioration only.
But the cases of wine that fermented, oil that putrefied and honey that spoiled show deterioration above the standard rate, so why are they treated as they are?
Those cases differ: once they spoil they remain spoiled and do not keep deteriorating, so selling them gains nothing.
What about the cases of oil that putrefied and honey that spoiled?

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: For what use are the spoiled oil and honey fit, if the Rabbis say they are sold in court?
Oil is fit for tanners who coat hides with it despite a foul odor, and honey serves as a salve for camels' wounds.
The baraita: the Rabbis say the bailee effects a remedy for the spoiled products and sells them in court.
What remedy does the bailee effect for those products?
Rav Ashi: the remedy is for the casks, since leaving spoiled contents in them would ruin the barrels.
On what point do Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree, if both agree on above-standard deterioration?
Rabbi Meir holds the Sages worried only about significant loss, while the Rabbis worried even about minor loss such as damage to barrels.
Mishna: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the bailee sells the produce before the court, like returning a lost item to its owner.
Rabbi Abba son of Rabbi Yaakov says Rabbi Yoḥanan rules like Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, while Rav Naḥman rules like the Rabbis.
Why does Rabbi Yoḥanan need to issue this ruling specifically here, if he already ruled generally for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
Rabba bar bar Ḥana quotes Rabbi Yoḥanan: wherever Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel taught in our mishna, the halakha follows him, except three cases.
Rabbi Abba and Rabba bar bar Ḥana are later amoraim who disagree about what Rabbi Yoḥanan actually held.
From Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel we learn that a relative may descend to a captive's property, and from the Rabbis that he may not.
Perhaps Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel speaks only here, because the produce would otherwise be destroyed, so the inference does not hold.
The two rulings rest on different reasons: spoiling produce versus fallow land, and the teruma concern or preference for one's own produce.
Are these two independent reasons, when Shmuel's ruling on both follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, implying one common reason?
No, the two halakhot rest on two unrelated reasons, and Shmuel ruled each one independently.
Rava reports Rav Naḥman's two rulings, which he says are unrelated, so the reasons must differ.
Amoraic dispute about a captive: Rav says the court does not authorize a relative to manage the property, while Shmuel says it does.
Everyone agrees the relative may manage the property when they heard the captive died.
They disagree only when they did not hear that the captive died and he may still return.
Rav holds the relative would devalue the property, since he is only a temporary manager who will return it.
Shmuel holds the relative tends the land well, since as a sharecropper he is paid for improving it, so he will not devalue it.
A baraita on Exodus 22:23 asks why the verse mentions wives becoming widows and children orphans, seemingly against the court authorizing a relative.
Rabbi Eliezer explains the verse adds a punishment: wives may not remarry without witnesses, and children may not inherit the property.
Rava holds we learned that courts do not let them descend and sell, but a relative may still manage the land.
An incident in Neharde'a: Rav Sheshet ruled from the baraita that the court does not authorize a relative to descend to a captive's property.
Rav Amram objects that the mishna may only mean that the court does not allow descending and selling.
Rav Sheshet mockingly replies, and argues from the juxtaposition of wives and children that both mean they may not descend at all.
The Gemara notes that whether a relative may manage a captive's property is a dispute between tannaim.
A baraita: one who descends to a captive's property and works it is not dispossessed, and even if he arrives first he profits.
A baraita on abandoned property: one who descends to it is removed, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds it is like captives' property.
A baraita on forsaken property: one who descends to it is removed, and everyone agrees the court does not authorize the relative.
What is different about abandoned property, and what is different about forsaken property, that they are named differently?

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Netushim means property abandoned by force, as in the seventh-year release by royal edict, while retushim means property abandoned voluntarily, as in Hosea.
