The baraita: all of them are appraised as a sharecropper appraises the work of a laborer, for one who works another's field.
To which kind of property does this ruling apply, given that captives' property is not removed and forsaken property is removed?
On whose opinion is the ruling about abandoned property based, the Rabbis or Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
If the Rabbis say the court removes it, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says abandoned property is like captives' property, neither reading fits the sharecropper rule.
For Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, abandoned property is like captives' property in not being removed, but unlike it in that the worker is appraised as a sharecropper.
What is different here from the mishna on a husband who improves his wife's usufruct property, where his labor is not appraised like a sharecropper's?
The case is comparable to a minor wife's property, where the husband is reimbursed to avoid devaluing it, so the worker too is reimbursed for the same reason.
What additional case does the phrase all of them are appraised as a sharecropper include, if it seems to apply only to abandoned property?
It includes Shmuel's ruling that a relative may manage a captive's property, and a fleeing person is treated as a captive if he fled from an accusation of murder.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: when a captive leaves standing crops, the court appoints a steward to harvest them and only then lets a relative manage the property.
If so, why not always appoint a steward to manage the captive's property?
A steward is appointed only for orphans, not for adults, so the court does not always appoint one.
Rav Huna rules that a minor may not descend to a captive's property, and a relative may not manage a minor's property.
Rav Huna's reasons: the minor might devalue the property, and a relative may come to claim presumptive ownership if the minor does not object in time.
Rava draws from Rav Huna that presumptive ownership of a minor's property cannot be acquired by use, even for three years.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A relative may not manage a minor's property, and the rule is limited to paternal brothers and to land without a division document.
The Gemara rejects those distinctions: whether paternal or maternal, land or houses, with or without a document, the court does not authorize the relative.
An old woman had three daughters; she and one were taken captive, one died leaving a minor son, and the third daughter remained.
Abaye asks what to do with the old woman's property, since either the surviving sister or the minor could be left in possession.
Abaye rules: half goes to the surviving sister, and a steward is appointed for the minor's half, since he may have inherited it.
Rava adds that once a steward is appointed for one half, he is appointed for the other half too, until the captives' fate is known.
When the old woman's death is learned, Abaye gives a third to the sister and a third to the minor, with a steward for the captive sister's share; Rava adds a parallel rule.
Mari bar Isak's brother from Bei Ḥozai demands half the inheritance, and Mari denies knowing him; the case goes before Rav Ḥisda.
Rav Ḥisda supports Mari from the verse about Joseph's brothers not recognizing him, showing that brothers may fail to recognize each other.
Rav Ḥisda orders the brother to bring witnesses, and when the witnesses are afraid of Mari, Mari must bring witnesses that he is not a brother.
Mari asks whether this is the halakha, since the burden of proof rests on the claimant.
Rav Ḥisda replies that this is how he judges Mari and all violent people like him.
Mari argues that witnesses will eventually come, and they will lie in his favor if the brother's witnesses fear him.
Rav Ḥisda replies that witnesses will not commit two wrongs, by both refraining from truth and testifying falsely.
Witnesses testify the brother is indeed Mari's brother, and the brother demands half of the orchards and gardens planted since their father's death.
Rav Ḥisda tells Mari the brother spoke well, since the mishna divides enhancements made by adult sons with minor sons.
A mishna in Bava Batra: adult sons who enhance inherited property share the profit with the minor sons, which supports the division.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabba says the profits of the enhanced property go to the middle, between adult and minor sons.
Abaye objects that the comparison fails, since adult brothers living with minors know of them, but here the older brother may not have known.
The matter developed further and was brought before Rabbi Ami.
Rabbi Ami argues that relatives tending captives' property are paid as sharecroppers, so Mari should be reimbursed for his expenditures.
The case was returned and presented before Rav Ḥisda.
Rav Ḥisda distinguishes: a captive's relative acts with court authorization, while Mari acted without it, and the brother was a minor.
Rabbi Ami accepts the reply, having been unaware that Mari's brother was a minor, and agrees Rav Ḥisda is correct.
Mishna: a bailee returning different produce deducts a fixed amount per kor according to the type of grain and the time elapsed.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri holds the deduction is only for one kor, since mice eat the same amount regardless of quantity.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that for a large measure the bailee does not deduct, since the increase offsets the decrease.
The Gemara challenges that after deduction, rice is short by more than the mishna's rate.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, explains the mishna's rice rule applies to shelled rice.
The mishna's rates for spelt and flaxseed are three se'a per kor.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, citing Rabbi Ḥiyya, explains that flaxseed on its stalks is intended, which accounts for the larger deduction.
A baraita teaches the same rates for spelt, flaxseed on its stalks, and unshelled rice, supporting that explanation.
The mishna states that the whole calculation follows the measure and follows the time elapsed.
A baraita adds that this is the decrease for each kor and for each year, supporting the mishna's formula.
Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri repeats his view that the mice do not care how much produce there is.
The Sages tell Rabbi Yoḥanan that much produce is lost and scattered, not only eaten by mice, which undercuts his view.
A baraita: the deduction applies when the bailee mixed the produce with his own, but if he designated a corner, he owes nothing.
If he mixed the produce with his own, why must he calculate the decrease rather than divide the loss proportionately?
Why not have him calculate how much he took as supplies and include that in the calculation?
Rabbi Yehuda holds that if the deposit was a large measure, the bailee does not deduct the decrease.
How large a measure counts as large?
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, says ten kor.
A baraita likewise states that a large measure is ten kor, supporting that figure.
A tanna taught before Rav Naḥman that the deduction applies when both measures came from the same threshing floor, not from a more precise house measure.
Rav Naḥman objects: are we dealing with fools who give a large measure and take back a small one?
Rav Naḥman reinterprets the ruling: it concerns different seasons, since produce absorbs moisture and expands in the rainy season.
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye: if grain expands in the rainy season, the jug should burst.
There was indeed an incident where the jug burst, or one may say the grain contracted from compression when repacked.
Mishna: for liquids the bailee deducts one-sixth for wine, three log per hundred for oil, with variations for refined oil and old casks, and Rabbi Yehuda's differing rates.
The first tanna and Rabbi Yehuda do not disagree: each follows the local custom of casks, sealing and clay quality.
Illustration: in Rav Yehuda's place, forty-eight pitchers were placed in a barrel, and he sold the oil at six pitchers per dinar.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda's calculation: thirty-six pitchers recoup the barrel price, eight are absorbed, and four pitchers remain as profit.
Does Shmuel not say that one may not profit from necessities by more than one-sixth, so why did Rav Yehuda sell at such low profit?
The barrel and sediment remain his, and his exertion and the tapping fee bring the profit to exactly one-sixth.
Mishna: if the oil was refined he does not deduct for sediment, and if stored in saturated old casks he does not deduct for absorption.
Is it not impossible that a saturated cask absorbed no oil at all?
Rav Naḥman says it concerns pitch-coated casks, and Abaye says once saturated they absorb nothing more.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that even a buyer of refined oil accepts a deduction of a log and a half of sediment per hundred log.
Abaye: on Rabbi Yehuda's view it is permitted to mix sediment into the oil, while on the Rabbis' view it is prohibited.
The seller reasons that since he could have mixed sediment in, the buyer should now accept the sediment deduction.
Why cannot the buyer reply that mixed sediment could be sold to another, leaving him with unsaleable residue?
The buyer is a homeowner who wants filtered oil for his own use, not a merchant who resells it.
Why cannot the buyer argue that the seller's not mixing sediment shows he renounced his claim to it?
Rabbi Yehuda does not presume renunciation, as the mishna on selling a yoke versus cattle shows that a sale is limited to its literal terms.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the price reveals the scope of the sale, while the Rabbis hold the money is not proof of the scope.
On the Rabbis' view, mixing sediment is prohibited, so the buyer refuses the deduction, asking whether the seller could mix it himself.
Rav Pappa replies that the reverse is reasonable: on the Rabbis' view mixing is allowed, and on Rabbi Yehuda's it is not, and the seller would earn nothing otherwise.
A baraita teaches that the buyer and the depositor of oil are alike regarding residue such as floating olive pits.
What is meant by residue, and why would the bailee not be able to return the oil with its residue removed?
Rather, the baraita teaches that the depositor accepts residue when returning the oil, and so the buyer accepts residue too.
Does the buyer really accept a deduction for residue?
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda says the loss for murky oil falls only on the seller, since the buyer accepts only the sediment deduction without residue.
The baraitot differ by season: one case is a purchase paid in Tishrei and delivered in Nisan, when the oil is murky; the other is paid and delivered in Nisan.
Mishna: a deposited barrel that breaks in the bailee's hands is liable only if he moved it for his own purposes, with a different rule when a place was designated.
In accordance with whose opinion is this mishna?
It follows Rabbi Yishmael, who holds that a thief's return does not require the owner's knowledge.
A baraita on a thief who returns a lamb or a sela to its place without informing the owner, as Rabbi Yishmael teaches.
Rabbi Akiva's opposing view begins here.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The rule: a bailee's return requires the owner's knowledge.
If the baraita follows Rabbi Yishmael, why does the mishna specify the case where no place was designated, when the bailee is exempt anyway?
The tanna does not need to state the case where a place was designated, since replacing it there is its place; in both cases replacement exempts him.
Consider the latter clause: where a place was designated and he moved it for his own purposes, he is liable, which seems to follow Rabbi Akiva.
So the latter clause follows Rabbi Akiva, who requires the owner's knowledge for return.
If the baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, why does the latter clause specify the case where a place was designated?
The tanna need not state the case with no designated place, since placing it elsewhere is not its place; with a designated place, the owner's knowledge is required.
So the first clause follows Rabbi Yishmael and the latter Rabbi Akiva?
Rabbi Yoḥanan says he will honor whoever explains both clauses of the mishna according to a single tanna.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba explains before Rav that the bailee took the barrel intending to rob the owner, so he must return it to its place.
Rabbi Natan bar Abba explains before Rav that the bailee took the barrel to misappropriate it, and misappropriators are liable for later damage.
On what point do Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Natan disagree?
They disagree on whether misappropriation requires loss: the robbery view says it does, and the misappropriation view says it does not.
Rav Sheshet objects: the mishna says the bailee moved the barrel, not that he took it, so neither robbery nor misappropriation is intended.
Rav Sheshet explains the bailee moved the barrel to stand on it and reach fledglings; both clauses follow Rabbi Yishmael, with the latter about a place not designated.
Why does Rabbi Yoḥanan not explain the mishna as following one tanna, given that placing it implies returning it to its place?
There is an amoraic dispute between Rav and Levi, one holding misappropriation requires loss and the other not; it is concluded Rav holds it does not.
A baraita about a shepherd who leaves his flock: he is liable if he places his staff and satchel on the animal that is later attacked.
Is he liable for placing the staff and satchel on the animal, since he already removed them?
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh and Rav, says the tanna means the staff and satchel were still on the animal when the wolf attacked.
What does it matter that the staff and satchel were still on the animal, since he did not pull it?
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzḥak, citing Rav, says the shepherd struck the animal with a staff and it ran before him, which is a form of pulling.
But causing the animal to run caused no loss, so why is he liable? Does this show Rav holds misappropriation needs no loss?
Rav may mean he weakened the animal with the staff, and his precise wording with a staff rather than a hand shows weakening, so Rav requires loss.
From Rav holding that misappropriation requires loss, it follows that Levi holds it does not.
What is the reason for Levi's opinion?
Rabbi Yoḥanan, citing Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai: the misappropriation rule for a paid bailee is repeated to teach he is liable even without loss.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan continues: misappropriation by a paid bailee is not different from that of an unpaid bailee.
What is meant by saying the paid bailee's misappropriation is different?
One could derive the paid bailee's liability a fortiori from the unpaid bailee, who is exempt for theft and loss yet liable for misappropriation.
For what halakha did the Merciful One write the paid bailee's misappropriation?
To teach that misappropriation does not require loss; intent to misappropriate suffices for liability.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, following Rabbi Elazar, holds that this case and that case are one.
What is meant by saying this case and that case are one?
Both must be taught because an a fortiori inference can be refuted: the unpaid bailee pays double for a false oath claim, which the paid bailee does not.
The one who does not refute the inference holds the paid bailee's stricter liability for principal makes the a fortiori inference valid.
Rava holds the verse need not state misappropriation at all, since it can be derived from the borrower by a fortiori reasoning.
Why then are the unpaid and paid bailees' halakhot stated in the verse?
One mention teaches that misappropriation does not require loss; the other prevents concluding the bailee is exempt like a partner-borrower.
On the view that misappropriation requires loss, why are two mentions needed?
One mention prevents applying the principle that the a fortiori conclusion must match its source.
A baraita reads the master of the house approaching the judges to determine misappropriation as referring to an oath, by comparison with a later verse.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a bailee who binds coins in a cloth, or entrusts them to minors, or secures them poorly is liable; proper safeguarding by bailee standards exempts him.
Granted the other cases make him liable, but if he bound the coins and slung them behind him, what more could he have done?
Rava cites Rabbi Yitzḥak: the verse says bind the money in your hand, so even bound money must remain in one's hand.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: a person's money should always be in his possession, as the verse says bind the money in your hand.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: a person should divide his money into three parts: one buried, one invested in business, and one kept at hand.
Rabbi Yitzḥak: blessing is found only in what is hidden from the eye, citing the verse about blessing in the storehouses.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: blessing is found only where the eye has no dominion, again citing the storehouse verse.
A baraita on measuring grain: blessing is found neither in what is weighed, measured or counted, but only in what is hidden from the eye.
Shmuel: money has safeguarding only when buried in the ground.
Rava: Shmuel concedes that on Shabbat eve at twilight the Rabbis did not require immediate burial, but delay past Shabbat makes the bailee liable.
If the depositor is a Torah scholar who needs money for havdala, the bailee may delay burial a bit longer.
Since rummagers are common, money is safeguarded only in the beams of a roof.
Since dismantlers are common, money is safeguarded only between the bricks of a wall.
Rava: Shmuel concedes money may be kept in the wall or between the corners of the house.
Since tappers are common, money is safeguarded only in the handbreadth next to the ground or next to the ceiling beam.
Rav Aḥa son of Rav Yosef brings a Pesaḥim mishna on bread under a rockslide, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel uses the dog's detection range.
Here, for money, must it be buried three handbreadths deep, or not?
Rav Ashi: for bread the concern is scent, which requires three handbreadths; for money the concern is sight, so one handbreadth suffices, per Rafram.
A man deposited money with another, who kept it in a willow hut, where it was stolen.
Rav Yosef: the hut is effective against thieves but negligent against fire, so the case is negligence followed by accident and the bailee is liable.
Others say the hut is effective against fire but negligent against thieves, so the bailee is exempt; the halakha follows that the bailee is liable.
A depositor asked a bailee to return his money, and the bailee said he did not know where he had placed it.
The matter came before Rava, who ruled that any claim by a bailee of not knowing is itself negligence, so he must pay.
A bailee gave the money to his mother, who placed it in a chest, where it was stolen.
How should the judges rule in the chest case?
Let us tell the bailee to go pay, but he may object that a principle protects him.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Anyone who deposits an item does so with awareness that the bailee's wife and children may safeguard it.
Let us tell the bailee's mother to go pay for the money.
She can reply that her son never told her the money was not his, so she buried it as if it were his.
Why did you not tell her the money was not yours?
The bailee replies that not saying so was better, since she was then more careful with money she thought was her son's.
Rava: the bailee swears he gave the money to his mother, and she swears she hid it in a chest where it was stolen, so the bailee is exempt.
A guardian for orphans bought an ox for them and gave it to a cowherd; the ox had no molars and died because it could not eat.
How should the judges rule in the case of the dead ox?
Let us tell the guardian to go pay for the dead ox.
The guardian replies that he gave the ox to the cowherd, expecting him to care for it.
Let us tell the cowherd to go pay for the dead ox.
The cowherd replies that he kept the ox with other oxen and threw food before it, and did not know it was not eating.
The cowherd is a paid bailee for the orphans, so should he have examined whether the ox was eating?
If the orphans suffered loss he would pay; here they suffered none, since they recovered the money from the original seller after discovering the defect.
Who then claims compensation from the cowherd, if the original seller claims from the guardian that he should have informed him?
The guardian need not inform the seller, who knows the transaction was mistaken; the trader swears he did not know of the defect and pays the meat value at the cheapest price.
A man deposited hops with another, who had his own hops; the bailee told his brewer to use the bailee's own pile, but the brewer used the deposited hops.
Rav Amram asks how the judges should rule in the hops case.
Let us tell the bailee to go pay for the deposited hops.
The bailee replies that he told the brewer to use his own pile, so he is not at fault.
Let us tell the brewer to go pay for the deposited hops.
The brewer replies that the bailee only gave advice and never insisted he avoid the deposited hops.
If the bailee's hops were closer, the bailee would be liable, since by not objecting he accepted brewing from the deposit; this applies only when he delayed or the piles were equidistant.
What loss is there in the end, since the bailee profits and could repay the owner with beer equal to the hops' value?
Rav Sama son of Rava: the beer turns to vinegar, so its value cannot be taken; Rav Ashi: the hops were mixed with thorns and did not improve the beer.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The conclusion of the prior case: the bailee pays the value of the hops mixed with thorns in accordance with his profit.
Mishna: a depositor's bound money at a money changer may not be used, so loss exempts him, while unbound money may be used and he is liable; a homeowner or storekeeper is treated differently.
Why may the money changer not use bound money, given that people typically bind their money?
Rav Asi, citing Rav Yehuda: bound and sealed money signals the depositor does not want it opened; Rav Mari adds an atypical knot, and his dilemma stands unresolved.
If the money is unbound, the money changer may use it.
Rav Huna says the money changer is liable even if the money was taken by force.
But the mishna teaches lost, which implies he is not liable for money taken by force?
Rabba's distinction: stolen means taken by armed bandits, and lost means the ship sank at sea.
Rav Naḥman says that if it was taken by circumstances beyond his control, the money changer is not liable.
Rava objects: if the money changer is not a borrower, he cannot be a paid bailee, so Rav Naḥman's position leaves him an unpaid bailee exempt.
Rav Naḥman replies he concedes the money changer is a paid bailee because he profits from using the deposit for a profitable purchase.
Rav Naḥman objects to Rav Huna from a Me'ila mishna on the Temple treasurer's money deposited with a money changer.
If the money changer is liable even when robbed, why does the mishna specify the treasurer's liability only for the money changer's spending?
Rav Huna replies that the treasurer is liable even without spending, and the latter clause mirrors the first clause's wording about spending.
Mishna: Beit Shammai hold the misappropriator pays by value at misappropriation or repayment; Beit Hillel by value at removal; Rabbi Akiva by value at the claim.
Rabba's example: a robber of a barrel of wine worth one dinar, now worth four, pays four if he broke it or drank it, and one if it broke by itself.
What is the reason for this difference?
Had the barrel been intact it would be returned as it was, so liability is fixed at the moment of robbery, when it was worth one dinar, as the mishna says for robbers.
Why is the robber liable at the moment of robbery if he did nothing to the barrel now?
Because the value at the moment of the robbery was one dinar, that is the value that governs his payment.
The mishna teaches that Beit Hillel hold payment is by value at the time of removal.
What does the time of removal mean, if it means the time the wine is removed from the world?
If the value decreased before removal, no one says the bailee pays less, since all robbers pay at the time of the robbery.
If the value increased before removal, that is the view of Beit Shammai, not Beit Hillel.

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Obviously Beit Hillel hold the bailee pays by value at removal from the owner's house, which is the time of misappropriation.
Shall we say Rabba's view follows Beit Shammai rather than Beit Hillel?
Rabba could reply that all agree on payment at the time of destruction when the value rose; they disagree only when the value falls.
Rabba explains: Beit Shammai hold misappropriation needs no loss and the robber bears a decrease in his possession; Beit Hillel require loss, so the decrease falls on the owner.
On that explanation, is Rava's view that misappropriation needs no loss a view of Beit Shammai?
The dispute concerns a bailee who moved the barrel to stand on it and reach fledglings from a nest.
They disagree about one who borrows an item without the owner's knowledge.
Beit Shammai hold such a borrower is a robber from the moment he moves the barrel, so the decrease falls on him; Beit Hillel hold he is a borrower liable only upon breakage.
On that explanation, is Rava's view that the borrower is a robber according to the Rabbis a view of Beit Shammai?
Instead, the dispute concerns the enhancement of stolen property: Beit Shammai give it to the owner, Beit Hillel give it to the robber.
A baraita on a robber of a ewe who sheared or sold its fleece and offspring: Rabbi Meir has the robber pay, and Rabbi Yehuda returns the stolen property as is.
The mishna's wording supports this: it says penalized for decrease and increase, not rise and fall in value, showing they dispute fleece and offspring.
Rabbi Akiva says payment is by value at the time of the claim.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva, who concedes where there are witnesses to the misappropriation.
The reason is the verse, to whom it appertains shall he give it on the day of his guilt, which makes him liable from the moment the witnesses saw him.
Rav Oshaya objects that Rabbi Yoḥanan in fact disagrees with Rabbi Akiva even when there are witnesses, since the court, not the witnesses, makes him liable.
Rabbi Zeira sends Rabbi Abba bar Pappa to ask Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva; he reports Rabbi Yoḥanan says always.
What is the meaning of always?
Rav Ashi: Rabbi Yoḥanan meant to exclude the view that the ruling applies only without witnesses.
Alternatively, the ruling excludes the case of returning the barrel to its place and breaking it, and rejects Rabbi Yishmael, requiring the owner's knowledge.
Rava says, contrary to Rabbi Yoḥanan, the halakha follows Beit Hillel.
Mishna: one who intends to misappropriate a deposit and states this before witnesses is liable for later damage per Beit Shammai, but only upon actual misappropriation per Beit Hillel.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: From where is it derived that one is liable for intent to misappropriate a deposit?
The Sages taught: Beit Shammai hold intent counts as action from the verse on every matter of trespass; Beit Hillel require actually sending a hand, citing the verse.
Each school challenges the other: Beit Shammai say the verse already states every matter, and Beit Hillel reply the other verse already states sending a hand.
If so, what is the purpose of the words for every matter of trespass?
It teaches that one's speech to a slave or agent to misappropriate also makes him liable.
Mishna: if one tilts the deposited barrel, he pays only for the wine he took.
Rabba: the mishna applies only if the barrel broke; if the wine soured, he pays for the entire barrel.
What is the reason for this ruling?
His own actions caused the spoiling, so the wine turned rancid because of his opening the cask.
Mishna: if one lifted the barrel and took a quarter-log, he pays for the whole barrel.
Shmuel: the phrase and took means that once he lifted it intending to take wine, he is liable if it breaks.
Shall we say Shmuel holds misappropriation does not require loss?
No: here the bailee prefers all the wine to serve as a base for the quarter-log, so it is as if he took the whole barrel.
If one lifts a purse to take one dinar, does intent count as taking all the coins, or does a purse differ from a single dinar?
The chapter ends and the next chapter, on the deposit, begins.
Mishna: payment of money does not complete a sale of movables; gold acquires silver, but silver does not acquire gold; Rabbi Shimon holds the one holding money has the advantage.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches his son Rabbi Shimon that gold coins acquire silver coins, in line with the mishna.
Rabbi Shimon objects that his father once taught the reverse in his youth, and now teaches differently in his old age.
What did Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi hold in his youth, and what in his old age?
In youth he held gold is currency and silver a commodity, since gold is more valuable; in old age he held silver is the currency and gold the commodity.

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gold coins that do not circulate are a commodity while circulating coins are currency; states the acquisition principle.
Rav Ashi says the halakha should follow the tanna's earlier, youthful teaching.
Supports Rav Ashi from the mishna's later wording that copper acquires silver.
Conditional argument that the mishna's ruling would be pointless unless silver were a commodity relative to gold.
Challenges the proof: why would the mishna need to state a ruling that would be self-evident?
Rejects the challenge: the tanna had to teach the copper-silver case, since copper might seem more readily accepted.
Rabbi Hiyya also holds that gold coins are currency relative to silver.
Rav's loan of gold dinars from Rabbi Hiyya's daughter, and the question of whether repaying them is interest.
Rejects the loan proof: Rav had dinars elsewhere, so the loan was a permitted borrow-and-repay case.
Rava says this tanna also holds that gold coins are currency.
A baraita giving the peruta, issar and dinar values and their practical consequences, supporting that gold is currency.
Asks how the baraita could value silver against gold if gold were a fluctuating commodity.
Concludes from the baraita that the tanna must hold gold coins are currency.
Cites a Ma'aser Sheni mishna as further support for the currency question.
Reports the mishna's Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute on exchanging sela coins for gold, and the Amoraim disagreeing.
One Amora explains the dispute as being about silver and gold currency status.
Beit Hillel's reasoning, and the agreed rule that produce can be exchanged for dinars.
Asks the reason for the difference between sela coins and produce.
Explains the reason by analogy to Beit Hillel's view on silver relative to produce, and Beit Shammai's on gold.
One view holds that the dispute applies even to exchanging produce for dinars.
Asks why, on that view, the dispute was not stated about the basic case of produce.
Answers that the dispute is stated for sela coins too, since Beit Hillel concede gold is a commodity relative to silver.
Concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds one does not desacralize produce with gold dinars.

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States the rule that one may not borrow a dinar and repay with a dinar, due to interest concerns.
Asks which metal the dinar in the rule refers to, and whether silver relative to silver is currency.
Concludes that the case must be a gold dinar repaid with gold dinar.
Asks in whose opinion the ruling stands, Beit Hillel's or Beit Shammai's.
Concludes from this that Rabbi Yochanan holds we do not desacralize produce with gold dinars.
Rejects that inference: Rabbi Yochanan holds we desacralize produce with gold even by Beit Shammai.
Explains that loans differ from tithe desacralization because gold is treated as a commodity in loans.
Cites Ravin's report of Rabbi Yochanan's view, then a Ma'aser Sheni mishna as support.
Challenges the mishna: if copper perutot desacralize, why mention gold coins at all?
Answers that perutot circulate more easily where they are used, so the case differs.
Offers another version: the dispute is whether desacralizing with silver for gold is allowed, per Beit Shammai's reading of the verse.
Beit Hillel read the superfluous word money to include second money.
Everyone agrees that desacralizing produce with dinars is valid, since gold is still first money.
One view says the dispute extends to desacralizing produce with dinars as well.
Challenges that view: if the dispute covers sela-for-dinar, it should cover sela-for-sela too.
Explains that the dispute is stated for sela-for-dinar because sela-for-sela is not in dispute.
Brings a further Ma'aser Sheni mishna, on exchanging silver sela for copper in Jerusalem.
Asks: if silver perutot may be exchanged, do we say gold is not first money for gold?
Rava replies that Jerusalem has a different legal status, from the verse permitting spending money freely there.
Cites the same mishna again, to show all agree second-tithe coins can be exchanged.
States that all agree on the mishna, then gives the alternative formulation of the Rabbi Yochanan dispute.

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beit Shammai's concern: a person might delay going up to Jerusalem while collecting enough silver for a gold dinar.
Beit Hillel reject that decree, and everyone agrees produce can be desacralized since it rots.
One view extends the dispute to exchanging produce for dinars too, to avoid delaying the produce.
Asks why the dispute is phrased as permitted or forbidden if it is only a Rabbinic decree, versus desacralize.
Records the dispute between Rav and Levi on whether money can effect an exchange acquisition.
Asks Rav Pappa's reason for the view that money cannot effect exchange acquisition.
Explains the reason: the value of a coin lies in its minted form, which authorities can cancel.
Cites the mishna that gold coins acquire silver coins, as support for money effecting exchange.
Asks whether the mishna's gold-acquires-silver rule refers to exchange rather than purchase by money.
Rejects that reading: the mishna refers to a standard money purchase, not an exchange of coins.
Objects that the mishna's wording would then be imprecise and should say the gold obligates the seller.
Proposes emending the text to say the gold obligates the other party to give the silver.
Argues from the mishna's latter clause that silver does not acquire gold, which fits a purchase by money.
Brings a baraita on selling silver for gold, where silver acquires only once gold is pulled, supporting purchase by money.
Asks what the nature of the transaction is in the baraita, if not exchange.
Challenges the purchase reading: the phrase wherever they are would be incorrect if this were purchase by money.
Rav Ashi explains wherever they are means exactly as agreed, so the buyer cannot substitute coins of different age.
Rav Pappa holds that even money that cannot effect exchange is acquired by exchange, as with produce.
Raises an objection to Rav Pappa from a baraita about desacralizing produce on a threshing floor without money.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: a person may desacralize produce on coins he has at home, by a set formula.
Explains the artifice is needed only when he has no coins in hand, and transfer to a stranger is preferable.
Objects that if coins are acquired by exchange, he could transfer them with a cloth or land, so the baraita's case would be unnecessary.
Asks why the baraita says he stands on a threshing floor, if he has nothing.
Replies that the threshing floor is not his own, so he has no property at all.
Asks whether the tanna would go to such trouble to teach the case of a man with nothing.
Concludes that the baraita proves money is not acquired by exchange, and that is the halakha.
Recounts that Rav Pappa retracted, transferring a loan's coins by granting acquisition of his threshold.
Ulla, Rav Asi, Rabba bar bar Chana and Rabbi Yochanan all hold that money cannot effect exchange.
Rabbi Abba objects from a baraita about wages paid with coins, which would be a loan if money cannot effect exchange.
Suggests the coins are unminted perutot, a commodity, so they are acquired by exchange and no loan arises.
Ulla agrees the baraita is precise. Rav Ashi explains it as a purchase with money, so it is not a loan.
Brings a mishna from Kiddushin, that items used as monetary value effect exchange, to show a coin can do so.
Rav Yehuda says this is what the mishna is saying, opening his interpretation.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: all appraisable items effect exchange acquisition, with coins excluded because their value is apparent.
Reads the mishna's latter clause, about exchanging animals, as showing the rule concerns movables, not coins.
Asks what the ox-for-cow example means for coins, and how Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman each explain it.
Explains the case as a purchase with money where the second animal is acquired by forgiving the debt.
Asks the reason for Rav Nachman's opinion.
Rav Nachman follows Rabbi Yochanan: money acquires by Torah law, and pulling was decreed lest the seller claim loss by fire.
Asks how Reish Lakish, who holds pulling is in the Torah, can explain the mishna under each of the two views.
Concludes that Reish Lakish must follow Rav Sheshet to explain the mishna.
Cites the mishna that all movables acquire each other, and Reish Lakish's view that this includes coin pouches.
Rav Aha explains the coins as anka and anigera dinars, invalidated by the kingdom or by a province.
Explains both cases must be taught, since each invalidated coin could still be a coin in some sense, so money is not acquired by exchange.
Rabba reports Rav Huna's ruling that a sale for coins in hand, with no price fixed, is complete.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna's ruling: the buyer acquires on receiving the money and the seller has an exploitation claim, as he said sell me.
Asks whether a sale for money with an unfixed price is like an exchange, and whether exchange with one party particular is a sale.
Rav Adda bar Ahava brings a baraita on a cow-for-donkey deal, to resolve the dilemma.
From the baraita, concludes that when parties are particular about value, acquisition waits until each pulls his item.
Rava rejects that inference: all exchanges involve particular parties, and the baraita concerns a donkey-for-cow-and-lamb case with incomplete pulling.
Suggests that Rav Huna holds a coin can effect an exchange, based on his ruling.
Rejects the suggestion: Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yochanan, money acquires by Torah law, and the decree does not apply here.
Asks with what vessel one effects the symbolic exchange in the transaction.
Rav says the buyer's vessel is used, Levi says the seller's vessel, each with a reason.
Objects to Levi from Kiddushin: a cloak transferring land would contradict the rule that unguaranteed property is acquired with guaranteed.
Rava replies that a cloak's transfer leads to the land's transfer through the owner's resolve, not simultaneously.
Cites verses in Ruth and Leviticus on the shoe and substitution, to show the tanna'im's dispute on sale and exchange.
Asks who gave the shoe to whom in the verse.
Rabbi Yehuda says the redeemer gave the shoe to Boaz, and the dispute parallels Rav and Levi.
A baraita says a symbolic exchange works with any vessel, and Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet differ on produce.
Asks the reason for Rav Nachman's opinion.
Derives from the verse 'his shoe' that only vessels, shoe-like items, can effect the symbolic exchange.
Asks the reason for Rav Sheshet's opinion.
Derives from 'to confirm all matters' that any item can effect the symbolic exchange.
Objects that each view also has a verse it must explain away, so neither reading is decisive.
Rav Sheshet explains that 'his shoe' excludes half a pomegranate or nut, which are not complete items.
Asks which opinion documents follow in saying the item is acquired by a fit vessel.
Explains the term 'with a vessel' excludes Rav Sheshet's view, and 'fit' excludes Shmuel's view.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the verse's wording excludes Levi's view and shows the vessel is given to acquire, not to transfer.
Rav Pappa, Rav Zevid and Rav Ashi each give a different reading of the terms in the verse.
Mishna: when one takes an asimon, the other party acquires the minted coin.
Asks what an asimon is.
Rav says an asimon is a token given at the bathhouse, paid for later.
Objects from a baraita that the bathhouse token is not an asimon, and a rival baraita with Rabbi Dosa seems to contradict it.
Rabbi Yochanan takes the opposite line, which is his usual reasoning.
Asks what an asimon is, on Rabbi Yochanan's reading.
An asimon is an unimprinted blank; Rabbi Dosa, Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute the desacralizing coin.
Explains the mishna's example, and that money acquires by Torah law but pulling was decreed against a fire loss.
Asks why such a decree was needed, since the buyer would be reimbursed for a fire.
Says the decree targets a fire outside anyone's liability, since the seller will rescue goods still his.
Reish Lakish holds pulling acquires by explicit Torah law, not only by decree.
Asks the reason for Reish Lakish's view.
Derives it from the verse in Leviticus about acquiring from a colleague's hand, meaning by pulling.
Rabbi Yochanan replies the phrase excludes land from exploitation, not that pulling acquires.
Reish Lakish agrees to that, and says the words or acquire would be superfluous unless pulling is taught.
Asks what Rabbi Yochanan derives from the phrase or acquire.
Rabbi Yochanan derives that the buyer may not exploit the seller, and Reish Lakish derives two rules from one phrase.
Mishna of Rabbi Shimon: whoever has the money has the advantage, so the seller may retract.
Asks why the buyer cannot also retract, if money does not acquire, by Rabbi Yochanan's account.
Reish Lakish replies he held the view of the Rabbis, not of Rabbi Shimon.
Asks how Rabbi Yochanan's view differs from the Rabbis' view on Rabbi Shimon's position.
Rav Chisda's ruling that pulling was instituted for buyers as well is the difference, which the Rabbis accept.
Cites the mishna of the generation of the flood, and argues from it that money acquires movables.
Explains the curse applies because the buyer reneged on a verbal commitment, not on a completed acquisition.
Asks whether one who reneged on a commitment is cursed, citing a baraita.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon: a garment is acquired by a gold dinar, but a dinar is not acquired by a garment, and this is the halakha.
The Sages: whoever reneges after pulling a gold dinar is cursed, and one who only negotiates is not bound.
Rava: the Sages are displeased with a reneger, but he is cursed only if money accompanied the commitment.
Rava brings the verse in Leviticus on deposit, pledge and oppression, to support Reish Lakish that pulling is needed.
Rav Pappa objects that the verse's omission of oppression suffices, and a pledge needs no pulling for the rule.
Rava replies the case is workers who took the item and deposited it back, so an actual item is denied.
Objects that this case is already a deposit in the verse, so it adds nothing new.
Asks: if so, why not have the verse repeat the pledge case as well?
If the verse repeated pledge, it would not decide the dispute, so its omission supports Reish Lakish.
Objects from a baraita of Rabbi Shimon that the verse does include a pledge, so the omission proves nothing.
Cites a baraita on consecrated money paid to a bathhouse attendant, and Rav's inference that pulling is needed for acquisition.
Objects from a baraita on consecrated money paid to a barber, who must pull the tools, which seems to contradict Rav's inference.
Gives a second baraita on paying a barber, sailor or craftsman, which is liable only once the item is pulled.
Resolves the contradiction: the first baraita concerns a gentile barber, the second a Jewish barber.
Rav Nachman holds, following Rabbi Yochanan, that by Torah law giving money effects acquisition.
Levi finds a baraita on paying a wholesaler as first payment for produce, liable before pulling, which supports that view.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita seems to contradict Reish Lakish's view on acquisition by money.
Replies that the baraita follows Rabbi Shimon, not the Rabbis.
Repeats the Sages' curse on a reneger, and the amoraic dispute between Abaye and Rava on informing or cursing him.
Abaye cites the verse forbidding cursing a ruler, and Rava cites the verse's wording among your people, and then the salt incident.
Objects that the incident shows the buyer only needed to be informed, and Rabbi Chiyya already knew the halakha.
Rejects that: the alternative is cursing, which Rabbi Chiyya would not accept as a Sages' curse.
Explains the incident was a down payment, and the dispute is whether it acquires its value or the whole amount.

Mishna: the accepted depreciation of a sela, as set by Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon.

Rav Pappa: the case is one of building stones delivered to the treasurer, following Shmuel that one builds before consecrating.
Mishna: such items carry no double payment, and so on.
Baraita derives from the verse on a pledge that a thing of movable value with a body is included, excluding land, slaves, deeds, and consecrated items.
Explains that the reason for no fourfold or fivefold payment is that the verse states those amounts.
A paid guard who is unpaid is not sworn, citing the Mishna.
Baraita on the verse about money or vessels given for safekeeping derives the same exclusions, including consecrated property.
Paid guard does not pay.
Baraita on the verse about giving a donkey, ox, or sheep for safekeeping derives the same exclusions and the consecrated category.
An unpaid guard is not sworn, as stated in the Mishna.
Objects with a baraita on townspeople who sent their shekels and they were stolen, on whether terumah was already set aside.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Those who take the oath to the treasurers, or the townspeople if not, and others pay in their place; the shekels are not carried over.
Shmuel: the case is one of a paid guard who swears to claim his wage, so the oath should be to the townspeople.
Rabbah: the townspeople swear in the presence of the treasurers, so they are not suspected or called negligent.
Objects that a paid guard is liable for theft and loss, so here too the wage should be lost, even if not paid.
Rabbah replies: the cases are robbery by armed bandits, or a ship sunk at sea.
R' Yohanan: this is R' Shimon's view, that consecrated property with liability has overreaching and an oath applies.
Baraita: one sets aside terumah on what is lost, what is collected, and what is yet to be collected.
R' Elazar: the oath is a rabbinic enactment so that people do not treat consecrated items lightly.
A paid guard does not pay.
Rav Yosef bar Hama objects to Rabbah with a baraita on hiring a worker to guard a cow, child, or produce.
Asks what the Mishna's ruling means and whether the worker who receives no sabbath wage is liable.
Rav Sheshet and R' Yohanan: the ruling applies where he acquired the item from his hand.
R' Shimon says consecrated items with liability have overreaching and oath, while those without liability do not.
A tanna recites before R' Yitzhak bar Abba on the parallels for consecrated property, and R' Yitzhak responds.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the view: consecrated items with liability are included by the verse on the fifth, while those without liability are excluded.
R' Yehuda: a Torah scroll, pearl, and animal also have no overreaching.
Baraita gives R' Yehuda's reasons and R' Yehuda ben Beteira's view on horses and weapons in war, citing life.
Mishna: just as there is overreaching in buying and selling, there is also verbal wronging, such as reminding a repentant person of his past.
Baraita: the verse forbidding wronging one another refers to verbal wronging, while monetary wronging is taught separately.
Examples of verbal wronging: a repentant person, a convert, a stranger learning Torah; one should not reproach them.
Cites Job's friends' words to show how reproaching someone in trouble is wrong, as a model for speech.
Do not send a buyer to a seller who you know never sold grain, as this is verbal wronging.
R' Yehuda: one should not fix one's eyes on a purchase when one lacks the money, since the matter is in the heart.
R' Yohanan in the name of R' Shimon bar Yochai: verbal wronging is greater than monetary wronging, since the fear of God is stated for it.
R' Elazar: one is bodily and the other monetary; R' Shmuel bar Nahmani: one can be restored and the other cannot.
A tanna recites before Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak that whitening a neighbor's face in public is like shedding blood.
Rav Dimi answers that he sees the man blush and turn pale, showing the shame of public embarrassment.
Abaye asks how they are careful; Rav Dimi replies that one whitens faces in public, and the wording of R' Hanina is corrected.
Lists those who go down to Gehenna and do not come up, including adultery and publicly whitening a neighbor's face.
Rava bar bar Hana reports R' Yohanan's teaching.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Better for a person to risk doubtful adultery than to publicly embarrass his neighbor.
Raba's exegesis of a psalm verse on mourners who tore their clothes without shedding blood, to ground the rule.
David speaks before God: even those who study purity laws call the adulterer's punishment strangling, while David says it is worse to embarrass publicly.
One who commits adultery has a share in the world to come, but one who publicly whitens a neighbor's face does not.
Attributes the saying about whitening a neighbor's face to several sages, in different versions.
Restates the saying that it is better to throw oneself into a furnace than to whiten a neighbor's face publicly.
Cites Tamar's verse, where she sends word to her father-in-law without shaming Judah in public.
Cites the verse forbidding wronging one another, applied to one who learns Torah with you.
Rav: one should be careful about wronging one's wife, since her tears come easily and her wronging is near.
R' Elazar: since the Temple was destroyed, the gates of prayer are locked, as the verse says.
Yet the gates of tears are not locked, as the psalm asks God to hear the prayer and the cry.
Rav: whoever follows his wife's counsel falls into Gehenna, citing the verse about Ahab.
Rav Papa objects to Abaye: people say a wife who bends and whispers; resolved by distinguishing kinds of matters.
Rav Hisda: all gates are locked except the gates of wronging.
Cites Amos's verse on the Lord standing by a wall with a plumb line, and R' Elazar's view that all is punished through an agent except wronging.
R' Abahu: three things do not let the curtain stay closed before them: wronging, theft, and idolatry, each with a verse.
Rav Yehuda: one should be careful with grain in one's house, since quarrels arise only over grain, citing a psalm.
Rav Papa: the saying applies to someone who pays with barley and brings a quarrel into the house.
Rav Hiyya bar Papa: one should be careful about grain, citing the verses in Judges on Israel's need and Midian.
One should honor one's wife, since blessing dwells in one's home only for the sake of one's wife, citing Abram's verse.
Raba tells the Mahoza people to honor their wives so that they become rich.
Mishna: where one cut the links and placed sand between them, R' Elazar deems it clean and the Sages impure.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates the oven of Akhnai, which the Sages declared impure, and that R' Eliezer's replies were all rejected.
R' Eliezer proves his view from a carob tree that was uprooted, but the Sages say a tree cannot prove a halakha.
R' Eliezer proves his view from a water channel, which flowed backward.
The Sages reject the water-channel proof as well: one cannot bring a proof from a water channel.
R' Eliezer proves his view from the walls of the study house, which leaned as if to fall.
R' Yehoshua rebukes them: when Sages argue, why interfere? The walls neither fell for his honor nor stood for R' Eliezer's.
R' Eliezer proves his view from heaven, asking for a sign from heaven.
A heavenly voice declares that the halakha follows R' Eliezer everywhere.
R' Yehoshua stands and cites the verse that the Torah is not in heaven, upholding the Sages' view.
R' Yirmiya explains that since the Torah was given at Sinai, one follows the majority, citing the verse.
Narrates that God laughed and said His children had defeated Him; R' Eliezer's purities were burned and he was excommunicated.
Asks who will go to inform R' Eliezer; R' Akiva volunteers, fearing an unfit person would destroy the world.
R' Akiva dressed in black and sat four cubits away from R' Eliezer.
R' Eliezer asks what day it is; R' Akiva answers; R' Eliezer weeps and the world loses a third of its olives, wheat, and barley.
Some say even dough in a woman's hands is affected; R' Eliezer was burned wherever he cast his eyes that day.
Rabban Gamaliel's ship was threatened by a wave; R' Eliezer ben Hyrcanus prayed that the quarrels not multiply in Israel.
The sea calmed; R' Eliezer's sister-in-law, Rabban Gamaliel's sister, stopped letting him fall on his face after that day.
A poor man came to the gate; the woman gave him bread, found him dead, and was told she had killed her brother.
Rabban Gamaliel's household was told by his wife that all gates are locked except the gates of wronging, per tradition.
Baraita: one who wrongs a convert transgresses three prohibitions, and one who oppresses him transgresses two.
Asks why wronging has three verses while oppressing has two.
Cites the verses forbidding wronging a convert, which includes him as a neighbor.
Cites the three verses on oppressing, concluding that wronging and oppressing each have three prohibitions.
R' Eliezer the Elder: the Torah warned about converts in thirty-six or thirty-six places because their inclinations are evil.
R' Natan: do not say to your neighbor the blemish you have; the saying applies to one with a stick in his eye.
Mishna: fruits are not mixed with fruits, even new with new.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one may not mix new with old, though one may give a merchant his lees; wine may be mixed only in limited cases.
Mishna: water mixed into wine may not be sold in a shop without notice, and a merchant may pour water in custom.
Baraita: one may not mix new wine with four-year-old wine, or old with three-year-old, because people prefer to keep them.
Repeats the Mishna that mixing wine is permitted but harms its quality.
R' Elazar, Rav Nahman, Rav Papa and Rav Aha son of Rav Ika explain which practice is allowed, citing R' Aha's view.
Mishna: one may not mix wine lees into wine, but one may give him his lees.
Objects: the first clause forbids mixing at all, so what does giving him his lees mean? The second clause implies otherwise.
Rav Yehuda explains: one may not mix yesterday's lees into today's wine, but may give him his lees.
Baraita of R' Yehuda: one who pours wine for a friend may not mix yesterday's into today's, but may mix like with like.
Mishna: water mixed into wine may not be sold in a shop unless he gives notice.
Raba's wine was brought from a shop and tasted watered; Abaye objects that the Mishna says not to a merchant even with notice.
The custom: where they pour water into wine, they may do so by half, third, or quarter; Rav says this applies to the vats.
Mishna: R' Yehuda forbids giving children nuts and parched grain; the Sages permit it, and beans are not to be mixed.
The Sages agree a man should not be cheated, but the swindler is like one who steals the eye; a person, animal, or utensils are not defrauded.
Asks the reasoning of the Rabbis, illustrated by a parable about nuts and oil.
Asks what the Rabbis' reason is for not reducing the measure.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the Sages permit mixing beans because it is evident; identifies the view of R' Aha who permits what is visible.
Baraita on animals and meat: one may not whip an animal or blow into its entrails; the Amoraim gloss the verbs with practices.
Objects that the Mishna forbids handling a person, an animal, or utensils, which seems to contradict the permitted practices.
Resolves the conflict: the forbidden case is new versus the permitted case of old, illustrated by a servant's dyed hair and beard.
Anecdote: Raba's sale; a servant asks Rav Pappa for water and then dyes his hair, citing Proverbs on the righteous escaping trouble.
Mishna defines neshekh and tarbit: lending a sela for two sela-worth of wheat, and selling wheat for wine with a pledge.
Asks why the Mishna leaves Torah-law interest aside, since neshekh and tarbit are one matter, and whether neshekh can exist without tarbit.
Gives an example of neshekh without tarbit: a lender charges a dinar's interest that is not deducted at the time of the loan.
Gives further cases of tarbit without neshekh, depending on whether the accrual happens before or after the loan.
Asks about tarbit without neshekh, using the example of lending a hundred for a hundred and twenty.
Raba answers: one cannot find neshekh without tarbit, nor the reverse, as the verse does not divide them.
Raba concludes that the verse was not meant to split them, so one who transgresses both violates two prohibitions.
Baraita: the verse forbids giving money with interest or usury, and derives that neshekh applies to food and tarbit applies to money.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Derives from the verses on lending with interest that the prohibition covers all things, not only money or food.
Ravina explains why two separate verses are needed: one for interest on money and one for food.
Objects that the tanna's teaching would make the verse unnecessary, since a gezera shava already covers the matter.
Raba explains why separate prohibitions are written: one for interest, one for robbery, one for overreaching, each derived by analogy.
Works out a series of a fortiori inferences to show which prohibitions can be derived from one another.
Objects to the inference that it can be refuted by the difference between the cases.
Resolves that the cases are not parallel, and the common element is that one who robs the other is the one to be compared.
Asks whether a robbery prohibition is needed, since withholding a worker's wage is explicitly written.
Cites the verse forbidding oppression of a poor hired worker, which is subject to two prohibitions, as a matter learned from its context.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yimar asks Rav Ashi why the verse on theft is needed; answer: one who hides weights in salt is committing outright robbery.
Baraita on the verse about just measures, with an a fortiori argument from the measure of a seah to the log.
Raba: why does the verse mention the Exodus with interest, with fringes, and with weights, each separately?
God says He distinguished in Egypt between the drop of the firstborn and the drop not; He will punish those who lend with interest and hide weights.
Rav Hanina tells Ravina that God will punish one who mixes the entrails of fish, which are impure, into pure ones and sells them to Israel.
Ravina asks what distinguishes the raising up mentioned here.
Explains that God brought Israel out of Egypt for this one matter, the impurity of creeping things, and that it is great.
Asks whether the cases of selling wheat for gold are not in fact interest.
R' Abahu and Raba: from here to the Torah's prohibition, and from here on it is rabbinic.
Cites the verse in Job on the wicked who prepare and the righteous who wear it, to support that only fixed interest is at issue.
R' Elazar: fixed interest is enforced by judges, but the accrued interest is not enforced by judges.
R' Yohanan: even fixed interest is not enforced by judges.
R' Yitzhak explains R' Yohanan's view from the verse in Ezekiel on one who lends with interest, that he is given to death, not to repayment.
R' Ada bar Ahava: the verse in Leviticus on not taking interest is given for awe, not for repayment.
Raba derives from the verse in Ezekiel that usurers are like murderers, who are not given to repayment.
R' Natan bar Yitzhak asks the reasoning of R' Elazar, citing a verse.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites the verse 'your brother shall live with you' and the baraita of two travelers with one jug: the one's life comes first, per R' Akiva.
Objects with a baraita: heirs who inherit interest money need not return it, though the father would have to return it.
Explains the wording: the later clause about the father's property is taught in the same way, with the reason of honoring the father.
Cites the verse forbidding cursing a leader, applied by R' Pinchas in Raba's name to one who has repented.
Asks what is required if the robber repented but died before fully returning the property.
Objects with a baraita: robbers and usurers return even after collection; the Gemara asks whether 'robbers' means something else.
It is a tannaitic dispute: R' Nehemiah and R' Eliezer ben Yaakov exempt the lender and guarantor, since there is an 'arise and do' obligation.
Asks what 'arise and do' means, and whether it implies the earlier Tanna holds they cannot be returned.
Asks what the Tanna holds: whether a bond that is to be collected counts as collected.
The Gemara concludes it is a matter of appraisal, citing the Mishna listing transgressors: lender, borrower, guarantor, and witnesses.
Explains that the case of witnesses shows that the matter is one of appraisal.
Rav Safra: what can be collected by their laws is collected from creditor to creditor, and vice versa, by our laws.
Abaye objects to Rav Yosef that this is a rule, and cites a pledge taken without a claim; Ravina objects to Rav Ashi.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains Rav Safra's rule: what is collected by their laws is collected by ours, which applies to fixed interest and earlier interest.
Mishna example: buying wheat for a dinar of gold per kor, and similarly for produce.
Asks: does one not then have wine? What is the ruling?
Objects with a baraita: one does not fix prices on produce until the market price has risen.
Rabbah: the Mishna deals with a case where the creditor is pressing for repayment in cash.
Baraita example: a creditor demands a mina, offered wheat at the current price for twelve months, which is forbidden as if it were interest.
Abaye asks why the rule is stated only when one has no wheat, and not also when he has it.
The Mishna is taught as R' Safra taught, in the interest case of the school of R' Hiyya.
Baraita: some things are permitted and forbidden because of the trick of interest: lend a mina, buy back wheat at a lower price.
Same case with thirty dinars: the lender sells back the wheat for a gold dinar, a trick that is forbidden.
Asks whether the case is interest if the borrower has wine, or if he takes coins that look like interest.
Raba replies: the wording should be 'the price of your wheat that you made for me', so it is a sale of the actual wheat.
Objects that the Mishna says a gold dinar per kor, but Raba says that when Rabbi Oshaya went out, he could not follow.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Recites R' Oshaya's version of the case: a creditor is offered wheat, wine, or oil at the current price for later delivery, forbidden if no one has it.
Asks what the word took means in the case of a loan.
Raba infers from R' Oshaya that a loan can be secured on produce, and that one who has the goods is not like one who has not.
R' Yannai's view: the same applies to produce and to its value, while Rav holds that one may make an agreement on produce but not on money.
Objects with a baraita: the entire case is permitted if he has it.
Rav Huna and Shmuel explain: the baraita is about a one-sided interest arrangement, following R' Yehuda's view.
Baraita: one who lent a mina and had a field sold to him; permitted if the seller eats the produce, forbidden if the buyer does; R' Yehuda permits both.
R' Yehuda tells the story of Bitos ben Zonin, whose field was sold on R' Elazar ben Azariah's ruling, with the seller eating the produce.
Abaye says the difference is one-sided interest, while Raba says it is interest on condition of return, citing R' Yannai's view.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States the principle: one may say the value is what counts, or that the goods count, and one may fix a price on the market rate.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua object to Raba with a baraita: all is permitted if he has it, forbidden if not.
Raba answers: there the case is a loan, here it is a sale.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain why the market rate may be fixed even without the goods: the lender benefits by having it at hand.
Abaye objects to Rav Yosef: then one may borrow a seah for a seah; the reply is that there it is a loan, here a sale.
Adda bar Abba asks Raba; Rav Ashi replies that people's coins are used to pay the agent's wages.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef analyze a lender's position: whether a creditor who lends coins to a buyer acquires them, or is merely guaranteed.
Rav Ashi: a creditor who is lent money does not owe if the buyer intended it; the case of a buyer who trusts the seller.
Rav Nahman's rule: whoever takes benefit from a loan has interest prohibited.
Rav Nahman: a lender who gives money for a fixed sum and has no further claim is forbidden, which is obvious.
Clarifies that the case is one where the borrower has standing in town; the loan is like not having it when collection is missing.
Rav Nahman: one who lends and later finds an overpayment must return it if the error was not intentional; otherwise it is a gift.
Asks what an error of wisdom is, as Rav Aha son of Rav Yosef answers.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Aha son of Raba asks Rav Ashi: if a person is strong and will not give a gift, what is the case? Perhaps he stole and offset it in the account.
Cites a baraita: one who robs his fellow and offsets it in an account is exempt.
Rav Ashi replies: perhaps another person stole and was offset in the account; the case is of one who comes and settles.
Rav Kahana recounts Rav's teaching on lending to a garden: when one lends and is repaid by increase, the lender may sell at the market price.
Asks whether the increase that comes automatically is permitted, and the Gemara resolves it.
Baraita on one who goes to milk goats, shear sheep, and sell honey: he may sell at the rate of the market for each.
If he fixes the price in advance for each, it is forbidden, even if the increase comes automatically.
Some say Raba holds that when the increase comes automatically it is permitted, as it is not at the time he has it.
Objects that a baraita forbids the case of 'so and so', and distinguishes the case where the other person takes the item.
Abaye permits one to say to a friend: here are four zuz for a jar of wine, and if it breaks it is at your risk.
Rav Sharvia objects to Abaye.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Raba's principle: one who takes on the work of a cheap item is near to profit and far from loss, so it is near to both.
Mishna: one who lends to another may not live in his courtyard for free, nor rent from him for less, because that is interest.
Rav Yosef bar Meniumi reports Rav Nahman: one who lives in a neighbor's courtyard without consent owes no rent, but if he borrowed and lives there, he owes rent.
Asks what the Gemara adds, since the Mishna already states the rule.
Explains that the Mishna's rule applies to a courtyard that rents out and a person who is accustomed to renting, not to an unrented yard.
Alternative version of Rav Nahman's ruling: one who lent and lives in the courtyard owes rent, but one who was lent to does not.
The reason: since at the start the lender did not lend with that intent, it is not interest.
Rav Yosef bar Hama is strict: people who lend money and do work with it, he holds them to rent.
Raba asks why he rules so; Rav Yosef replies that Rav Nahman's view applies; Raba suggests Rav Nahman meant a specific case of a worker.
Rav Yosef bar Hama's view is supported by Rav: one who forces his neighbor's servant to work for him is exempt.

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Notes that these rules apply where no money was lent; where money was lent, it appears as interest, as Rav Nahman's ruling shows.
Abaye's example: one lends four zuz with a grain price arrangement, so the lender's gain is counted as interest and must be deducted.
Raba rules that five are deducted, since the original was in the form of interest.
Abaye's ruling: for four zuz lent with a cloak given in return, deduct four but not the cloak.
Raba explains: the cloak is deducted so that it cannot be said the cloak covering is merely a cloak, when it is interest.
Raba's case: one lends twelve zuz and rents a courtyard for ten, then rents it back at twelve; the twelve are deducted.
Rav Aha of Difti objects to Ravina: the renter should be paid as the wage is; this is what the worker claimed and accepted.
Mishna: one may increase the rent but not the price of sale; a rent of ten silver per year for a courtyard is permitted, but a field sold for a thousand zuz is forbidden.
Asks why the first clause is different from the second.
Rabbah and Rav Yosef explain: wages are paid only at the end, so withholding them is loss; the later clause concerns a sale that is already final.
Raba: the Sages discussed this matter and derived it from the verse on a hired worker, year by year, that this year's wages are paid only in another year.
If the sale is for twelve mina at the threshing floor, it is forbidden.
Rami bar Hama objects to Rav Nahman with the Mishna's wording of a threshing-floor sale; Abaye distinguishes that one the case was ended.
Rav Papa answers that his own field is permitted; the difference is whether the matter was ended at the outset.
Explains the reason: the worker does not lose money; the seller is not short of money, and performs the matter with the buyer.
Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi asks Rav Papa what he sees in following his own interest, and whether the buyer would have paid cash.
Rav Hama: the rule is clear for his field; the reason is that the buyers prefer to be lit in his place and not go elsewhere.

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rules as Rav Hama, as R' Elazar, and as R' Yannai: what counts is the value or the item itself, as the case requires.
Mishna: one who sells a field and receives part of the price, or lends on his field with a deadline of three years, and Ben Zonin acted on the Sages' ruling.
Reconciles Rav Huna's view that the seller eats the produce with Rav Anan's view that it is split three ways, by R' Ilai's and R' Yohanan's readings.
Rav Safra's teaching in the school of R' Hiyya lists four cases: both permitted, both forbidden, seller permitted, and buyer permitted.
Raba answers that both are permitted when the lender says the title passes according to the amount of his money.
Gives the cases where the title passes now or upon payment, with and without a loan, and which party is permitted.
Asks which Tanna holds that both are forbidden.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua rules not as R' Yehuda, since if R' Yehuda held one-sided interest is permitted, the case would differ.
Rav Huna applies the same reasoning to a pledged house or field, where the lender is told he cannot sell except to him at that price.
Sold a house and field, and said: when I have money, return it to me, forbidden; when you have money, I will return it to you, permitted.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua repeats that the rule is not R' Yehuda's, since on R' Yehuda's view one-sided interest would be permitted.
Raba distinguishes: the first clause is where the lender did not speak of his own intent, the second where he did.
Anecdote: a man sold land to a friend without warranty; when the friend was upset, the seller said it is a good bargain, and Ameimar concurred.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi tells Ammi the reason: the buyer wants to attach a condition, but the Mishna speaks of the seller; the statement is a mere formality.
Anecdote of a dying man who wrote a bill of divorce for his wife; Rav Aha of Difti asks whether a condition can be placed in the document.
Rav Huna: if he lends on his field, the sale is complete at the time of paying the money; Rav Nahman says it is complete even after.
Account of Rav Yehuda tearing up the document of the exilarch, and Rav Nahman's ruling that even at the time of payment nothing is acquired.
Raba objects to Rav Nahman with the case: if you do not give me within three years, it is mine; Rav Nahman says it is a conditional promise, and Raba finds a difficulty.
The Mishna is according to R' Yosei, who holds that a conditional promise is valid.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Offers an alternative: the Nehardeans report Rav Nahman's view that a conditional promise is valid when the time arrives, not before.
Rav Nahman's view as heard by the Gemara: the sale is valid only at the time set, and not before, because the speaker wished to soften the statement.
Explains why the speaker says it takes effect, since he thinks that when the time comes the other will not come to claim it.
Rav Papa: a conditional promise is sometimes valid and sometimes not, depending on the case, such as one who drinks beer and gives coins.
Rav Aha of Difti objects to Ravina that the borrower may be drinking to annoy the lender; Ravina replies that if he cares about the money it is valid.
Rav Aha of Difti objects again: perhaps he wants to prevent the land from being lost; Rav Papa replies that if he cares about the land it is valid.
Rav Papa: even though the Sages say a conditional promise is not valid, it is a pledge for collection.
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan objects to Rav Papa: does he say it is valid for collection?
Mar Zutra son of Rav Mari objects to Ravina: if the creditor can collect from him, the conditional promise is valid, so it is a pledge.
Explains the pledge that Rav Papa spoke of: the creditor is told the debt will be paid only from this property.
Anecdote: a man sold land to a friend with warranty; if the claimant takes it, the buyer will give him better land, and the claimant later seized it from him.
Rav Papa thought to say the case is about better land, which is the claimed property.
Rav Aha of Difti tells Ravina to say: when I said I would give you, I meant the good land still existing, and the good land is now in its place.
Rav Bar Shava borrowed from Rav Kahana; Rav Papa: a conditional promise is not valid for land, but for wine, which is for sale, it is like money.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua reports Rabbah: whatever is not valid without the condition is invalid.
Rav Nahman: since the Sages said a conditional promise is not valid, the land returns and the fruits too, implying he holds that a mistaken waiver is not a waiver.
Objects with a parallel dispute: one who sold date-palm produce to another; Rav Huna says he may retract before it comes into being, Rav Nahman says also after.
Rav Nahman concedes that if the buyer ate, the seller cannot collect; there it is a sale, and here it is a loan.
Raba's statement on the distinction.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara recounts an objection to Rav Nahman about overreaching and waiver of a childless wife, where waiver by mistake is not valid.
Objects with a Mishna on a woman who refuses, a second wife, and a childless wife, who receive no ketubah or maintenance.
Anecdote of a woman who told a man to buy land for her; he bought it and she asked him to return the money, and he said you are a fool.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna: if a man says you are a fool, a brother lends the money, and the land returns with its fruits.
Asks whether the interest is fixed interest, which is enforced by judges, or accrued interest, which is not.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna and Raba: it is reasonable that accrued interest is not enforced by judges.
Abaye objects to Rabbah: why is a pledged house not collected? The reason is that the term was not set.
Rav Pappi says Ravina acted on the case, counting and taking the fruits, unlike Rabbah bar Rav Huna.
Mar son of Rav Yosef reports Raba: where a pledge is set against the sum, one collects up to the sum; if more, one does not take it, nor credit one document against another.
Rav Ashi: now that you say one does not collect more than the sum, one also does not collect the sum without money.
Explains that the removal without money is taking out interest, and accrued interest is not enforced by judges.
Rav Ashi ruled in the case of minor orphans.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Raba's ruling, from Raba bar Rav Yosef: a creditor holding a pledge in a place where it is taken may eat only with a deduction, and a scholar only with a deduction.
Asks what the dispute is if one who permits the quitzuta has no other way.
Rav Aha and Ravina dispute whether quitzuta is permitted, one saying yes and one saying no.
Explains the example of quitzuta: one says he will eat for five years without deduction and then pay, and the views differ.
Asks which view forbids the second case and how it could be permitted, as in a pledge where the deed states the terms.
