Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua: in a place where it is taken, the creditor collects from it, and the firstborn takes double, but the seventh year releases it.
Mar Zutra reports Rav Pappa: in a place where it is taken, one takes it even from fallen dates, and if the buyer took it by the scraps, he acquires it.
Asks whether a creditor who says he will not take it may do so, and whether he needs to acquire it from the owner.
Rav Pappa says he need not acquire it; Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi says he does; the halakha is that he must acquire it.
Ravina says he may eat it, while Mar Zutra says he may not; the halakha is that he may not eat.
Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi do not eat from the pledge with a deduction.
Ravina eats with a deduction; Mar Zutra asks why one who eats with a deduction is like an inherited field.
Explains that the inherited field is different, since the Torah says what it says despite the large produce it yields.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the distinction: one who forbids treats the field as consecrated or redemption, while here it is a loan that looks like interest.
Rav Ashi reports the elders of the town: a pledge without a stated term matters for whether the owner may eat the produce for a year.
Rav Ashi reports the elders: the question is whether a pledge that was left there matters for a legal claim.
Raba rules: the halakha follows neither the Pappunai, nor the Mehoznai, nor the Narshai; a deed written for a stated increase is not valid.
Mar bar Amemar asks Rav Ashi: granted where the document is held by the owner, but what if it fell before orphans?
Cites the Ecclesiastes verse about an error that comes from the ruler, and mentions Ameimar's death.
Ameimar and the Narshai: a field pledged to a person and leased back; the claim is not a serious matter.
Mishna: one may not set a shopkeeper up for half the profit, nor give money to buy produce for half the profit, unless he is paid his wage as a worker.
Mishna: one may not set up hens or appraise calves for half the profit, but one may take calves and foals for half the profit and raise them until they are three, and a donkey until it carries.
A tanna teaches: like an idle worker; asks what the phrase like an idle worker means.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye explains why the Mishna needs both cases: a shopkeeper with little work is paid like an idle worker, while buying produce for profit is more work.
A mnemonic note on how much wage goats and hens yield.
Baraita on how much a worker is paid: R' Meir, R' Yehuda, and R' Shimon ben Yohai disagree on the wage for a hired laborer.
Baraita: one may not appraise goats, sheep, or anything that does not work and eat; R' Yosei ben R' Yehuda permits appraisal where they produce.
Explains that the first Tanna's view on milk and wool is agreed; they differ on newborn animals, where the first Tanna follows R' Shimon ben Yohai.
R' Yosei ben R' Yehuda follows his father, who holds the worker is paid even for a small amount.
Baraita on a woman who lends a hen for two chicks: R' Yehuda permits, R' Shimon forbids; R' Yehuda holds no wage for effort is owed.
Baraita: where the custom is to pay a porter's wage for money, one follows the local custom and does not change it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: one appraises a calf with its mother and a foal with its mother, even where the custom is to pay the porter's wage; he holds no wage owed for effort.
Rav Nahman rules: the halakha follows R' Yehuda, the halakha follows R' Yosei ben R' Yehuda, and the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
Raba evaluates a deed of Rav Ilish's sons where half is for hire and half for loss: it is not forbidden, since either way the loss can be computed.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Kahana recounts a ruling heard before Rav Zvid of Neharda about a partner who worked with a worker's share in the wage.
Rav Nahman says the halakha follows R' Yehuda, and Rav Nahman answers that it is a shita, not a ruling; the reasoning supports R' Yehuda's lenient view.
Rav holds that if he gives a third of the wage he is permitted; Shmuel says if he cannot find work, he should be paid a dinar.
Objects that Rav says one does not fix a dinar for him, yet Rav said a third is permitted, which seems contradictory.
Resolves: Rav's statement refers to one who owns an animal himself, as people say one ties a bull to the bull.
R' Elazar of Hagronya bought an animal, gave it to his tenant, and divided the profit; his wife sought a share of his partnership.
Dialogue: the tenant asks to divide the profit as before; the partner says it would look like interest; the sharing is partnership.
Explains the proverb that a tenant binds himself to the landowner to bring him a shepherd.
Baraita on how long one must care for another's animal: Sumchus holds eighteen months for a donkey and twenty-four for a horse.
Explains that the care varies year to year, so the division is by each year's care.
Baraita: one must care for a calf for thirty days when young and fifty days when grown; R' Yosei says three months for a young animal, after which one takes half.
Rav Mansia bar Gada took half of his own and a half of his partner's share.
Abaye asks who gave the claimant a share, and objects that the place where it is customary to rear animals is a different matter.
Rav Pappa asks what difference it makes, and whether the partner's claim counts in the case of a sale of wine.
Rav Nahman: the money is like the case of the disputed parties, a sale of wine bought together, where one partner divides it without the other's knowledge.
Rav Pappa answers: I see that the one who came first is behind my own case, and so the claim is to be decided.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Nahman's rule: money lent follows the case of those who dispute the value: for good wine and good wine, or cheap and cheap, but not mixed.
Rav Hamma used to lend money openly; the reason given is whether the money is returned in its original form or its loss is known.
Raba: one may tell his friend to take four zuz and to lend them to someone else; the Torah forbids only interest of a loan upon a loan.
The reason: he takes a wage for the act of speaking, which is permitted.
Anecdote: the son of Rav Pappa took a share of the spinning wages and told his father to lend the money; the Sages told Rav Pappa.
Rav Pappa replies that such interest is permitted, since the loan is not lent to the lender, and the wage for the speaking is taken.
Mishna: one may appraise a cow, donkey, and any animal that works and eats for half; where the custom is to share the offspring, one shares immediately.
Baraita: one who leases a field from his fellow for ten kor of wheat a year and says give me two hundred zuz, and I will work it and give you twelve kor, is permitted.
Rav Nahman and Rabbah bar Abuha: sometimes one may lease a shop to make a bench or a ship to make a ladder, since the rent is higher when the work is done.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav: if the wage is the payment, is the cost also? Rav is silent.
Rav Sheshet explains Rav's silence: he had not heard the baraita.
Baraita: though one may not accept iron sheep from a Jew, one may accept them from gentiles.

Baraita: one who lends a cow to a friend and says the cow's worth thirty dinar, and I will pay a sela monthly, is permitted, since the price was not fixed; Rav Sheshet says it is fixed only after death.
Rav Pappa rules: the halakha is that a ship carries the wage and the cost.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara notes that the wage at drawing and the cost at breaking depend on local custom.
Explains that the matter depends on custom, because the Mishna itself taught it.
Rav Anan reports Shmuel: orphans' money may be lent at interest.
Rav Nahman objects that the money belongs to orphans, so the loan is forbidden, since the orphans would lose it.
Anecdote of Rabbah son of Rav Yosef: Shmuel's sale of a kettle, where the buyer takes the wage and the seller the loss.
Shmuel replies that even if you examine him, it is permitted, since they accept the copper's loss on the difference.
Rav Sheshet: orphans' money may be lent at interest, near for gain and far for loss.
Baraita: one who is near to gain and far from loss is wicked; near to loss and far from gain is pious; near to both and far from neither is the normal character.
Rava asks Rav Yosef how orphans' money is handled; Rav Yosef says it is placed before the court and given to them in coins, after checking the borrower's gold.
Explains that a specific item is different, since it may be a deposit, and the owner comes with signs and takes it back.
Rav Ashi asks: if one cannot find a man with gold, will the orphans' money be lost?
Rav Ashi: we see a man whose property is in order and who is trustworthy and hears the law of the Torah, so we give the money to him before the court.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one may not accept iron-sheep from a Jew because it is interest, but one may accept from gentiles and lend to them at interest.
Objects: does this mean the acceptance stands; a baraita says offspring of iron-sheep taken from gentiles are exempt from firstborn.
Abaye: no difficulty; the baraita concerns one who accepts risk and loss, and the other does not.
Raba objects to Abaye: if he accepts the risk, the iron-sheep is the case, and the Mishna's later clause should settle it differently.
Raba resolves: in both cases the acceptance of risk is not taken, and the firstborn exemption follows since the gentile holds a hand in the middle.
Cites the verse: one who multiplies wealth through interest gathers it for one who is gracious to the poor; Rav explains it is a king's case.
Rav Nahman reports Huna: the rule is needed even for interest taken from a gentile.
Raba objects to Rav Nahman with a verse: to a gentile you may lend at interest, which implies the rule is only about the brother.
Objects with a baraita that a Jew may lend to a gentile at interest and so on.
Rav Hiyya bar Rav Huna answers that the baraita is needed only for the case of a gentile who is a resident alien.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina explains the case: the Sages decreed lest a student learn from another's deeds, so it concerns scholars, and it fits the view of Rav Huna.
Cites the verse on lending to the poor, to show that one's own poor and the poor of the city and the poor of another city have priority.
Rav Nahman reports Huna: the rule is needed even for lending to a gentile at interest and to a Jew free of interest.
Baraita: R' Yosei says: come and see how the eyes of those who lend at interest are blind; one calls a neighbor and they bring witnesses.
Baraita of R' Shimon ben Elazar: the verse about one who does not give money at interest shall not totter; so those who lend at interest collapse.
Objects: but we see those who lend at interest who do not collapse.
R' Elazar: some collapse and rise, and some collapse and do not rise.
Cites the verse in Habakkuk on the wicked swallowing the righteous; Rav Huna says a righteous person swallows the wicked but a complete righteous one does not.
Baraita of R' Yehuda: the convert of righteousness in sale and the resident alien in interest; the verse for sale refers to a resident alien.
Objects with a baraita: a convert is not acquired with a Hebrew slave, while a woman and a convert acquire a Hebrew slave.
Explains that a convert acquires as a matter of course, and that one who acquires is as one who has no acquisition.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: a convert who acquires has the status of a Jew, but in acquisition has the status of a gentile.
Objects that the baraita may be against Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds a woman acquires even Hebrew slaves.
Resolves: the Hebrew slave is a different case from the Canaanite slave; Rav Yosef taught that a widow should not raise a dog at an inn.
Continues: the case of a dog is one where, once it is fed, it follows, since it is because of the food the person follows.
Cites the verse on one who falls and his hand grows weak, that a convert and resident alien are not to take interest.
Objects with a baraita: one may lend at interest to a gentile and a resident alien.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: the verse says not from them but from him, which is written of Israel.
Baraita: do not take interest from him, but you may become his guarantor.

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks: is the guarantor meant to be a Jew, when the Mishna lists the guarantor among those who transgress a prohibition?
Answers: the guarantor is a gentile, since a gentile's court follows the guarantor, who collects the interest.
Rav Sheshet: if one accepted to judge by Jewish law, he may not take interest; if he accepted only for one, not for the other.
Mishna: a Jew who lends money belonging to a gentile, with the gentile's consent, is permitted.
Baraita: a Jew lending a gentile's money is permitted with the gentile's consent, but not without it.
Baraita cases: a Jew who borrowed from a gentile at interest and asked to return it; or a gentile who borrowed from a Jew; placing them with another changes the outcome.
Asks: granted the second clause is stringent, but the first clause: since a gentile has no agency, the one who takes the interest is the Jew.
Rav Huna son of Manoah in Rav Aha's name: the case is where he said leave them on the ground and be off.
Objects: if so, what is it teaching? Rav Pappa says the case is where he took and gave by hand, yet what does this teach?
Explains the point: lest one think the gentile acts with the intention of the Jew, so the teaching clarifies it.
Rav Ashi: the rule that a gentile has no agency applies only to terumah; in all of Torah a gentile has agency.
Objects that Rav Ashi's view is a baraita, since terumah derives from the verse about you and your agents being children of the covenant.
Another version: Rav Ashi said the rule that a gentile has no agency applies to them for us, but for them we are their agents.
Objects that the baraita of Rav Ashi is a clear teaching, since the verse includes agents for the sake of inclusion.
Ravina: the gentile has no agency under rabbinic law, but has something like a minor's status; the gentile lacks agency even though...

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina: a Jew can come under agency, but a gentile cannot come under agency, so the rule applies here too.
Baraita on a Jew who borrowed from a gentile at interest and converted: the outcome depends on whether the conversion came before or after the loan is credited.
R' Yosei: a gentile who borrowed from a Jew at interest collects both principal and interest in any case.
Raba, reporting Rav Hisda and Rav Huna: the halakha follows R' Yosei; Raba explains R' Yosei's reason is so people do not say he converted for his money.
Baraita: a document that includes interest is penalized; the lender collects neither principal nor interest, per R' Meir; the Sages say he collects principal but not interest.
Explains the dispute: R' Meir holds that penalties are imposed to deter the permitted from the forbidden; the Sages do not impose such penalties.
Asks why earlier documents are invalid, since even if they were not collected from the first, they are collected from the second.
Resh Lakish: this is a tannaitic dispute, and it is the view of R' Meir.
R' Yohanan: even if the Sages were to hold, it is a decree lest one collect from the earlier document.
Anecdote: a man pledged an orchard to a friend, who ate its fruit for three years; the lender asks whether it can be sold, or is a loan on a document.
Abaye: this is not the same as R' Asi's view, which the speaker reported.

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One who admits a document need not confirm it and may collect from encumbered property; Raba notes the cases differ, and Ravina challenges Merimar.
Ravina objects with R' Yohanan's decree lest one collect from an earlier document; Raba says there the document can be written from a later time.
Baraita on improving land: a thief who sold a field and the buyer improved it; the owner may collect from the thief's property.
Mishna: one may not fix prices on produce until the market price is set; the reaper may fix a price on the sheaf, the vat, and the lime, and R' Yosei and R' Yehuda disagree on the high price.
R' Asi reports R' Yohanan that one may not fix a price on the market price; R' Zeira challenges that even like this; R' Yohanan spoke of town markets with fixed gates.
Asks how the Mishna can be understood, illustrated by wheat being sold in a market with fixed gates.
Baraita: one may not fix prices until the market price is set, for new and old produce, and for gleaners and sellers.
Rav Nahman: one may fix prices for gleaned produce at the price of the gleaned produce.
Raba objects to Rav Nahman: why may the gleaner borrow from another gleaner, but the owner may also borrow from a gleaner?
Explains: the one who gave money to the owner gives him the choicest produce.
Rav Sheshet reports Rav Huna: one may not lend in the market for a price; Rav Yosef bar Hama challenges him.
Objects that Rav Huna himself allowed the sons of Rav's house to borrow in Tishrei and repay in Tevet, so the view changed.
Baraita: one who carries a bundle from place to place and meets a friend, who says give me and I will carry for you as you do for others at that place.

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: one may move produce from place to place with the owner's consent; if the other has produce there, it is permitted, and merchants raise prices where it is dear.
Rav Pappa and Rav Aha of Difti explain why merchants prefer the cheap price, and give examples of groups of traders traveling to villages.
Rav lent money to donkey drivers and took on the risk of the road; a respected person is different.
Rav Asi asked R' Yohanan whether one may do the same with broken vessels; anecdotes of R' Yishmael and R' Yosei's sons and of R' Yohanan.
Explains the dispute between Rav, who forbids, and Shmuel, who permits, about whether the lease appears as interest or is protected.
Rav Shimi bar Hiyya: Rav agrees about oxen where the loss is great.
Shmuel tells those who plow to turn the earth so that they acquire the land, or else it is as a loan and forbidden.
Raba tells the watchmen of the fields to turn over the house of the ruler, so that the wage is not paid until the end of the period.
The rabbis object to Raba: you take interest, since everyone takes four from the tenant in Nisan while you keep the money until Iyar.
Raba answers: you do wrong, since the tenant is bound to the land; if you pay in Nisan you lose, while I keep it until Iyar and gain.

73b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Anecdote: Rav Mari bar Rahel pledged a house to a gentile, who sold it to Raba; Raba's collection of rent and the Gemara's view on who collects.
Raba tells Ravina's teacher that Sages who lend money in Tishrei for wine, and redeem it in Tevet, are lending at interest.
Anecdote of Ravina, who lent money to the sons of Akra and took back more than he gave.
Rav Ashi explains: the land is not theirs; the land is pledged to the tax, and the king says whoever pays the tax may eat the land.
Rav Pappa tells Raba that these scholars lend money for the taxes people pay and take security.
Rav Sheshet: the king's seal is placed on the seal, and the king says whoever does not pay the tax may be punished for one who pays.
Rav Sa'orem, Raba's brother, was strong and used to bring people in through Raba's gate.
Raba praises him, citing the verse that one may hold a non-Jew in servitude but not his brother, which includes one who does not behave properly.
Rav Hama: one who gives money to his friend to buy wine and fails to buy it must repay him, as with a donkey driver.
Ameimar reports Rav Zvid of Neharda: Rav Hama's rule applies to ordinary wine, not to this specific wine.
Rav Ashi: even ordinary wine is not, because it is an acquisition based on a promise, and such does not acquire.
Asks what distinguishes Rav Ashi's view from the Mishna: if I bring and do not do, I pay with the best, where the goods are in his hand.

74a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Raba: when three people give money to one to buy for them, and he buys for one, the sale is valid for all only if no one is pressing; if each is pressing, only the one who bought benefits.
Rav Pappi reports Raba: a sale by sign is binding; Rav Hiyya says it acquires actually, the Sages say it binds one who pays; the halakha is that it binds only if one pays.
Mishna opens: one may fix a price on the harvest with the reapers, at the beginning.

Rav holds that one who has not yet reached the second stage may fix a price for the third, but not for the first; Shmuel holds that by human hand even a hundred may be fixed, but by heaven's hand not even one.
Objects to Shmuel: the Mishna says one may fix on the sheaf, though the grain lacks drying and threshing, which is in heaven's hand.
Objects with the Mishna on the vat of grapes and the olive press, citing R' Hiyya's teaching, and asks whether these are in heaven's hand.
Objects that the olive press and the potter's eggs lack a press, and that the baraita's examples are inconsistent.
Asks why the Mishna is not inconsistent with the lacking of drying, baking, and the lime, as with the potter's eggs.
Explains: for Shmuel, who holds by human hand, the lime may be fixed once it is ready to be put in the kiln, not only once it is in.
The Mishna on potter's eggs recites: one may fix on the potter's eggs.
Baraita: one may not fix on the potter's eggs until they are made; R' Meir and R' Yosei disagree on white and black earth.
Ameimar lent money at the time of carrying earth; asks whether this follows R' Meir or R' Yosei, and what the practice is in his town.
The Mishna's permission to fix on the manure all year round follows the first Tanna, as Raba explains.

74b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishna on fixing a price at the high rate during the rainy season, which the Gemara identifies.
Anecdote: a man gave money for his mother-in-law's dowry; when the dowry was lost, the case came before Rav Pappa about the price and whether the money was acquired.
Rav Pappa: if one fixed the high price, the seller may retract and the buyer accepts, and if not, the buyer may retract.
Ravina objects: how do you know the Sages disagree with R' Shimon, who holds that money is not acquired; perhaps R' Shimon holds money is acquired.
Rav Pappa explains that for the Sages, whether one fixed or did not fix, one takes the current price, since the buyer's intention is weakened.
Ravina objects: let us say R' Shimon holds one gate versus two gates; if so, the buyer does not take on the seller's risk.
Objects with a baraita: in any case, so the halakha is; the Sages say the buyer and seller both accept the risk; what does R' Shimon hold?
Rav Aha son of Raba asks Rav Ashi: the agent appointed from the start would suffice; Rav Ashi replies: it is a merchant who buys and sells.
Mishna: one may lend his tenant wheat for wheat for seed, but not for eating; Rabban Gamliel lent to his tenants, taking the cheaper price.
Baraita: one may lend a tenant wheat for seed, and this applies only if the tenant has not gone down; if he went down, it is forbidden.
Asks why the first Tanna does not distinguish between whether the tenant went down or not, while the other Tanna does.
Raba explains: the first Tanna's tenant gives the lender a sum, whether he goes down or not; it depends on whether the lender can take it back.
Baraita: one person says to his friend, the rule is ...

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet explains the Mishna's case: if one did not fix a price, when grain falls he takes the grain, and when it rises he pays the price.
Mishna: one may not tell a friend to lend a kor of wheat with the promise to return it at threshing; Hillel forbids, and a woman may not lend a loaf to her friend.
Rav Huna: if one has a seah, he may borrow a seah or two seahs; R' Yitzhak says even one with a seah may borrow many kors.
R' Hiyya teaches in support of R' Yitzhak: one who has no drop of wine or oil may borrow, and one who has may borrow for as many drops.
Rav Nahman: Shmuel said the halakha follows Hillel, but the halakha is not so.
Rav Yehuda: Shmuel said this is Hillel's view; the Sages say one lends and repays in general.
Rav Yehuda: Shmuel said companies that are scrupulous with each other transgress measure, weight, count, and interest when they lend and repay on the festival.
Rav Yehuda: Shmuel said scholars may borrow from one another with interest, since they know interest is forbidden and it is a gift they give each other.
Shmuel tells his father to lend a hundred peppers for a hundred and twenty peppers and be sure.
Rav Yehuda: a man may lend to his children and household with interest to teach them the taste of interest, lest they be drawn in.
Mishna: one may not tell a friend to weed my field and I will weed yours; one may not say weed my field and I will weed yours.

75b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one may not tell a neighbor to plow with me in the rainy season and I will plow with you in the dry; Rabban Gamliel explains early and late interest.
Mishna: an example of early interest and late interest, and R' Shimon's view that there is interest in words.
Mishna: one may not say that so-and-so came from a place, since the lender, borrower, guarantor and witnesses transgress; the Sages add the scribe.
Lists the verses forbidding giving interest, taking interest, and putting a stumbling block before the blind.
Baraita: R' Shimon ben Yohai derives from the verse that one may not greet a debtor, since even speech is forbidden.
Abaye: the lender transgresses all of these; the borrower transgresses the prohibition on interest; the guarantor and witnesses transgress only the verse about giving interest.
R' Shimon: interest is worse than what the lenders profit; it lays a charge on Moses, whom the Torah calls wise, and his teaching is true.
Rav Dimi: from where do we learn that one who owes a debtor a mina and knows he has none may not pass before him; Rav Ami and Rav Asi say it is as if they judged two cases.
Rav Yehuda: whoever has money and lends it without witnesses violates the prohibition on giving a stumbling block before the blind.
Resh Lakish: one who lends without witnesses brings a curse on himself; the Sages say Ravina sent money to Rav Ashi as a witness for the case.
Ravina sent to ask Rav Ashi to bring witnesses and have a document drawn up, since he might forget and bring a curse on himself.
Baraita: three cry out and are not answered: one who lends without witnesses, one who makes a master of himself, and one whose wife rules him; explanations follow.
Heading: the chapter 'Which is interest', with the first Mishna.
Mishna: laborers who mislead one another have only a complaint against each other; one who hires a donkey or a potter for a wedding or funeral, and the laborers pay on the lower rate.

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: if the employer retracts, the hand is on the bottom; whoever changes his mind, the hand is on the bottom.
Asks how the case of laborers misleading one another should be understood.
Gemara's cases: the employer says to hire laborers, and the agent goes and misleads them with a different wage; or the employer offers four and the agent says three.
Baraita: one who hires a worker to work on his own land and shows him another's land, pays the wage and recovers from the employer.
Explains that the case is one where the employer said the wage is on him, and the laborers differ in how they bargain.
Further resolutions: the case may be one where the employer said four or three, or laborers who are reliable in their work.
Another resolution: the employer said four and the agent said three; the laborers believed the agent's claim of three.
Asks whether the laborers rely on the agent's word that the employer said so, or on the employer's own word.
Cites a baraita about a husband who brings a bill of divorce and the wife says receive it for me.
Rabbah bar Avuha: even if the bill reaches her hand she is not divorced, which shows she relies on the speaker's word.
Rav Ashi's remark on the case.

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the divorce analogy: Rav holds that the wife relies on the husband's words; the difference is whether the agent was appointed to receive or to deliver; the baraita applies the same logic.
Baraita: laborers who misled the employer or the employer who misled them have only a complaint; but when laborers go and find no grain, they are paid if they found a wet field.
Baraita: this applies only where they did not start; if they started, the work already done is valued, e.g., half the reaping or half the weaving.
Baraita: if the cloth would have been worth six dinar, he pays one sela or they finish and take two; R' Dosa says value what would be made.
Baraita: for lost items, one may hire a porter with a fixed fee; the porter may be paid a sum up to forty or fifty zuz.
Baraita: where there are other laborers available to hire, the employer who tells the worker to go and hire from these has only a complaint.
A tanna recites before Rav: the employer pays them their wage.
Objects: but the Mishna teaches it is not similar: a laborer who comes laden to one who sits and does nothing.
Resolves: the case of a worker who is paid in the evening is different from one who is paid per day, as the field is watched in the evening.
Raba's example: one who hires workers to fill a cistern and rain comes and fills it with water, if he watches the field at night.

77a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Raba's illustration: if the laborers lose the day because the field was not watered at night, the owner pays them as idle workers.
Raba's further cases: one who hires workers to a task, and the river or rain interferes, so loss falls on the laborers or the owner.
Explains that the task-wage is paid to the workers in the case where the owner can make the work worthwhile, by bread and meals, as in Mahoza.
The Mishna's ruling: the workers may pay six dinar, or finish and take two selas; this needs stating for when the work became dearer and they asked for more.
Clarifies: the owner appeased the workers, who said he would pay more; the Gemara asks whether they might claim it was for their food and drink.
If the workers asked for a higher wage, he must pay it, since he said it was a surplus.
R' Dosa: value what the work will become; the six dinar piece is what the worker sets, and the work may be ruined and the owner would have to pay.
Explains that a worker told the owner it is for good work; the owner gives a sela for a sela.
R' Huna son of Rav Natan: the case is where they lowered their price at first and the work fell; the Gemara explains whether it means less.
Rav says the halakha follows R' Dosa, and a worker may retract even in the middle of the day; objects that the owner who hires for half a day may be different.

77b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whose view this is, since if it were the Sages, why is only death or heat named; it must be R' Dosa, who distinguishes wage from contract.
R' Nahman bar Yitzhak: the Mishna speaks of lost items, and everyone agrees the rule is that one who reverses pays the lower price.
Asks why the Mishna says any one who reverses, unless it is included to cover the worker and R' Dosa's view; Rav holds part of R' Dosa's view.
Alternatively: any one who reverses means the seller or buyer who withdraws, as the baraita explains.
Baraita on sale of a field for a thousand zuz, with two hundred paid: if the seller retracts, the buyer's hand is on top, and vice versa; R' Shimon ben Gamliel says they are taught to be firm.
R' Shimon ben Gamliel's form of document: one may write that the buyer paid two hundred and owes the rest, so the purchase is valid even after years.
Objects: if the money is drawn from better property, should not the lender collect from the middling; the Mishna says a debtor collects from middling; and the land given money.
R' Nahman bar Yitzhak: the better property or the middling property; R' Aha: even if you say from better property.
Explains that one who buys land for a thousand zuz and sells property cheaply is like one who suffers damage, and the damaged are valued at the better property.
R' Shimon ben Gamliel's form continues: if the document does not contain this wording, the buyer does not acquire.
Objects with a baraita: one who gives a deposit and says if I retract, the deposit is canceled; R' Yosei holds such conditions stand, since a conditional promise acquires.
R' Yehuda: it is enough for the buyer to acquire to the extent of the deposit.
R' Shimon ben Gamliel: when he says my deposit should be returned, but if he sold a field for a thousand zuz and took five hundred, the buyer acquires and returns the rest, even years later.
Resolves: one who sells something and comes in and goes out with zuz does not acquire, while one who does not come in and go out with zuz does acquire.
Raba: one who lends a hundred zuz to his fellow and is repaid zuz by zuz, the repayment is a repayment, with a complaint against him; Rav Ashi examines an example of a wine sale.
Asks whether such a case acquires or does not acquire.
Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Abimi of Hagronya reported Raba: a zuz is like a zuz and does not acquire.
Rav Aha son of Rav Yosef objects to Rav Ashi that it was said in Raba's name that it acquires; Rav Ashi retorts about translating his teachings for the seller of the field.

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether one who sells a field in the case of a loss is like one who sells: where he wanted to sell for a hundred and could not, and sold for two hundred, the question is left undecided.
Rav Nahman reads the Mishna about hiring a donkey, a potter, or a carrier: the hirer owes the carrier up to the amount of the wage.
Raba objects to Rav Nahman: the baraita says up to forty or fifty zuz; Rav Nahman answers that the case is when a bundle came into his hand.
Mishna: one who hires a donkey to carry it uphill and carries it on the plain, or the reverse, is liable if it dies; the distinctions depend on slipping versus heat, and on the donkey's loss.
Asks why the first case is not distinguished while the second case is, as the house of R' Yannai says.
The first case, where the donkey died from the air: the air of the hill killed it, or the air of the plain killed it.
R' Yosei bar Hanina: the case is where it died from thirst, or hardship.
Rabbah: the case is where a snake bit it.
R' Hiyya bar Abba says R' Yohanan: this is R' Meir's view, who holds that one who transgresses against the owner's wishes is liable.

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the one who is called a robber is R' Meir.
Mishna of the dyer: one gives wool to a dyer to dye red and he dyes it black; R' Meir says he pays the value of the wool.
R' Yehuda: if the gain exceeds the expense, he pays the expense; if the expense exceeds the gain, he pays the gain.
Objects: perhaps the dyer case is different because it is acquired by an act of change; cites R' Meir on Purim funds going to Purim.
R' Eliezer: Purim funds may be used only for Purim, and the poor may not take a strap for a sandal unless so stipulated; R' Yaakov cites R' Meir, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is lenient.
Explains that the Purim case is one where the giver intended for Purim, and not for other items; so it does not contradict R' Meir.
Baraita from R' Shimon ben Elazar in R' Meir's name: one who gives a dinar to a poor man to buy a cloak may not buy a robe, since he goes against the owner's intent.
Objects: perhaps the case is different because people would suspect; if so, the Mishna should say because of suspicion, not because he goes against intent.
One who acts against the intent of the owner of the house is called a robber.
Asks what 'and it was made bright' means, and whether it is translated as a bright thing.
Raba: a case of a man who was tormented by a king's matter; they asked whether he was tormented by silver or gold.
Rav: this applies only to a donkey that returns; but if the donkey does not return, one must replace it.
Shmuel: whether the donkey returns or not, if it is taken on the road one says here is yours; if not, one must replace the donkey.
Objects with a baraita: one who hires a donkey which became bright, or went mad, says here is yours; if dead or turned into a bag, one must replace it.
Rav's view resolves the baraita; for Shmuel there is a difficulty, which is answered by a case on the road versus off it.
Objects that the same reasoning applies to Shmuel: the final clause teaches R' Shimon ben Elazar's view.
Explains the first Tanna's view: the difference is whether the donkey's going was taken away, as R' Shimon ben Elazar holds.
Shmuel holds the view of R' Shimon ben Elazar, and Rav holds with him too, as the law is stated.
Alternatively, the whole Mishna is R' Shimon ben Elazar's, with a gap in the text that is supplied.
Mishna: one who hires a donkey which became bright or went mad, says here is yours; if dead or turned into a bag, one must replace it; if it was taken on the road, one says here is yours.

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: R' Shimon ben Elazar: if the donkey is taken on the road, one says here is yours; otherwise one must replace the donkey.
Asks whether this can be reconciled with R' Shimon ben Elazar, since the Mishna says one says here is yours when the donkey is made bright or mad.
Baraita: one who hires a donkey to ride on, and it became bright or mad, must replace it, per R' Shimon ben Elazar.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna: riding is different, as with glass vessels; Rav Pappa notes the same.
Hired a donkey to ride and it died halfway: he pays for half the trip, and the hirer has only a complaint.
Explains the cases: whether the hirer can easily complain, and whether one who did not come here would have paid the wage anyway.
Rav holds one may not hire a replacement after the donkey dies halfway; Shmuel says one may hire, and their dispute concerns that.
Objects with a baraita: if a tree dried or was cut, both are forbidden; how can one buy land and eat its fruits, since the land returns at Jubilee.
Rav Hasda: from where do we learn the seller of land for sixty years cannot retrieve it in Jubilee? The verse says land shall not be sold forever.
Explains that when the Jubilee does not apply, the land is not forever sold; the case is when the Jubilee is not in force.
Reasons that if the Jubilee applied, one would have a claim on the land and take it, so the case must be otherwise.
Explains that sometimes the mortgage is paid before Jubilee, or the debt is repaid four or five years before Jubilee.
Baraita: R' Natan: one who hires a boat which sank halfway; if he paid, he does not take back; if not, he need not pay.
Asks how the case should be understood: is it a boat with wine in general, or with a specific boat?
Objects: say give me the boat, since I am bringing wine; if the boat is general with wine, why does the one who did not pay not pay?

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa: the case of say give me the boat and I will bring wine applies only to this boat and this wine; for a general boat and general wine, the cargo is shared.
Baraita: one who hires a boat and it breaks down halfway pays for half the trip, and the boat owner has only a complaint.
Asks how the case is to be understood: if the owner can gather the cargo, why does he have a complaint; the reason may be the loss of the boat's cargo.
Explains the complaint as due to a change of the owner's intention, or because the boat's burden was thrown out.
Baraita on hiring a donkey to ride: the hirer may place his clothing and his mattress, and the feed for the way; afterward the donkey owner withholds the hirer's feed.
Rav Pappa: the case where the donkey owner is able to buy and sell from one shop to another; the donkey's needs and the sale ability decide.
Baraita: a man may not ride a donkey hired by a woman, nor a woman by a man; the rule covers an adult or a minor, pregnant or nursing.
Rav Pappa: the case is pregnant and nursing; Abaye: from this we learn the womb is delicate and ruined.
Asks what the difference is for sale and purchase.

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one who hires a cow to plow on the hill and plows in the valley, if the jug breaks he is exempt; if the reverse, he is liable, since legumes are divided.
Rav Pappa: who pays depends on who holds the item; the halakha is that whoever holds the vessel pays; if the place is one where both are liable, both pay.
R' Yohanan: one who sells a cow saying it is a gorer, a biter, a kicker, or a lier-down, and it has one defect; if he dismisses the defects, it is a mistake only if the defect is one.
A baraita says likewise: one who sells a maidservant saying she is foolish, fits, or dull, with one defect and the rest, it is a mistake only for one defect.
Rav Aha son of Raba asks Rav Ashi whether all the defects are present; Rav Mordechai reports Raba: if all defects are present, it is not a mistake.
Mishna: one who hires a donkey to bring wheat and brings barley is liable; wheat-and-straw is liable; the rule on overloading depends on the measure, per Symmachus.
Abaye and Raba dispute whether the Mishna's 'heavy like a load' applies to the stone-carrier's weight; they disagree on how to read the wording.
Mishna: one who hires to bring wheat and brings barley is exempt, but if he adds more than his load, he is liable.
Asks whether the case means three kab, not a seah; the Mishna says a seah, so the question is how many to add.
Explains Symmachus's view: the case where he did not change wheat, and brought barley, and how much more to add; the measures follow R' Meir.
Begins a baraita citing a case where one hires a donkey to bring wheat and brings wheat.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the measures of the boat and the donkey, and Abaye and Raba's distinctions about when a carrier is liable; Rav Pappa concludes that ships hold about thirty kor.
Mishna: all craftsmen are paid guards, and in all of these cases one says take your wage and bring the money.
Mishna: a borrower who says keep this for me and I will keep yours is an unpaid guard; one who says keep it for me is a paid guard.
Mishna: one who lends on a pledge is a paid guard; R' Yehuda says lending money is an unpaid guard; Abba Shaul says one may rent a poor man's pledge.
Asks whether the Mishna is not like R' Meir, since the Mishna does not follow R' Meir.
Baraita: R' Meir holds the hirer pays as an unpaid guard, and R' Yehuda holds as a paid guard.
Objects: if R' Meir holds that the hirer benefits, then a hirer too is a paid guard; the question is whether one pays more.
Explains: R' Meir may hold that one who takes a rent for the pledge in advance is a paid guard; so the Mishna may be read differently.
Baraita: R' Meir holds a paid guard pays as a paid guard, and R' Yehuda holds as an unpaid guard; all the craftsmen say take your wage.
The Mishna in the earlier chapter: all craftsmen are paid guards, as stated.
Rav Hisda: a borrower who lends the item back, and it dies, is liable; but after the loan period, the borrower is exempt.
Rav Nahman bar Pappa objects with the Mishna: in all of these cases, one says take your wage and bring the money; this is an unpaid guard.

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the Mishna: the case of a borrower who says take your wage and bring money is a paid guard; the Gemara explains why the Mishna must state it.
Rav Nahman bar Pappa: we also learned that in all these cases, one says take your wage and bring money, an unpaid guard.
Asks whether the case is the same as the lender's case, where one may not take his wage.
Huna son of Marimar before Ravina: the Mishnas seem to contradict each other; the answer is that the Mishna teaches the same for the lender.
Objects with a baraita: a borrower who sends and it dies is liable, and so too when he returns it late.
Rafram bar Pappa, citing Rav Hisda: the baraita speaks of returning within the loan period; after it, he is exempt.
Asks whether a borrower is exempt like a borrower but liable like a paid guard, or whether a paid guard too is not liable.
Ameimar: it is reasonable that the borrower is exempt and liable as a paid guard, since he benefits from the benefit.

Baraita: one who takes utensils from a craftsman to send to his father-in-law's house: if they are not accepted, he pays by the value of the benefit; if they are lost on the way, he is liable on the return but exempt as a carrier.
Case of a man who bought wine from his friend: he would bring it to a certain place; the wine was lost on the way, and the case came before Rav Nahman who held him liable.
Rabbah objects to Rav Nahman: lost on the way he is liable, and on the return he is exempt, since he is a carrier.
Rav Nahman: the return is part of the journey, and the reason is that if he had found a buyer, would he have sold?
Asks why the guarding of 'keep for me and I will keep for you' is a paid guard, since the guard is for the owner.
Rav Pappa: when one says keep for me today and I will keep for you tomorrow.
Baraita: keep for me and I'll keep for you; lend to me and I'll lend to you; all become paid guards for each other.
Asks why the guarding is the owner's responsibility.
Rav Pappa: the one who says keep for me today and I will keep for you tomorrow; these guarded for each other daily.
Anecdote: one of them was asked to guard a cloak; the cloak was neglected and stolen; the case came before Rav Pappa, who held them liable.
The Sages objected to Rav Pappa: why is neglect the owner's? Then the matter became clear: at that time he was drinking beer.
Rav Pappa's explanation: for one who holds neglect by the owner is exempt, which explains the embarrassment; for one who holds liable, that day was not his.
Another anecdote: they said to the guard, go and guard for us; he said, guard my cloak; I will pay you.

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Anecdote: two men traveling with a donkey and a cloak; the cloak was taken and washed, and the case came before Raba, who held the borrower liable.
The Sages say to Raba: why is the borrower liable, since the guardianship is the owner's; the matter turned out that the item was taken without the owner's consent.
Case of a man who hired a donkey from his friend: he was told to avoid the river road and take the dry road; he went by the river, and the donkey died.
Raba: why would he lie, if he wanted? Abaye: why would I lie in a place without witnesses; we do not say keep for me and he says leave it before me.
Abaye and Rav Huna: if one says leave it before you, he is neither an unpaid guard nor a paid guard.
Asks whether 'leave it' without more is an unpaid guard, from the baraita.
Cites the baraita: keep for me and he says leave it before me, an unpaid guard; the bare case is not evidence, since the baraita means something else.
Explains R' Yohanan's view: one who enters another's courtyard is liable only if the owner accepted to guard it, since the owner has his own guard; in the market there is no guard.
Asks whether the Mishna is not like R' Eliezer, since the lender on a pledge does not take his money.

Baraita: one who lends to his friend on a pledge, and the pledge is lost: R' Eliezer says he swears and takes his money; R' Akiva says he cannot claim the money; but if he lent a thousand zuz on a document, the pledge lost means the money i
Resolves that the two cases differ: one where the pledge was taken at the time of the loan, one where it was taken afterward; both cases are the same.

82a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves the apparent conflict: the Mishna's case is where the lender lends produce, and the second clause is R' Yehuda's view with the omitted words supplied.
Mishna: one who lends on a pledge is a paid guard, unless he lent money, when he is an unpaid guard; R' Yehuda's rule is stated.
The Mishna is not like R' Akiva but more clearly it is not like R' Eliezer.
Asks whether the dispute is about whether a pledge has a stated value, citing Shmuel's case of a thousand zuz and a rope lost.
R' Yitzhak derives from the verse that a creditor acquires a pledge: it says the pledge shall be righteous to you, so the verse shows acquisition.
Objects: perhaps R' Yitzhak speaks of a pledge taken after the loan, but one taken at the loan itself, all agree that the creditor does not acquire.
Explains that here the pledge is taken at the time of the loan, and so the dispute is on that point.
The dispute about a guard of a lost item: Rabbah says as an unpaid guard, Rav Yosef says as a paid guard; the Gemara asks whether this is a tannaitic dispute.

82b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Disagreement over whether a lender holding collateral is a paid or unpaid bailee.
Mishna's ruling that Abba Shaul permits renting out a poor man's collateral to reduce the debt.
Shmuel rules the halakha follows Abba Shaul, limited to tools with high rent and low wear.
Mishna: a bailee who breaks a transported barrel is exempt upon swearing he was not negligent.
Rabbi Eliezer says both bailees must swear, but he doubts whether both can.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir holds that either kind of bailee swears and is exempt.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda holds an unpaid bailee swears while a paid bailee pays.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says both bailees swear, doubting whether both can.
Asks whether this means Rabbi Meir holds that one who stumbles is not negligent.
Objection: a baraita shows Rabbi Meir holds the stumbler liable, contradicting that reading.
Resolves the contradiction: the Sages disagree on whether one who stumbles is negligent.
Rabbi Elazar says the mishna must be broken, since the two rulings come from different traditions.
Rabbi Yehuda's ruling, with each bailee judged by the law that applies to him.
Rabbi Eliezer agrees the halakha follows Rabbi Meir but still doubts both can swear.
Why does a paid bailee swear at all, since he pays even without negligence?
Even an unpaid bailee seems unable to swear on a level surface where the loss was caused by him.

83a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenge: even on an incline the oath seems unnecessary where evidence exists, so why swear?
Isi ben Yehuda's baraita: with an eyewitness, the bailee brings evidence rather than taking an oath.
Rabbi Yohanan explains the oath is a Sages' decree, since otherwise no one would transport barrels.
Asks how exactly the bailee takes the oath.
Rava says the oath is that he broke it unintentionally.
Rabbi Yehuda: an unpaid bailee swears and a paid bailee pays, each under his own law.
Rabbi Elazar: the halakha follows Rabbi Meir, but he doubts whether both can swear.
Asks why a paid bailee swears at all, since he pays even without negligence.
Asks how an unpaid bailee can swear on level ground where negligence is evident.
Restates the challenge: on an incline, evidence should be brought, so no oath is needed.
Isi ben Yehuda's baraita again, supporting evidence in place of an oath when there is an eyewitness.
A broken wine barrel in Mehoza's market: Rava rules the bailee brings evidence and is exempt.
Rav Yosef asks whether Rava ruled according to Isi ben Yehuda.
Rava confirms he ruled following Isi, which is the accepted halakha.
A man had wine bought for him that later fermented, and the buyer returned to dispute the matter.
Rava rules the buyer must prove the wine was good when bought, which exempts him.
Rav Yosef again asks whether the ruling follows Isi ben Yehuda.
Rava again confirms the ruling follows Isi ben Yehuda.
Rav Hiyya bar Yosef in Sikhra decrees that porters breaking a pole-carried load pay half.
Explains: a pole load is near both accident and negligence, so half; a digla means full payment.
Rabba bar bar Hanan keeps the porters' cloaks for a broken barrel; Rav orders them returned.
Rabba asks whether this is the halakha.
Rav says yes, citing Proverbs on walking in the way of good men.
Rabba bar bar Hanan returns the cloaks.
The porters plead that they are poor, toiled all day, are hungry, and have nothing.
Rav orders Rabba to pay the porters their wages.
Rabba asks again whether this is the halakha.
Rav says yes, citing Proverbs on keeping the paths of the righteous.
Mishna: an employer cannot force laborers to start early or work late beyond local custom, including meals.
Story: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya's son hires laborers and promises them sustenance without details.
Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya says the promise was insufficient; he must first state only bread and legumes.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the son needn't have specified, since regional custom governs.
Asks whether the mishna's rule is obvious, since an employer cannot compel workers.
The rule is needed only where wages were raised above the local standard.
Laborers may reply that the raise was for quality work, not for longer hours.
Reish Lakish begins a new teaching.

83b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A laborer's trip home is at his own expense, while his trip to work is paid by the employer.
Psalm 104 verse cited as the source: people go out to work from sunrise and labor until evening.
Asks how a verse can ground the rule if local custom governs, and where a new city's workers come from.
Reish Lakish refers to a new city or mixed workers; alternatively, the employer hired him as a Torah-law laborer.
Rabbi Zeira, or Rav Yosef in a baraita, offers a homiletic reading of the next verse.
Psalm 104:20 read as referring to this world and to the wicked, who resemble beasts.
Psalm 104:22 read as referring to the righteous and the wicked in the World-to-Come.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon finds an officer whose job is to arrest thieves.
Asks how the officer can catch thieves, since they are like beasts, per the same verse.
Some say he argued from Psalm 10:9 that the officer may catch the righteous and leave the wicked.
The officer replies that the king's decree requires him to arrest thieves, and he does his job.
Elazar's instruction: enter a tavern at the fourth hour and tell scholars, laborers and thieves apart.
The court hears of the advice and appoints Elazar to carry out the arrests.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha rebukes him for handing the people of God to a gentile court for execution.
Elazar answers that he is only removing thorns, the wicked, from the vineyard of the Jewish people.
Yehoshua replies that the owner of the vineyard, God, should remove His own thorns.
A laundryman insults Elazar, who concludes he is wicked and has him arrested and executed.
Elazar regrets his hasty decision and tries, unsuccessfully, to ransom the laundryman.
Elazar cites Proverbs 21:23 on guarding one's mouth to show the insult caused the man's death.
The laundryman is hanged; bystanders console Elazar, saying he was wholly wicked and sinned on Yom Kippur.
Elazar places his hand on his belly and reasons that his certainties, like his suspicions, must be right.
Still unsettled, he undergoes a test: his fat is removed and left in the sun, and it does not putrefy.
Asks whether this proves anything, since fat not attached to flesh does not putrefy in any case.
Red veins in fat do putrefy; here they did not, which shows Elazar's righteousness.
Elazar applies Psalm 16:8-9 to himself, saying his flesh dwells in safety.
A similar incident is related about Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei, who was appointed head officer.

84a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A similar incident: Elijah the prophet encounters Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.
Elijah rebukes him: how long will you hand over the people of God to execution?
Rabbi Yishmael replies that the king's edict obliges him to take the post.
Elijah advises him to flee the way his father did, to Laodicea rather than accept the post.
The Sages were so obese that a pair of oxen could pass between them without touching them.
A Roman noblewoman says their children cannot be theirs, given their obesity.
They reply that their wives' bellies are larger than theirs, so all the more so they could not have done so.
They cite Judges 8:21: as the man is, so is his strength, meaning their organs match their bellies.
An alternative reply: love compresses the flesh, so their bodies were not an obstacle.
Asks why they answered her foolishness, since Proverbs 26:4 says not to answer a fool; answer was to avoid slander on their children.
Sizes of the Sages' organs are reported: Rabbi Yishmael's, Rabbi Yohanan's, and Rav Pappa's belly.
Rabbi Yohanan says he is the last of Jerusalem's beautiful men, and his radiance is described by a silver goblet image.
Asks whether Rabbi Yohanan was so beautiful, since he is not included in the chain of beautiful men.
Rabbi Yohanan differed from them because he had no beard, so his beauty lacked the countenance of the others.
Rabbi Yohanan sits at the ritual bath entrance so women see him and bear children like him.
The Rabbis ask whether he fears the evil eye when displaying himself so openly.
He replies that he descends from Joseph, over whom the evil eye has no dominion.
Genesis 49:22 is cited: Joseph is a fruitful vine by a fountain, which supports his claim.
Rabbi Abbahu reads alei ayin as olei ayin, those who rise above the evil eye.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina derives the same idea from Genesis 48:16 about fish covered by water.
Reish Lakish, a bandit leader, is recruited to Torah by Rabbi Yohanan, who promises him his sister in marriage.
Baraita dispute: from when are metal weapons and sickles susceptible to impurity, from firing or from scouring?
Rabbi Yohanan holds firing in the furnace completes manufacture; Reish Lakish holds scouring in water.
Rabbi Yohanan jabs that a bandit knows about banditry, so Reish Lakish is an expert in weapons.
Reish Lakish objects that Torah brought him only the name of leader of bandits, as before.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that he brought him close to God, under the wings of the Divine Presence.
Reish Lakish falls ill after the quarrel; his sister pleads with Rabbi Yohanan for his sake and her children's.
Rabbi Yohanan replies with Jeremiah 49:11 that he will rear the orphans and the widows can trust God.
Reish Lakish dies, and Rabbi Yohanan is terribly grieved.
The Rabbis send Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat, whose teachings are sharp, to console him.
Elazar sits before Rabbi Yohanan and cites a baraita supporting each of his statements.
Rabbi Yohanan explains that Reish Lakish's twenty-four objections sharpened the halakha, unlike Elazar's proofs.
Rabbi Yohanan rebukes him: do I not know my own view is correct without your baraita?
Rabbi Yohanan rends his clothes calling for Reish Lakish, goes mad, and dies after the Rabbis pray for him.

84b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Elazar accepts afflictions as atonement for possible errors in his rulings, and his attendants tend him nightly.
His wife prepares sixty relishes for him and keeps him from the study hall to protect his health.
He summons his pains by night and dismisses them by day; his wife rebels and returns to her father's house.
Sixty sailors visit him with gifts, having prayed for rescue at sea in his merit.
His wife sends their daughter to check on him; he answers that his means exceed hers and resumes his studies.
Students bring sixty blood samples for inspection, and he declares them all pure.
The Rabbis object that it cannot be that not one sample is uncertain, so he must be mistaken.
Elazar replies that if his ruling is correct, every child born from these women will be male.
It turns out all the children were male, and they were named Elazar after him.
A baraita records Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi lamenting the wife who kept Elazar from the study hall.
Dying, Elazar tells his wife to lay him in the attic; Shmuel bar Nahmani reports her account of eighteen to twenty-two years.
The wife describes the uncorrupted body and a worm from his ear, explained as punishment for not protesting an insult.
Litigants are judged by a voice from the attic; after a neighbor's curse, the Rabbis bury him.
Dream of his father, and the townspeople of Akhbaria refusing burial because of the protection he gave them.
On Yom Kippur eve, a serpent blocks the cave until the Rabbis address it and it lets them bury him.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sends an emissary to propose marriage to Elazar's widow.
She refuses: a vessel used for the sacred should not serve the profane, as the adage holds.
Rabbi Yehuda replies that Elazar was greater in Torah, but asks whether he was greater in good deeds.
She replies she does not know whether he was greater in Torah, but he was greater in good deeds, accepting afflictions.
Asks what event showed Elazar's superiority to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi in Torah knowledge.
The two youths sat on the ground before the elders, who had benches; the elders then promoted them.
The elders praise the youths's brilliance, and benches are prepared for them beside the Sages.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel protests that they are seeking to take his only son from him.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha argues that the one with a father should live, the orphan may be demoted.
Elazar is also demoted without explanation and is offended.
Elazar protests that they treat Yehuda HaNasi as equal to him, though he is far greater.
From then on, Elazar stopped supporting Yehuda HaNasi's views and began preempting his responses.
Elazar refutes Yehuda's planned response in advance, calling his answers bundles of worthless refutations.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi is offended and reports the incident to his father.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says Elazar is a lion, son of a lion, while Yehuda is a lion, son of a fox.
The background to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's saying that the three most modest people are Father and others.

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The sons of Beteira appointed Hillel as Nasi over them, showing their modesty.
Jonathan son of Saul tells David he will be second to him, cited from I Samuel 23:17.
Asks how we know these men were truly modest, or whether they merely yielded to stronger rivals.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was certainly truly modest.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepts afflictions as precious: thirteen years of kidney stones and scurvy.
His stableman's wealth and the lowing of livestock to mask Rabbi Yehuda's cries of pain.
Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon's afflictions were greater than Rabbi Yehuda's.
Elazar's afflictions came and went out of love, while Rabbi Yehuda's came and went due to incidents.
Asks what the incident was that brought Rabbi Yehuda's suffering.
A calf hangs its head on his garment, and he tells it to go; so affliction comes upon him.
His maidservant sweeps out young weasels, and he tells her to leave them be.
Psalm 145:9 is cited; heaven says since he was compassionate, they will be compassionate to him.
During Elazar's suffering no one died early, and during Rabbi Yehuda's no rain was needed.
Sayings on rain: a rainy day is as hard as judgment; the Sages would pray to annul it if not needed.
Despite the drought, water remained in holes left by uprooted radishes.
Rabbi Yehuda visits Elazar's town and learns his son is wayward and costs prostitutes a lot.
Rabbi Yehuda rescues the son, ordains him, and assigns him to Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya.
The son repeatedly wants to go home; his teacher rebukes him, and he vows to stay and improve.
The son matures, sits in Rabbi Yehuda's academy, and his voice resembles his father's.
Rabbi Yehuda is told the voice is the son of Elazar, and he recognizes him.
Proverbs 11:30 is applied: the fruit of the righteous is Yosei, and the wise one is Shimon ben Isi.
When Yosei dies, a serpent blocks the cave; people assume Elazar was greater than Yosei.
A divine voice explains Elazar suffered in the cave for thirteen years, while Yosei did not.
Rabbi Yehuda visits Rabbi Tarfon's town and learns his grandson is wayward and costs prostitutes a lot.
Rabbi Yehuda offers his daughter if the grandson repents; sources differ on whether they married.
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda exerted himself so much to save these wayward sons.
Anyone who teaches Torah to another's son merits sitting in the heavenly academy, citing Jeremiah 15:19.
Teaching Torah to an ignoramus's son lets God annul a decree for his sake, citing Jeremiah 15:19.
Rabbi Yohanan: if a scholar, his son, and his grandson are scholars, Torah never leaves his seed.
Isaiah 59:21 is cited as the basis: My words shall not depart from your mouth or your seed's.
Asks what the words from now and forever mean in God's guarantee.
Rabbi Yirmiyah explains: from now on Torah wanders in search of its host.
Rav Yosef fasts forty fasts, and each time the verse is read; he concludes Torah seeks a host.
Rabbi Zeira's fasts so Babylonian learning would be found and Elazar's sleep is not disturbed.
Thirty days of fasting so the fire of Gehinnom would not rule him.
Rabbis secretly watch him, notice his skin is burned, and Rav Yehuda cites Rav's reading of a verse.
Jeremiah 9:11 is cited: who is the wise man that will understand this, and why the land perished.

85b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages and prophets could not explain the verse until God Himself explained it.
Jeremiah 9:12 is cited: they forsook My Torah which I set before them.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, explains that they did not recite the blessing over Torah study first.
Rav Hama reads Proverbs 14:33 as describing a scholar, son of a scholar or of an ignoramus.
Ulla explains the adage that a small coin in an empty barrel makes a loud noise.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira why Job 3:19 says the great and small are there, if we already know that.
Those who humble themselves over Torah become great in the World-to-Come; those who serve it become free.
Reish Lakish cannot find Rabbi Hiyya's grave and laments that he analyzed Torah as well as he did.
A divine voice tells him he analyzed Torah like Hiyya but did not disseminate it like him.
Rabbi Hanina boasts he could restore Torah by his analytic power if it were forgotten.
Rabbi Hiyya rebuts: you cannot compare, since I act to ensure Torah is not forgotten.
Hiyya describes his work: making flax nets, hunting deer, writing the Torah and teaching children to keep it alive.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says how great are Hiyya's deeds.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei asks whether his deeds exceed those of the Master.
Rabbi Yehuda affirms it and says there is no one like him in Israel, not even among fathers.
Rabbi Zeira dreams of Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and the others' places in the heavenly academy are described.
Rabbi Hiyya's place is among the furnace-workers, since a smith's son enters there.
Rav Hviva relates that a Sage saw Elijah, whose face glowed by day and burned like fire at night.
Elijah explains that the Sages' academy in heaven is entered, but not Rabbi Hiyya's radiant cave.
Asks what the signs are that distinguish the places in heaven.
Angels go up and down, but Rabbi Hiyya ascends and descends himself, so the Sage could not identify the spot.
Two fiery spirits strike a man and blind him; he goes to the cave, says he learned a teaching, and is healed.
Elijah regularly attended Rabbi Yehuda's academy, but one new moon he did not come.
Rabbi Yehuda asks why the new moon shone on him.
Elijah explains he stands with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who sought the Messiah before his time.
Asks whether there are counterparts to these men in this world.
Yes, Rabbi Hiyya and his sons; Rabbi Yehuda decrees a fast, and they bring rain.
Hiyya's sons pray, the wind blows and rain falls, and the world is stirred by the revival of the dead.
Asks who revealed the secret in the world, that a wind blows and rain falls.
They say it is Elijah; the men are brought to Elijah, who strikes them.
Sixty fiery spirits come upon them like a fire-bear and scatter them, as Shmuel Yarhinah is mentioned.
Shmuel Yarhinah was Rabbi's physician, and Rabbi weakened in his eyes.
Shmuel asks if he should anoint Rabbi's eyes with a salve.
Rabbi replies that he cannot, and Shmuel says he cannot treat him with a salve.
He places a salve underneath his bed, and Rabbi is healed.
Rabbi was tormented trying to fix him, but the matter was not working.
Shmuel says Rabbi should not trouble himself, since he sees the book of Adam the first man, written by Shmuel Yarhinah.

86a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A gloss records the final tanna'im and amora'im: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Natan, then Rav Ashi and Ravina.
Psalm 73:17 is offered as a mnemonic: the sanctuary alludes to Rav Ashi and the word considered to Ravina.
Rav Kahana reports that Rabba bar Nahmani died from fear of a decree of religious persecution.
His enemies accuse him before the king of exempting twelve thousand Jewish men from the head tax.
The king's messenger is sent after him, since many men study in his academy during Adar and Elul.
Rabba flees from town to town and is finally found hiding back in Pumbedita.
The king's messenger lodges at Rabba's inn, where the tray and cups turn his face backward.
The attendants ask what they should do, since the man is the king's agent.
Rabba instructs them to serve one cup and remove the tray, and the messenger is healed.
The messenger realizes Rabba is nearby and promises not to reveal him unless he is beaten.
Rabba is brought before the messenger, prays, and the wall crumbles so he can escape.
Rabba hides in a swamp studying Torah, where the heavenly academy is debating a leprosy question.
Leviticus 13:2 is cited: if the white spot precedes the white hair the person is impure, otherwise pure.
In heaven, God holds the person pure while the rest of the academy holds him impure.
They ask who can arbitrate this dispute.
Rabba bar Nahmani is chosen, as he said he is preeminent in leprosy and tent impurity.
The Angel of Death cannot approach him while he studies; a wind startles him into thinking soldiers come, so he dies.
Dying, he declares it pure; a Divine Voice praises him, and a note falls in Pumbedita announcing his summons.
Abaye and Rava search for his place, and birds in the marsh reveal where the body is.
They mourn him for three days and three nights, with a ban on anyone who withdraws from the mourning.
A note falls telling them to return home in peace.
On the day he died, a wind knocked a traveler from his camel as it crossed the river, and the traveler was cast across.
Asks what this is.
They tell him Rabba bar Nahmani has died.
Rabba prays to God: all the world is Yours, and Rabba is Yours, so why destroy the world for him?
Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta is introduced as a man of the flesh, meaning corpulent, in a story about heat.
On a hot day he sits in the mountain shade and asks his daughter to fan him, promising her a quantity of nard.
A wind blows; he asks how much nard he should buy, and the answer is in accordance with local custom.
Asks what must be brought in a place where bread and drink are customarily provided.
If you tell them to hurry, they will bring it to you; they reply that not everyone is like you.
The story of Rabban Yohanan ben Matya, who told his son to hire workers and sustain them.
The Gemara notes the mishna's wording: if he has stipulated provisions for them, they are owed as stated.

86b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's supporting incident: Rabban Yohanan ben Matya's son hires workers and promises them unspecified sustenance.
The father replies that even a feast like Solomon's would not discharge the duty to the descendants of the patriarchs.
Asks whether Abraham's feast was superior to Solomon's, given the lavish provisions described for Solomon.
I Kings 5:2-3 is cited to describe the daily provisions of Solomon's table.
Guryon in Rav's name and Rabbi Yitzhak explain the flour was for baked dough and meat pudding.
Rabbi Yitzhak explains that Solomon's thousand wives each prepared a feast, each hoping he would dine with her.
Genesis 18:7 is read by Rav: a tender and good calf means three calves, a meal for three men.
Solomon's feast was for all Israel and Judah, whereas Abraham's was for three guests, citing I Kings 4:20.
Asks what the fattened fowl mentioned in the verse are.
Rav says they were force-fed, while Shmuel says they were fattened and standing on their own.
Rabbi Yohanan says the choicest animal is an ox and the choicest fowl is a hen, with particular sources.
Amemar describes black fowl found among hens and the details of the fattened birds.
Genesis 18:7 is cited again, with Rav's reading that a single calf 'tender and good' is three calves.
Objects that one could read 'tender and good' as a single calf, as people say, so why three?
Asks why the verse writes 'tender and good' if the meaning is only for exposition.
Rabba bar Ulla raises an objection against this reading, attributed to Rav Hoshaya or Rav Natan.
Genesis 18:7-8 is cited: the servant hurries to prepare the calf, and each guest was given a portion.
Asks why three portions are needed when one would suffice.
Rav Hanan bar Rava says three are needed so they can feed the guests three kinds of relish, including mustard.
Rabbi Tanhum says one should never depart from custom, since Moses ascended and ate no bread of the angels.
Moses and the angels' bread are cited, and it is argued the text only says they appeared to eat and drink.
Rav Yehuda says what Abraham did personally God did personally for his children, and what he did through an agent, God did through an agent.
Genesis 18:7 is cited: Abraham ran to the herd, showing the personal act.
Verses are cited showing God personally providing quail, manna and the cloud for the people.
Verses are cited where God stands before them at the rock and sits under the tree.
Verses are cited showing Abraham walking with his guests and the Lord leading the people by day and water from the rock.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina's view differs, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches the same.
Each merit's reward is listed: three received three, manna and the cloud, and Miriam's well for the washing of feet.
Rabbi Yannai son of Rabbi Yishmael offers a teaching about washing feet.
Objection: the teaching seems to suspect them of conduct like Arabs who bow to dust, which Ishmael's school rejects.
Genesis 18:1 is cited: the Lord appeared to Abraham at the oaks of Mamre while he sat in the tent entrance in the heat of the day.
Asks what the heat of the day means.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina says that was the third day after Abraham's circumcision, and God removed the sun to spare him guests.
God comes to visit Abraham; the sun is removed, Eliezer goes out and finds no one, and says he is not trusted.
This is the saying: there is no faith in servants.
Genesis 18:3 is cited: the servant went out, saw God standing at the door, and Abraham asked God to pass by.
When Abraham saw God prostrate before him, he said it is not proper to stand here.
Genesis 18:2 is cited: Abraham lifted his eyes and saw three men standing over him, and ran to meet them.
Earlier they came to stand, but when they saw he was in pain, they said it is not proper to stand here.
Asks who the three men were.
Michael brought Sarah the news, Raphael healed Abraham, and Gabriel went to overturn Sodom.
Objection: Genesis 19:1 says two angels came to Sodom, while Michael went with him to save Lot.
Michael went with Lot to save him, and so the verse says He overturned the cities, not they.
Asks why the verse's wording for Abraham's words differs from the wording for Lot's words in the same context.

87a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Genesis 19:3 is cited: Lot urged the angels greatly, and they acquiesced.
Rabbi Elazar derives that one may decline a lesser man's request, but not a greater man's.
Genesis 18:5 and 18:7 are cited: a morsel of bread, and the calf Abraham ran to fetch.
Rabbi Elazar says the righteous say little and do much, while the wicked say much and do not even a little.
Ephron's example is cited: he asked four hundred shekels, then took them in centenarii coins from Abraham.
Rabbi Yitzhak derives that a woman is more stingy toward guests than a man, since Sarah wanted only flour.
Asks why Abraham did not serve bread, given that he told Sarah to bake cakes.
Efrayim Miksha'a says in Rabbi Meir's name that Abraham ate only in ritual purity, and Sarah was menstruating.
Genesis 18:9 is cited: they asked where Sarah was, and he said she was in the tent, to show her modesty.
Rav Yehuda, or Rabbi Yitzhak, says the angels knew Sarah was in the tent.
Asks what the point of saying in the tent is.
To make her beloved to her husband.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina gives other reasons, and a teaching in Rabbi Yosei's name notes the verse teaches courtesy.
Shmuel holds one may not ask about a woman's welfare through her husband, which seems to conflict.
It is different because the verse reports Sarah saying: after I have withered, shall I have pleasure?
Rav Hisda explains: after the flesh was spent and wrinkles grew, the flesh was restored and beauty returned.
Asks how to reconcile Abraham's words, My lord is old, with the verse stating I am old.
A teaching of Rabbi Yishmael's school: it is proper to avoid saying something unpleasant, as God also altered the words to spare Sarah.
Genesis 18:12-13 and 21:7 are cited to show the verses' wording about Sarah's age.
Genesis 21:7 is cited: who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?
Rabbi Levi says on the day Abraham weaned Isaac, the nations mocked that an old couple had adopted a foundling.
Abraham gathers the great men of the generation, and Sarah miraculously nurses all the children.
