Isaac's face changes to resemble Abraham's, and they all declare Abraham fathered Isaac.
Genesis 25:19 is cited: Abraham fathered Isaac, showing Abraham was not old before that.
Whoever spoke with Abraham then spoke with Isaac, and Abraham's prayer made old age come.
Genesis 24:1 is cited: Abraham was old and advanced in days, and Jacob had no illness.
Jacob prays and illness comes upon him.
Genesis 48:1 is cited: Joseph was told his father was ill.
Elisha was not ill until he came, prayed, and was healed.
2 Kings 13:14 is cited: Elisha fell ill with the illness of which he would die, inferring another illness.
A baraita: Elisha had three illnesses: one who pushed Gehazi, one who sent bears among children, and one who died.
2 Kings 13:14 is cited for the illness of which he died.
The mishna: go out and say to them, on condition you owe me only bread and legumes.
Rav Aha son of Rav Yosef asks whether the mishna says bread and legumes, or bread with legumes.
Rav Hisda answers with an idiom about the vav in the mishna's wording.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says there is no need to state that everything follows local custom.
Asks what the word all is meant to include.
The mishna case: a worker hired as one of the city's residents is paid the lowest of the wage, per Rabbi Yehoshua.
The mishna opens its list of those who may eat from the produce of their labor, including one who works on attached or detached produce.

87b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna continues: a laborer may not eat produce while its work is incomplete, nor from non-land-grown items.
Asks from where this rule that a laborer may eat from attached produce is derived.
Deuteronomy 23:25 is cited: when you enter your neighbor's vineyard you may eat grapes.
Asks, since the vineyard is the source, from where the rule extends to all other produce.
Derived by analogy to a vineyard: any produce grown from the ground, at its completion, may be eaten by the laborer.
Objection: a vineyard is special because its owner must leave olelot for the poor.
The rule is instead derived from standing grain, Deuteronomy 23:25-26, which allows plucking ears by hand.
Asks why standing grain must be the same grain liable for ḥalla, rather than any standing produce.
A verbal analogy to the word standing in Deuteronomy 16:9 about the omer shows it means grain liable to ḥalla.
Objection: the comparison fails, since a vineyard is not liable for ḥalla, and standing grain is not liable for olelot.
No single case fits; their common feature is growth from the earth and that a laborer may eat at completion.
Asks what is unique about their common feature.
Both have an altar aspect, since wine and flour are offered, so an olive, with its oil in offerings, should also qualify.
Objection: the olive is itself called a vineyard in the verse, so it cannot be derived from the common feature.
Judges 15:5 is cited: the standing grain and the olive yards, kerem zayit, are burned.
Rav Pappa says an olive is called kerem zayit, not kerem, so the olive is derived from the common feature.
Notes the difficulty that no source yet shows a laborer may eat all produce while he works.
Shmuel says the word sickle includes all sickle owners, while the verse about a sickle is needed for the harvest.
Asks, granting the sickle derivation, from where is it derived for one who does not harvest.
Rabbi Yitzhak says the verse standing grain includes all owners of standing grain.
Objects that standing grain is already liable for ḥalla, so why needs the verse to include all owners.
Rava cites a baraita: when you come is written here and shall not the sun go down over him is written there.
As there the verse refers to a worker, so here it refers to a worker in your neighbor's vineyard, not a Samaritan's.
Discussion of whether it is permitted to eat from stolen goods of a Samaritan, according to differing views.
It is established that the verse refers to a neighbor's vineyard, not consecrated produce.
Verses cited on the worker's appetite: he may eat his fill but not by gorging, and may not suck grapes.
The worker may eat when he gives to the owner's tools and may not eat when he does not.
Rabbi Yannai says untithed produce, tevel, is not liable for tithes.

88a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Produce is subject to tithes only once it has been brought until it sees the front of the house.
Deuteronomy 26:13 is cited: I have removed the consecrated from the house.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that even bringing produce into the courtyard makes it subject to tithes.
Deuteronomy 26:12 is cited: they shall eat in your gates and be satisfied.
Asks whether Rabbi Yohanan too must accept the wording from the house.
The house is not meant literally: a courtyard must be secured like a house, not open to the public.
Asks whether Rabbi Yannai must accept the verse's wording in your gates.
The word gates teaches that completion applies only when produce enters through the gate, not via roofs or enclosures.
Rav Hanina Hoza'a objects: an owner and laborer may eat untithed, so a buyer should be liable even before it enters the house.
Asks whether the case must be one in a field.
Rav Pappa says the case is a fig tree in a garden whose branches lean into the courtyard.
Asks whether the owner should then also be liable, since the produce is in the courtyard or house.
The owner's eyes are on the tree, while the buyer's eyes are on the purchase inside the courtyard or house.
Asks whether a buyer is actually liable for tithes by Torah law.
A baraita holds that the shops of Beit Hino were destroyed for strictly following Torah law over rabbinic safeguards.

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Deuteronomy 14:22 is cited: tithe and eat, so the buyer's duty to tithe is only a rabbinic support verse.
Asks what the word kenafshekha, as you are, is meant to teach if not the laborer's right to eat.
A baraita: if you muzzled yourself, you are exempt from muzzling, so a laborer you muzzle is exempt likewise.
Mar Zutra objects from a mishna on when cucumbers and gourds become subject to tithes.
No: the mishna means from the blossom falling inside the house or courtyard.
Asks why the mishna did not say until they lose their blossom if that is the intended meaning.
Had it said until, one might think tithes wait until all the blossoms are gone; from when teaches it starts at the first loss.
Mar Zutra son of Rav Nahman objects from a baraita: the granary point is completion of work, meaning bringing in.
Olives and grapes lack a granary, so bringing into a house fixes tithes; wheat and barley have a granary explicitly.
Asks where we derive a person's right to eat detached produce while working.
Derived by a fortiori from an ox, but the ox case is not a fair comparison since one must muzzle an ox.
Asks why an employer should not be commanded about his laborer's muzzling, by a fortiori from an ox.
Deuteronomy 23:25 is cited: as the laborer's soul, if you muzzle him he is exempt.
Deuteronomy 23:26 is cited: standing grain twice, showing a person may eat detached produce.
Rabbi Ami says a person eating detached produce needs no verse, since the verse concerns attached produce.
Deuteronomy 23:25 is cited: when you enter your neighbor's vineyard, as the scriptural basis for oxen.
Asks, given the case of one hired to carry, from where we know an ox may eat attached produce.
Explains a fortiori arguments from the ox and a person, and why the commands about sustaining and muzzling differ.
Leviticus 25:36 is cited: that your brother may live with you, applying to a person and not an ox.
The repeated word neighbor is used to derive that an ox may eat attached produce.
Ravina holds both the detached-person and attached-ox rules need their own verses, citing Deuteronomy 25:4.

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why the word ox is needed if all animals are included, as Shabbat shows.
The word ox juxtaposes the muzzler and the muzzled animal, so each may eat attached and detached produce.
A baraita: threshing applies to produce grown from the ground at completion, excluding milking, butter and cheese.
Asks why this exclusion is needed, since the vineyard verse already excludes such work.
Standing grain is written to include all standing produce, so it is needed to exclude items not grown from the ground.
Another baraita: threshing includes any completed item, excluding weeding garlic and onions, which are not yet complete.
Asks why this is needed, since not putting produce into the owner's vessel already bars eating.
It is needed because the small garlic and onions are not yet complete for the whole field, though they are picked.
Another baraita: separating dates and dried figs, already complete for tithes, bars the laborer from eating.
Objection: a baraita says a laborer may eat from one who separates dates and dried figs.
Rav Pappa says that baraita concerns unripe dates left on the ground to ripen, not complete for tithes.
Another baraita: a laborer may not eat from items whose work is complete for ḥalla, such as kneaded or baked dough.
Objection: why is this needed, if the work is already complete for tithes once brought into the house?
The baraita refers to places outside Eretz Yisrael, where tithes do not apply.
If so, ḥalla also does not apply outside Eretz Yisrael, so the case must be in the land itself.
It refers to the seven years of conquest and the seven of division, when ḥalla applied but tithes did not.
Objection: tithes are not the decisive factor for the laborer, since completion of work is.
Ravina proposes combining the two baraitot into one: a laborer may eat items not complete for tithes or ḥalla.
Asks whether a laborer may roast produce over fire and eat it, whether that is like grapes.
A baraita permits the owner to give workers wine so they do not eat many grapes, and to dip bread in vinegar.

ranges.en: The Gemara refutes the proof: the issue was whether the produce itself may be singed, not the worker's fitness.
A baraita: laborers may eat grapes at the ends of the rows, provided they do not singe them in fire.
The prohibition there is due to neglecting work, not the fire; the real dilemma is when his family can singe for him.
A baraita: a laborer may not singe, heat in the ground, or break produce on rocks, but may break it bit by bit.
There too the reason is neglect of work; sweetening by rock is not a clear argument, since the fruit is always sweetened a little.
A baraita on laborers plucking figs and dates: they may not dip the fruit in salt and eat, implying sweetening is prohibited.
Salt adds an ingredient, unlike singeing, so the baraita's prohibition does not settle the question.
A contradictory baraita permits a worker hired to harvest to dip the fruit in salt and eat.
Asks which clause of that baraita the dipping permission refers to, the agreement clause or the Torah-entitled clause.
Abaye: in Eretz Yisrael dipping fixes consumption as a meal; outside it does not, since tithes apply only in the land.
Rava objects: no produce is a meal in Eretz Yisrael by Torah law yet permitted outside it, as the Sages model enactments on Torah law.
Rava: one fruit dipped in salt is only a casual meal, but two make a meal, so two-by-two eating requires tithes.
Asks from where we derive that dipping two fruits in salt establishes them as subject to tithes.
Rav Mattana cites Micah 4:12: he gathered them like sheaves to the threshing floor, so gathering two counts as storing.
The Sages taught: cows that tread on produce already completed but threshed again as part of its preparation for food.

ranges.en: Threshing teruma or tithe does not violate the prohibition on muzzling, but for appearances one brings a similar produce; Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai adds vetches.
A contradictory baraita: a Jew threshing with a gentile's cow violates muzzling, while a gentile with a Jew's cow does not.
Notes the difficulty of conflicting rulings on teruma and tithe across the two baraitot.
Teruma is resolved by distinguishing actual teruma from its growths, but tithe is not resolved that way yet.
Rejects the suggestion that tithe growths are like teruma growths, since growths of tithe are non-sacred produce.
Resolved by first versus second tithe, or by the views of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on second tithe.
Asks what the circumstances of a cow threshing tithe are.
Tithe separated before teruma while still on the stalks; or threshing inside the wall of Beit Pagei near Jerusalem.
Definite tithe versus demai: the ruling of one baraita concerns certain produce, the other doubtfully tithed produce.
Asks whether there is such a thing as demai teruma, given that demai tithe exists by rabbinic decree.
A baraita: Yohanan the High Priest annulled the tithe declaration and decreed demai, having found Jews separating only teruma.
The baraita refers to demai teruma in the case of tithe.
The question put to Rav Sheshet: whether a cow that eats and grows fat is because the food benefits it.
Objects that the food does not benefit the animal, since it is a beast that suffers from the work.
Rav Sheshet cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: he brings vetches because they are better for it than anything, showing benefit.
Asks whether a person may tell a gentile to muzzle his cow and thresh, since telling a gentile is only rabbinic on Shabbat.
A baraita: a gentile threshing with a Jew's cow does not violate muzzling, so the matter has no prohibition.
The first clause of the baraita is taught because the last clause concerns a Jew threshing a gentile's cow.
Shmuel's father is sent oxen, reported as part of the discussion.

ranges.en: Asks the halakha when gentiles steal and castrate animals on a Jew's behalf
Shmuel's father rules that they must use artifice in return and make the gentiles sell the animal
Rav Pappa says the proof is inconclusive, since Eretz Yisrael holds Noahides are bound by the castration prohibition
Rava proposes that the owners must sell castrated animals only for slaughter, not for plowing
Abaye objects that penalizing them by requiring a sale is enough, so no further restriction is needed
It is obvious that selling to an adult son counts as selling to a stranger
Asks the halakha when the buyer is a minor son
Rav Aḥai prohibits such a sale to a minor son while Rav Ashi permits it, with Mareimar and Mar Zutra following each view
Some say a pair of pious men would swap such oxen with each other
Rami bar Ḥama asks the halakha if one placed a thorn in a threshing animal's mouth
Placing a thorn would be proper muzzling, so the case is framed wrongly
Reformulates the dilemma: a thorn that settled in the mouth and was not removed
Asks the halakha if a lion was made to crouch over the animal from outside
Making a lion crouch would be proper muzzling, so the case is framed wrongly
Reformulated dilemmas: a lion crouching outside, its young placed outside, thirst, or a blanket spread over the grain
Resolves one dilemma from a baraita: the owner may starve his animal, and the homeowner may untie straw before it
The proof fails, since in that case the animal does get to eat from the produce
Alternatively the baraita means untying straw before threshing begins, so the animal fills up beforehand
Rabbi Yonatan asks Rabbi Simai about muzzling from outside before threshing and lays out the two sides
Rabbi Simai says Rabbi Yonatan can learn it from priests, citing Leviticus 10:9
Quotes the verse forbidding wine and strong drink when the priests come into the Tent of Meeting
A plain reading of the verse forbids only drinking before entry, so the proof does not work
Cites the next verse in Leviticus 10:10 about distinguishing sacred from non-sacred
Just as drinking is barred only at the time of entry, muzzling is barred only at the time of threshing
A baraita: one who muzzles another's cow or mixes kinds is exempt, and only threshing muzzled or mixing kinds is flogged
Asks the halakha when one muzzles or leads animals by voice alone
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that such a person is liable
Reish Lakish holds that such a person is exempt
Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that twisting the mouth to speak counts as an action
Reish Lakish explains that a mere voice does not count as an action
Rabbi Yoḥanan raises an objection against Reish Lakish

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah in Temura: one may not substitute, but if he does the substitute is sacred and he receives forty lashes
Reish Lakish asks whose opinion this mishnah follows
Explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds one is flogged for a prohibition with no action involved
Asks whether the mishnah can be established as Rabbi Yehuda's view
The mishnah's first clause says everyone, men and women, may substitute, which conflicts with Rabbi Yehuda
Recalls the earlier question of what the word everyone is meant to add
It adds an heir who substitutes an animal he inherited
So the mishnah does not follow Rabbi Yehuda
If it followed Rabbi Yehuda, an heir could neither substitute nor lean on an offering
The anonymous tanna may agree with Rabbi Yehuda on one point and differ on another
A baraita: one who muzzles and threshes is flogged and pays four kav for a cow and three for a donkey
By the principle that one is not both flogged and liable to pay, the baraita contradicts itself
Abaye answers that this is Rabbi Meir's view, who allows both flogging and payment
Rava explains that the prohibition on the prostitute's wages applies even to one who committed incest
Rav Pappa explains the payment begins at pulling the cow, while flogging begins only at muzzling
Rav Pappa reports two dilemmas raised by his students and resolved as prohibitions, one correct and one not
Asks whether one may knead dough with milk
Resolves it as prohibited, in accordance with the halakha
A baraita: kneading with milk or smearing the oven with tail fat makes the whole loaf forbidden
Asks whether one may place a male and female of different species into the same pen
Resolves it as prohibited, though this ruling is not in accordance with the halakha
Shmuel holds adulterers must be seen behaving as such, but crossbreeding requires insertion like a brush into a tube
Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami objects from a baraita that the verse would otherwise prohibit mere holding
The verse in Leviticus 19:19 limits the prohibition to crossbreeding diverse kinds only
By inference, holding diverse kinds must also be prohibited, which undermines Shmuel's view
Asks what holding means and why the term is used for insertion
Holding is a euphemism for insertion, a fine expression
Rav Yehuda rules that mating within one species is permitted, since the worker is occupied and not licentious
Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami raises an objection against this ruling

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita's verse: had it said only do not mate, one might forbid holding, so the verse limits the prohibition to diverse kinds
From the verse it follows that mating within one species is permitted, and also holding within a species
Holding is allowed within a species but inserting is not, since the tanna specifies holding
Holding means inserting, a euphemism the tanna uses, so the objection fails
Rav Ashi reports that the house of Rav Neḥemya the Exilarch asked him this question
Asks whether one may put a same-species animal and a different-species animal into one pen, given the same-species one draws the other
Rules it prohibited though not in accordance with the halakha, because the slaves would deliberately crossbreed
Mishnah: a laborer who works with only hands or only feet, or even shoulders, may eat the produce
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda requires labor with both hands and feet to eat
Asks the reason for the Rabbis' ruling in the first clause
The verse about entering a neighbor's vineyard does not specify a kind of labor, so any labor suffices
Restates Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda's view that both hands and feet are required
Asks the reasoning behind Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
An ox threshes with all four legs, so a laborer likewise must work with both hands and feet
Rabba bar Rav Huna asks whether threshing with geese and chickens qualifies, and the dilemma is left unresolved
Rabba bar Avuh rules that laborers may eat grapes before treading, but drink wine only after they tread
Mishnah: a laborer working on figs may not eat grapes, and may eat only while working, though he may eat while walking
Asks whether a laborer on one vine may eat from another vine of the same kind as the owner's food
If not, asks how an ox tied to a wagon can eat from the vine it works on
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi says the ox works one end of long branches while eating from the other
A mishna permits eating figs while working on figs, so same-kind produce is allowed
Asks how such a case can arise if a laborer may not eat from another vine
Rav Sheisha says the mishna concerns a hanging vine, eating from one edge while working the other
The mishna says the laborer may hold back until reaching good fruit and eat there
If one may eat from another vine, he could simply go and eat there
There the concern is neglecting work, so the dilemma only arises when his wife and children are present
Another mishna: laborers may eat while walking to other rows and on return, out of duty to restore lost property
The Gemara reasons that walking is not labor, so one working on this vine may not eat from another
Rejects that conclusion: the one working may eat from another vine, and walking alone is what bars eating
An alternative version attributes the prohibition to walking not counting as work, implying work on this vine permits another vine
Rejects that inference, since the other version may still hold that one working on this vine may not eat from another

ranges.en: A walking laborer counts as one who is working, but he may eat only by rabbinic ordinance
Mishnah: a donkey may eat while being unloaded
Asks how the donkey can eat from the load if the load is being removed
Suggests the mishna means the donkey may eat until it is fully unloaded
A baraita says donkeys and camels may eat from their load, provided the owner does not feed them by hand
Mishnah: a laborer may eat cucumbers or dates worth a dinar, and Rabbi Elazar Ḥisma limits this, though the Rabbis allow it
Asks how the Rabbis differ from the first tanna if both say the same thing
The difference is whether one teaches a person not to be a glutton
Explains the difference through Rav Asi's rulings on eating a single cluster, and why both rulings are needed
Rav reports a concealed scroll in which Isi ben Yehuda says the verse covers any passerby, not only laborers
Rav responds that Isi has left no livelihood for anyone, since passersby would consume the whole vineyard
Rav Ashi suggests Isi meant only laborers who work for their meal
Rav Kahana objects that owners prefer hired laborers to strangers, so the reading does not hold
Asks whether a laborer eats from his own property or from property of Heaven, and what difference that makes
Explains the difference: if he gives food to his wife and children, it is valid only if it is his own property
A mishna says a laborer may eat cucumbers or dates worth a dinar, suggesting the food is his own
If the food is his own, how can a sixth-of-a-dinar wage allow eating a full dinar's worth
Replies that the Merciful One grants him the right to eat more than his wages
Rabbi Elazar Ḥisma limits eating to the wages, and the dispute appears to turn on whether the food is his own
Everyone agrees the food is his own, and the dispute is about the meaning of kenafshekha in the verse
Rabbi Elazar reads kenafshekha as in accordance with his soul, the risk he takes, while the Rabbis read it like your own person
A baraita: a nazirite laborer's request to give grapes to his family is not heeded
If the laborer eats from his own property, why would his request not be heeded
The nazirite case differs because of the proverb telling a nazirite not to approach a vineyard
A baraita: a laborer's request to give produce to his family is not heeded
If the laborer eats from his own property, why would his request not be heeded
A laborer here means a nazirite laborer
Asks why two baraitot use different terms, nazirite and laborer, if they are taught separately
A baraita derives from the verse about not putting produce in your vessel that the laborer's family may not receive it
If the reason is the nazirite proverb rather than the verse, the baraita's source is a decree on nazirites
Accepts the nazirite reading, so the baraita does not show that laborers in general may not share their food
Next, a mishna about a laborer hired to pick figs is brought to test the same question

ranges.en: A laborer who stipulates that he and his sons may eat is exempt from tithing, but his son who eats must tithe
If the laborer eats from his own property, asks why the son is obligated to tithe
Ravina says it looks like a sale, so the son must tithe to avoid misunderstanding
A mishna: a laborer hired to work fourth-year produce may not eat it, and the owner must redeem and feed them if not informed
If the laborer eats from Heaven's property, the Merciful One would not entitle him to violate a prohibition
The mishna differs because it looks like a mistaken transaction
The latter clause of the same mishna: laborers hired to reseal broken cakes or barrels of tithed produce may not eat
Suggests the same mistaken-transaction explanation applies to the barrels as well
The mistaken-transaction explanation fails for barrels, since the laborers would know the wine was already tithed
Explains they knew the wine was tithed, and Rav Sheshet says the wine fell back into the pit it came from
A baraita says wine is tithed from descent into the pit, which contradicts Rav Sheshet
Rabbi Akiva's view explains the laborers' ignorance, and the mishna concerns one man who does both tasks
Rav Zevid taught the dispute in a version heard from Rabbi Hoshaya's school, where tithing begins when waste is drained
Barrels were opened not into the pit but for draining, and the same man both plugs and drains, so the laborers assumed both tasks
A mishna: a man may stipulate a wage increase in place of eating for adult children, slaves, and wife, but not minors or animals
If the laborer eats from Heaven's property, minors cannot waive their right, which explains why minors are excluded
If he eats from his own property, minors should also be stipulated for; asks what case the mishna concerns
A baraita of Rabbi Hoshaya seems to contradict the mishna about stipulating for minor slaves
Asks whether the two sources disagree on whether a laborer eats from his own property or from Heaven's
No, everyone agrees he eats from his own property, and the mishna and baraita concern different food provision
Asks what case the baraita concerns, and whether minors would then also be stipulated for
The Merciful One does not allow waiving the suffering of minor children who see food before them
Asks whether the mishna concerns a case where the father does not provide food

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how the mishna's rule fits the view that a master may say he will not feed his slave
Both sources concern a case where the master gives no food, and the tannaim disagree on whether he may withhold it
Rabbi Yoḥanan would then have ignored the mishna and ruled like the baraita, which seems unlikely
Retracts: everyone agrees a laborer eats from Heaven's property, so stipulating means feeding the slave beforehand
Then the same reasoning should apply to an animal, which would make the dispute pointless
Retracts again: the tannaim really dispute whether a laborer eats from his own property or from Heaven's
Mishna: a man may stipulate a wage increase in place of produce for adult dependents, but not for minors or animals
Mishna: laborers hired on fourth-year produce or broken cakes and barrels may not eat, and the owner must tithe and feed them if uninformed
Mishna: watchmen of produce may eat by local custom but not by Torah law
Rav holds only garden and orchard watchmen are limited, since a watchman counts as a laborer for eating
Shmuel holds only watchmen of winepresses and piles may eat, since watching does not count as doing labor
Rav Aḥa bar Rav Huna objects: if watching is not labor, why does watching the red heifer render garments impure
Rabba bar Ulla says it is a rabbinic decree lest the watchman move a limb of the heifer
Rav Kahana objects: a watchman of mixed cucumbers should not eat, so watching is not labor
Those cucumbers were uprooted, so their blossoms had not been removed and tithes did not yet apply
Rav Ashi adopts Shmuel's view, citing a mishna whose inference shows some watchers eat only by local custom
Mishna: four types of bailees, an unpaid bailee, a borrower, a paid bailee and a renter, each with different oath and payment rules
Asks which tanna taught the mishna about four types of bailees
Rav Naḥman says Rabba bar Avuh identified the tanna as Rabbi Meir
Rava objects that all Sages accept four types of bailees, so the attribution is unclear
Rav Naḥman clarifies that Rabbi Meir holds a renter is treated like a paid bailee
Yet a baraita has Rabbi Meir holding a renter pays like an unpaid bailee, which contradicts this
Rabba bar Avuh teaches that baraita in reversed order
If renters and paid bailees share one rule, why does the mishna count four types
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the mishna lists four types but there are only three sets of rules
A shepherd's animal drowned in the river and Rabba exempted him, since a paid bailee is not liable for unavoidable loss

ranges.en: Rabba holds a paid bailee need only guard as people normally guard
Abaye asks: then a shepherd who enters at the usual hour should be exempt from a theft that occurs then
Rabba agrees that such a shepherd is exempt
Abaye asks whether a bailee who dozes at the usual time is also exempt
Rabba agrees that he is exempt
Abaye cites a baraita that exempts only robbery by an army, as in the Job verse about the Sabeans
Rabba says the baraita concerns city watchmen, who are exempt only from attacks of that scale
Abaye cites a baraita on how far a paid bailee must guard, with Jacob's words to Laban as the standard
Rava says that baraita too concerns city watchmen, who must guard further
Abaye asks whether Jacob was himself a city watchman
Rava explains Jacob meant he gave Laban an extra level of guarding like city watchmen
Abaye cites a baraita: a shepherd who leaves his flock is liable only if he could have saved it
Asks whether the baraita refers to a shepherd who enters the city at usual hours
Rabba says no, it refers to one who enters when people do not usually enter
Abaye objects: then why is he exempt, since his negligence started the loss before it became an accident
Rabba explains the shepherd entered the city to save himself after hearing a lion roar, so it was not initially negligent
Abaye asks what the shepherd could have done about a lion
Rabba says he should have faced the lion with other shepherds and sticks
Abaye asks why the rule is stated for paid bailees, since an unpaid bailee who did not confront the lion is also liable
Rabba: an unpaid bailee is liable only if he could gather helpers for free, while a paid bailee must do so even for payment
Asks how far a paid bailee must pay for extra guards, and where else a paid bailee bears unavoidable losses
The bailee may recover the cost of the extra guards from the owner
Rav Pappa asks what the owner gains if he must pay the extra guards anyway
Abaye says the difference lies in the owner's familiarity with his animals and the extra effort of replacing them
Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna hold that the owner paid for extra guarding, so the bailee must give it
Story: a porter's animal drowned on a narrow bridge, and Rav Pappa held him liable
The porter asks what else he should have done
Rav Pappa says he should have transported the animals one by one
The porter asks whether anyone can transport animals one by one
Rav Pappa says earlier scholars complained, but since he is the expert hired for this, the responsibility is his
Story: flax left with a bailee was stolen by a robber, and Rav Naḥman held the bailee liable
Asks whether Rav Naḥman disagrees with Rav Huna bar Avin
Rav Huna bar Avin's ruling: an unpaid bailee may take an oath or sue the thief, while a paid bailee sues and takes no oath
Rava says the cases differ because government men stood nearby, so the bailee's own negligence caused the theft
Mishna: one wolf is not an unavoidable loss but two are; Rabbi Yehuda and others add cases of bandits, beasts, and deaths
Asks why a baraita says one wolf is an unavoidable loss, against the mishna
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says that baraita refers to a time of wolf attacks, following Rabbi Yehuda
Mishna: bandits count as an unavoidable loss
Asks why, since the shepherd should fight the bandit as one man against another
Rav says the mishna refers to armed bandits, whom the shepherd cannot reasonably resist
Dilemma: if both bandit and shepherd are armed, must one man stand against another, or does one risk his life more
It stands to reason the bandit risks his life while the shepherd does not, so the shepherd is not liable for refusing to fight
Abaye asks the halakha if a shepherd finds a known thief sitting in his place

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Case: a bailee taunts a thief that he has guards and dogs, then the thief steals; asks the halakha
Rava says it is as if the bailee led the animals to a place of beasts and bandits, since his taunt provoked the theft
Mishna: bailees may stipulate monetary exemptions, but a condition against the Torah is void unless made before the action
Asks why bailees may stipulate against what the Torah says, when such stipulations are normally void
The mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds a condition against the Torah is valid in monetary matters
Baraita on betrothal with a condition: Rabbi Meir voids it, while Rabbi Yehuda upholds it in monetary matters
But the mishna's latter clause, voiding such conditions, is Rabbi Meir's view, not Rabbi Yehuda's
The latter clause concerns non-monetary matters, so the mishna still follows Rabbi Yehuda
The mishna's clause voiding conditions preceded by action is Rabbi Meir's view, so the explanation fails
Baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir: a condition stated before the action is valid, one after the action is not
The whole mishna follows Rabbi Meir; the bailee here never bound himself to the Torah's bailee liabilities
Baraita: a paid bailee may take on a borrower's liability; Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute how it binds, and Rav discusses Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima
Baraita on a bill of divorce conditioned on impossible acts: valid only if the condition is met, per one tanna
Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima holds such a bill is valid, since an impossible condition is mere exaggeration
Rav Naḥman says the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the mishna does too
The mishna's wording, that a condition is valid only if it can be kept, implies an impossible condition is void
Chapter end marker, then mishna: a borrower who borrows a cow with its owner is exempt if it dies, based on Exodus 22:14

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a borrower who first borrows the cow and later the owner's services is liable if the cow dies, per Exodus 22:13
Asks whether the first clause can mean borrowing the owner's services literally at the same moment as the cow
The cow standing in the borrower's courtyard allows simultaneous acquisition, or the owner's services are lent only at the moment of pulling
Recalls the mishna on the four bailees: oath and payment rules for unpaid bailee, borrower, paid bailee and renter
A baraita divides the bailee passages in Exodus 22 into three: unpaid, paid, and borrower
Asks how the baraita knows which passage covers which bailee, since the first two are not explicit
A paid bailee bears more liability, so the second passage about theft and loss concerns him
Rather, the first passage concerns a paid bailee, since double payment for a false oath is also a stringency
Paying principal without an oath is a greater stringency than double payment, which arises only from a false oath
A borrower bears all the cost of the benefit for himself, so he alone pays the principal even for theft
But the animal needs food and guarding, which the borrower must provide, so not all the benefit is his
The borrower's rule still holds where food is free, or where guarding is minimal, or for borrowed vessels
Mishna: paid bailees and renters swear over injury, capture or death, but pay for loss and theft
Asks the source for a paid bailee's liability for loss, since theft is explicit in Exodus 22:11
A baraita derives loss from the repeated verb ganov yigganev, which teaches liability for any case
Asks the source for loss liability if the Torah does not use repeated verbs for emphasis
Eretz Yisrael derives it a fortiori: if theft, nearer to unavoidable, is paid, loss, nearer to negligence, must be too
If a fortiori suffices, why does the verse also state the rule explicitly
Sometimes the Torah derives a point by a fortiori but still writes it out explicitly
Asks the source for a borrower's liability when the animal is captured, as Exodus 22:13 lists only injury and death
Deriving capture from injury or death fails, since injury is foreseeable while capture is not
Capture is included in the paid bailee passage, so it is included in the borrower passage by analogy
The analogy fails: for a paid bailee the cases exempt him, while for a borrower they make him liable
Rabbi Natan derives it from the word or in Exodus 22:13, which separates injury and death into distinct cases
This works for Rabbi Yonatan, but Rabbi Yoshiya would need the word or for a different purpose, so what can be said
Rabbi Yoshiya's baraita: the verse on cursing father and mother covers cursing either parent alone
Rabbi Yonatan says the phrase father and mother means both together and also either one alone

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that the word together is needed only if the verse specifies liability only when both are cursed
Rabbi Natan's derivation from or follows Rabbi Yoshiya: injury and death alone create liability, since the animal is no longer as borrowed
Asks the source for a borrower's liability in cases of theft or loss
Deriving it from injury or death is refuted: the animal can still be sought after theft or loss, unlike injury
A baraita: an a fortiori inference from the paid bailee shows a borrower is liable for theft and loss, with no refutation
Asks what the baraita adds by saying the a fortiori has no refutation
The refutation: a paid bailee pays double for a false oath about armed bandits, so a borrower is not always stricter

Oaths normally exempt a person from paying; the Sages imposed one on the laborer because the employer is busy, while a renter is trusted with his oath
Rav Nachman: a renter with an undated lease who is told he already used five of ten years is believed to have been paid
Rav Acha of Difti objects: by that logic a borrower with a note who claims half repaid should be believed, and that is not the halakha
Ravina: a loan note serves collection and a receipt could be written, whereas a lease document is only meant to prevent claims of ownership
Rav Nachman: one may borrow a utensil in good condition indefinitely, with Rav Mari son of Shmuel and Rav Mari son of Rav Ashi adding conditions and limits
Rava and Rav Pappa limit borrowing rights to the specific orchard, well, or land named, and the right to dig new wells needs an act of acquisition
Mishna: if a rented house falls, the landlord must provide a replacement of similar size, rooms and windows, changing these only with both parties' consent
What are the circumstances of the mishna, since if the landlord merely rented a house without specification, the size rules seem unexplained
Reish Lakish: the landlord specified dimensions, so the replacement must be of a similar size and structure
If that is so, what is the purpose of stating this ruling, since it is obvious
Ravin reports Reish Lakish: the landlord said he rents a house like this one
But still, what is the purpose of stating this ruling, since it is obvious
It is needed where the house stood on a riverbank, so the words like this are taken to refer to dimensions and structure, not location
The chapter ends; Mishna on a tenant or sharecropper of a field, who must follow local custom for cutting, uprooting and plowing, and the produce, stubble and wine are divided

103b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Closing words of the previous mishna: vine branches and poles are divided, and both parties supply the poles.
Baraita: where custom is to cut, one may not uproot, and where custom is to uproot, one may not cut; each can block the other.
Gemara explains the first case: owner wants stubble left, cultivator objects that uprooting is too laborious, so neither may deviate.
Reverse case: owner wants the land cleared, cultivator wants the stubble kept, so neither may deviate from the custom.
Baraita conclusion: each party may prevent the other from deviating from the local custom.
Why does the baraita need to state that both parties can block each other? What is its purpose?
The baraita states the reason: each party can block the other's deviation, so neither may change the local practice.
Mishna: if plowing after harvest is customary, the cultivator must plow the field after the harvest.
Isn't this obvious? The Gemara asks why the ruling needs stating.
It is needed for a place where weeding is not customary, and this cultivator weeded anyway.
Objection: the cultivator might claim he weeded intending never to plow, so he should not be required to plow.
The mishna teaches that the cultivator had to state this intention to the owner beforehand to be exempt.
Mishna: all farming follows the local custom of the region.
What is the word all coming to add to the mishna's ruling?
Baraita: where custom is to rent trees with the land, they are rented; where custom is not to, they are not.
Isn't this obvious? The Gemara asks why a case of renting trees needs to be stated.
Case: everyone gives a third of the yield, but this landowner gave the field for only a quarter.
Objection: the owner may claim his reduced share was meant to exclude any share of the trees.
The baraita teaches that the owner should have specified this intention to the cultivator in advance.
Baraita: where custom is not to rent trees with the land, the trees are not presumed to be rented.
Isn't this obvious? The Gemara asks why the ruling needs stating.
Case: everyone accepts land for a quarter of the yield, but this cultivator took it for a third.
Objection: the cultivator may claim his added share was meant to get him a share of the trees.
The baraita teaches that the cultivator should have stated this intention to the owner in advance.
Mishna: just as the produce is divided, the straw and stubble are divided between owner and cultivator.
Rav Yosef says that in Babylonia the custom is not to give stubble to the sharecropper.
What is the practical difference resulting from this statement about Babylonian custom?
If one owner gives stubble, that is merely generosity, and his conduct does not establish a general custom.
Rav Yosef lists the boundary elements and fences that the owner of the land must supply for the field.
The general principle: the main boundary of the field is the owner's duty, and extra protection is the sharecropper's duty.
Rav Yosef specifies that the owner provides the hoe, shovel, bucket and irrigation device, while the sharecropper makes the channels.
Mishna: just as wine is divided, so the vine branches and poles are divided between owner and cultivator.
What are the poles used for? The Gemara asks what their purpose is.
Rabbi Yannai's school explains these are long poles split in half, used to support the vines.
Mishna: both the owner and the cultivator supply the poles.
Why do I need the mishna to state this? What is the reason it says so?
The reason is that both supply the poles, so both divide them.
Mishna: a cultivator whose irrigation spring dried up or whose trees were cut cannot deduct from rent unless explicitly promised them.
What are the circumstances of the mishna? If the large river dried up, why can't he deduct from his rent?
Objection: the cultivator could say it was a regional calamity, so he should be able to deduct from his rent.
Rav Pappa says the mishna refers to a small river that irrigates only this field, which the owner can tell him to deal with.

104a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Opening remark that the bucket example should have been brought to illustrate the point.
Rav Pappa says the first two mishnayot apply to tenancy and to contracting, but the later rules each apply to only one of them.
Mishna: if the cultivator asked explicitly to lease an irrigated field or a field with trees, he may deduct losses from his rent.
Objection: why can't the owner say he only named the type of field and never meant it would actually be irrigated?
Baraita: a seller of a beit kor of dirt may not retract, since he sold it only by name, provided the field is called that.
Baraita continues: the same applies to a vineyard sold by name, even if it has no vines, when it is called a vineyard.
Baraita continues: the same applies to an orchard sold by name, even without pomegranates, when it is called an orchard.
Objection: apparently the seller can say he meant only the name, so here too the owner can say the same.
Shmuel resolves it: the baraita concerns the owner naming the terms to the tenant, who then cannot object; the mishna concerns the tenant naming them.
Ravina says both the baraita and the mishna concern an owner who named the field, and the mishna's wording implies this.
Why does the owner need to state that the field is irrigated, when it is obvious from looking at it?
The owner must have said it by way of emphasis, to affirm that he is providing an irrigated field as it currently stands.
Mishna: a contractor who lets the field lie fallow pays a share based on what it could have produced, as the contract states.
Rabbi Meir expounded the common language used in ordinary legal documents to derive halakhic conclusions.
Baraita supports Rabbi Meir: he says the contractor is liable, since the document says he pays best produce if he fails to cultivate.
Rabbi Yehuda likewise expounded common language, as is taught in a baraita.
Baraita: a rich husband brings his wife's offerings, since his marriage contract makes him responsible for all her obligations.
Hillel the Elder likewise expounded common language.
Baraita: Alexandrian men betrothed women early, and others snatched them, so the Sages sought to make their children mamzerim.
Hillel asked the children to bring their mother's marriage contract, and found it contained a condition.
The wording of the contract shows the marriage took effect only upon entering the canopy, so the children are not mamzerim.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha also expounded common language, as is taught in a baraita.
Baraita: a creditor may not take collateral worth more than the debt, as he cannot exceed the debt's value.
The debtor's written receipt shows the collateral is limited to the value of the debt, as the document states.
If the creditor did not write this to the debtor, would the creditor not acquire the collateral anyway?
Objection: Rabbi Yohanan says a creditor who returned collateral and then the debtor died still keeps it against the heirs.

104b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Writing the sum in the document is effective for depreciation: if the collateral loses value, the rest is collected from the debtor's property.
Rabbi Yosei likewise expounded common language, as is taught in a baraita.
Baraita: where the custom is to write a dowry as a loan, the wife collects the full sum; where the custom is to double it, she collects only half.
The Sages of Neharbela collected one-third of the sum, and Mareimar also allowed collecting the added value written in honor of the daughter.
Objection by Ravina: but a baraita says that where the custom is to double the sum, she collects only half, so Mareimar contradicts it.
Not difficult: there the husband acquired the entire written sum from the bride's father, while here he did not, so the cases differ.
Ravina wrote an enhanced dowry for his daughter, and the groom's family asked to perform an act of acquisition on the full sum.
Ravina replies: if they want acquisition, the sum recorded will be the actual sum, not the doubled one; otherwise no acquisition is made.
A man told his heirs to give four hundred dinars to his daughter in her marriage contract, leaving the intended amount unclear.
Rav Aha sent to ask Rav Ashi: did the man mean four hundred actual dinars written as eight hundred, or four hundred written, meaning two hundred?
Rav Ashi: if he said give her, the full four hundred is intended and written as eight hundred; if he said write for her, four hundred is written as two hundred.
Some report a different version of Rav Ashi's ruling, depending on whether he said for her or in her marriage contract.
The Gemara rejects that version: the wording for or in makes no difference; only a plain give her yields the full sum.
A man received land and promised one thousand dinars if he left it fallow; he left one-third of it fallow.
The Sages of Neharde'a ruled he pays one-third of the stipulated sum, 333 and one-third dinars, for the neglected portion.
Rava says this is an asmakhta, a conditional promise lacking firm consent, so it does not effect acquisition and no payment is due.
According to Rava, how does this differ from the mishna's case of promising best-quality produce for leaving the field fallow?
There the promise was ordinary; here the extra large sum is an exaggeration, so it is an asmakhta and not a real monetary obligation.
A sharecropper planted wheat instead of sesame; Rav Kahana thought the owner should deduct the usual damage that sesame would have caused.
Rav Ashi objects with a proverb: let the land be weakened but not its owner; people discount land damage for quick profit.
Another sharecropper planted wheat on land meant for sesame, and it yielded more wheat than the usual value of sesame.
Ravina thought the owner should give the cultivator the added value of the wheat over the expected value of the sesame.
Rav Aha of Difti objects: the cultivator alone did not enhance the value, so the extra sum should be divided between them.
Neharde'a Sages: a joint venture is half loan and half deposit, an arrangement satisfactory to both the borrower and the lender.
If half the capital is a loan, the manager may use it as he likes, even to buy alcohol, since it is his money.
Rava: the venture is called a joint venture because the investor can say the money was given for business and not for drinking.
Rav Idi bar Avin: if the manager dies, the venture becomes movable property held by his children and liable for his debts.
Rava objects: it is called a joint venture so that on the manager's death it does not become movable property of his children.
Rava: if two parties drafted one venture as two separate documents, each is treated separately, so the lender bears the loss on one.

105a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If two joint ventures are recorded in one document, losses are netted together, which harms the borrower.
Rava: a manager who lost money, then made up the loss without telling the investor, cannot later ask the investor to share the original loss.
The investor's reply: the manager made up the loss only to protect his reputation, not to be reimbursed, so he cannot claim it.
Two managers in a joint venture who profited: if one proposes dividing now and the other wants to wait for more profit, the second may block the division.
If one asks for half the profits, the other may refuse, since the profit is tied to the principal as security.
If one asks for half the profits and half the principal, the other may refuse, since the capital is held jointly by both.
If one offers to share any loss, the other may refuse, since two people's luck is better than one's alone.
Mishna: a cultivator who will not weed the field and promises the owner his rent regardless is not heard, since weeds will spread to the owner's land.
If the cultivator promises to plow and weed after reaping, the owner may refuse, wanting his own superior wheat rather than wheat sprouting among weeds.
If the cultivator offers to buy good wheat from the market, the owner may refuse, wanting produce from his own land.
If the cultivator offers to weed only to the measure of his portion, the owner may refuse, since weeds would still spoil the field's reputation.
Why does the mishna give the weeds reason, if the other claims are not accepted? The Gemara asks what the real reason is.
Mishna: a cultivator whose field did not yield enough to make a pile must tend the field if there is enough produce to form a pile.
Rabbi Yehuda: a pile's measure is not fixed; it depends on whether the crop equals the seed needed to sow the field.
The Sages taught the mishna: if the crop is enough to form a pile, the cultivator must tend the field and give the owner his share.
The contract the cultivator writes shows he commits to plow, plant, reap and winnow, with the owner taking half, so the duty is contractual.
The contract continues: the owner takes half of the pile, and the cultivator takes the other half for his work and expenses.
How large must the pile be to count as enough to form a pile? The Gemara asks for the measure.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina: a pile is large enough when a winnowing shovel can stand in it unsupported.
What if a winnowing shovel protrudes from one side of the pile to the other? Is such a pile still large enough?
Come and hear a proof: Rabbi Abbahu had this explained to him by Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina.
Any pile that hides the sun from the shovel's blade is considered significant, which was said by Abbahu's tradition.
Levi says three se'a; the school of Rabbi Yannai says two se'a; Reish Lakish says two se'a exclusive of expenses.
A mishna in Ohalot supports the dispute: Beit Shammai hold unruly olives and grapes are susceptible to impurity, Beit Hillel say no.
What does the word unruly, peritzei, mean for olives?
Rav Huna: unruly olives are wicked olives that yield very little oil.
Rav Yosef asks what verse Rav Huna's explanation is derived from.
Rav Yosef cites Daniel: the wicked among your people shall rise up, supporting that peritzei means wicked.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak derives the meaning from Ezekiel: a son who is a robber, a shedder of blood.
How much oil must the olives yield for them to be classified as unruly?
Rabbi Elazar says four kav from one press; the school of Rabbi Yannai says two se'a from one press.
The Sages do not really disagree: each rules for a different local practice, with one kor versus three kor brought into the press.
The Sages taught: opening words of the next baraita.

105b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A zav and a pure person who climbed a weak tree or branch: the pure person becomes impure, since the zav moved him.
What are the circumstances of a tree with little strength?
The school of Rabbi Yannai: a tree is weak if its trunk is too narrow to hollow out a quarter-kav vessel from it.
And what are the circumstances of a weak branch or sukkah?
Reish Lakish: a branch is weak if its circumference fits inside a person's fist.
A mishna in Oholot supports the rule: one who walks on stones over a possible grave, or rides a weak animal, is impure as having moved the impurity.
What are the circumstances of a weak person?
Reish Lakish: a person is weak if his knees knock together when someone rides on him.
What are the circumstances of a weak animal?
The school of Rabbi Yannai: an animal is weak if it releases dung under strain when a person rides it.
The school of Rabbi Yannai states that the measure for prayer and for phylacteries is four kav.
What is the relevance of this measure for prayer?
Baraita: someone carrying a load on his shoulder when prayer time arrives lowers it behind him if under four kav, and puts it down if four kav.
What is the relevance of this measure for phylacteries?
Baraita: a load on the head that crushes phylacteries is forbidden if it is four kav, and permitted if it does not crush them.
Rabbi Hiyya teaches: one carrying refuse on his head may not move or tie his head phylacteries, but may tie them on his arm.
The Sages said in the name of the school of Sheila: even the cloth wrapping phylacteries may not be placed on the head of one wearing them.
And how much does Rabbi Sheila permit one to place on his head?
Abaye: even a tiny fraction, one-quarter of one-quarter of the smallest measure in Pumbedita, is still forbidden.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says the pile's measure is not fixed; it depends on whether it has enough crop to equal the seed needed to sow.
And how much is the amount equal to the seed needed to sow?
Rabbi Ami reports Rabbi Yohanan's view: four se'a of seed for a kor of land.
Rabbi Ami's own view is eight se'a of seed for a kor of land.
An elder explains the difference: in Rabbi Yohanan's years the land was rich, and in Rabbi Ami's years it was poor, so more seed was needed.
A mishna in Peah supports the rule: when wind scatters the sheaves, the owner gives the poor the amount of gleanings the field could yield.
And how much is the amount equal to the seed dropped during harvesting?
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Elazar, or possibly Rabbi Yohanan, said four kav for a kor.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma: is the measure for a field sown with a kor of seed, and is it for hand sowing or sowing by oxen?
Ravin's report of the same teaching is brought, but the dilemma about hand or ox sowing remains unresolved.
Mishna: if grasshoppers or wind destroyed a field, the cultivator deducts only if it is a regional disaster affecting the whole area.
Rabbi Yehuda: if the cultivator paid the owner a fixed sum, he never deducts, whether or not it is a regional disaster.
What are the circumstances of a regional disaster?
Rav Yehuda: most of the valley destroyed counts; Ulla: four surrounding fields destroyed on all four sides counts.
Ulla raises dilemmas in the West: a single furrow destroyed, a single furrow surviving, or a fallow or fodder field between destroyed fields.

106a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dilemmas about other seed types, and whether blight in one area and windblast in another count as a regional disaster; left unresolved.
If the owner told the cultivator to plant wheat, but he planted barley, which was blasted, is the barley damage counted as regional?
The cultivator's argument: even had he planted wheat, it would also have been blasted, since the whole region was hit.
The owner's counter: had the cultivator planted wheat, the verse of Job about decreeing a matter would have been fulfilled for him.
It stands to reason that the owner can answer that the wheat would have fulfilled the verse about the light shining upon his ways.
If the owner's fields were blasted along with this one, but most of the valley was not, is it a regional disaster or the owner's bad luck?
The owner can answer that a little would have been left for him, as Jeremiah says that a few were left from many.
If the tenant's fields were all blasted, is the damage a regional disaster that he may deduct, or his own bad luck?
It stands to reason that the owner can say the damage was due to the tenant's own bad luck, since all his fields were hit.
Why should this be so? Here too, let us say to the owner that a little would have been left for him.
Objection: the tenant's loss could be claimed as the owner's bad luck, so the owner should be able to argue a little would be left for him.
The tenant can answer: if you deserved something left over, it would have been left from your own land, not from the field you lease.
An objection from a mishna on the Jubilee repurchase: wind-blasted and mildewed years do not count toward the tally of years.
Analysis: the mishna's windblast and mildew cases are like the years of Elijah, when no produce at all grew, so partial produce does not count.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: the sold field differs, since the verse on years of crops refers to years with produce anywhere in the world.
Rav Ashi objects to Rav Kahana: then the Sabbatical Year should count, since there is produce outside Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Kahana: the Sabbatical Year is an abrogation of the King, that is God, so it does not count in the tally.
Mar Zutra's objection: then the Sabbatical Year should not count for redeeming a consecrated field, yet a mishna gives a sela per year including it.
Ravina: that case differs, since the field can still be used to lay out produce on, even though it may not be planted.
Shmuel: the cultivator deducts for a regional disaster only if he planted, since the owner could claim his planting would have spared the field.
Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita about a shepherd who left his flock: the owner could say his presence would have saved the animals, as in the verse about David.
The shepherd can reply that if the owner had merited a miracle, one would have occurred, as with Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's goats.
And let the owner say: granted that I did not merit a great miracle, but a small miracle should have happened for me.

106b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara notes that the apparent contradiction is indeed difficult.
Baraita: if a cultivator's crops are destroyed, he replants the first and second time, but not the third time.
A second baraita: he replants on the third occasion, but not after the fourth destruction.
The baraitot are not contradictory: one follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who makes a presumption after two occasions; the other follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who needs three.
Reish Lakish: the limit applies only if crops sprouted and locusts ate them; if they never sprouted, the owner may insist he keep planting.
Until when does the planting period last?
Rav Pappa: until the sharecroppers come in from the field, around the month of Shevat, when Pleiades stands over their heads.
Objection from a baraita on the six seasons: it attributes a planting period in Tishrei, Marheshvan and early Kislev to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in the name of Rabbi Meir.
The baraita lists the six seasons: planting, winter, cold, harvest, summer and heat, each divided at the half-month marks.
Rabbi Yehuda counts the year from Tishrei and Rabbi Shimon from Marheshvan, so the seasons shift accordingly.
Who is the most lenient about planting, extending it to the latest time, and was it really Rabbi Shimon?
Not difficult: one case concerns early crops accepted for planting, the other late crops planted at a much later date.
Mishna: Rabbi Yehuda says if the cultivator accepted the land for a fixed sum of money, he never subtracts the loss from his rent.
Story: a man leased land on the bank of the river Malka Sava for a fixed sum, and the river dammed up, the case reaching Rava.
Rava rules: the Malka Sava does not usually dam up, so it is a regional disaster, and the cultivator may subtract the loss.
The Rabbis object to Rava from the mishna: a cultivator paying a fixed sum never subtracts, whether or not a regional disaster occurred.
Rava: no one needs to heed Rabbi Yehuda's view, since it is a minority opinion that is rejected.
Mishna: a cultivator who pays ten kor of wheat may pay from the blighted field's produce, but need not supply high-quality wheat from the market.
Story: a man leased land to grow hay, then sowed barley, which was blighted, and the worker wanted to pay from that barley.
Rav Haviva asks Ravina whether this is like the mishna's case of paying from the field's own produce when blighted.
Ravina: it is not comparable, since here the land performed its owner's mission of hay, and the extra barley was outside the agreement.
Story: a man leased an orchard for wine, which soured; Rav Kahana thought this matched the mishna's rule of paying from the field itself.
Rav Ashi: not comparable, since the grapes were sound and the wine soured later, while the mishna's crop was blighted; Rav Ashi concedes the grapes that shrank.
Mishna: a cultivator may not plant wheat where barley was agreed, as wheat weakens the field; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forbids switching even when permitted.
What is the reason for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling?
Rav Hisda: a cultivator may not retract from a self-accepted obligation, supported by the verse that the remnant of Israel shall speak no deceit.
Objection from a baraita on the Purim collection for the poor: a poor person may not take even a sandal strap unless he stipulated he could spend freely.

107a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye explains Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reason via Rabba: alternate wheat and barley, and plant lengthwise and crosswise, to avoid weakening the field.
The Gemara clarifies the earlier point: weakening happens only without repeated plowing; with repeated plowing there is no problem.
Mishna: one who leases a field to plant grain may not plant legumes instead.
Rav Yehuda taught Ravin that one leasing a field for grain may plant legumes instead.
Ravin objects that the mishna says a grain field may not be planted with legumes.
Rav Yehuda: not difficult, since the Babylonian rule differs from the Land of Israel rule because the land there is weaker.
Rav Yehuda on cress growing among flax: taking it is not robbery unless it grew on the boundary, or was fully grown and hardened with seed.
The reason: the flax was already damaged by the cress, so removing the cress only takes something from the owner.
Rav Yehuda tells Ravin that neighbors' trees leaning over the boundary: fruit belongs to whichever side it tilts toward, by local custom.
Amoraic dispute on a tree on the boundary: Rav says fruit goes to the side it tilts toward; Shmuel says the two owners divide all the fruit.
Objection from a baraita: the fruit of a boundary tree is divided, apparently refuting Rav.
Shmuel reads the baraita as referring to a tree filling the whole boundary, which belongs to both, consistent with Rav.
If so, this is obvious, so what is the purpose of stating the baraita's ruling?
No, it is needed when the boughs hang more to one side, which the baraita addresses.
But still, what is the novelty of this ruling?
A hypothetical claim: the owner above could say to the other owner, let us divide the fruit by where each boughs hang over his own land.
The baraita teaches that the other owner may reply: why prefer that division, and instead divide by bisecting the tree the other way.
Rav Yehuda advises Ravin not to buy land near a town, and Rabbi Abbahu cites Rav that one may not stand by another's field while it is ripe.
Is that so? Yet Rabbi Abba found Rav's students and asked what Rav meant by the blessings in Deuteronomy about city and field.
Rav's students report Rav's explanation: a house near a synagogue, land near the city, a wife free of uncertain impurity, and righteous descendants.
Rabbi Abba says Rabbi Yohanan did not hold this, but read the city blessing as a bathroom near one's table, and a reward for walking to a mitzva.
Rabbi Yohanan's reading: field property divided into thirds among grain, olives and vines, and a departure from the world as sinless as one's entry.

107b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Not difficult: the evil-eye concern applies where no wall and partition surround the plot, while the other statement covers a walled plot.
Rav reads the verse about the Lord removing all sickness as referring to the evil eye, and shows it by consulting the dead in a graveyard.
Shmuel reads all sickness as referring to wind, consistent with his view that all harm comes from the wind.
Objection: according to Shmuel, those executed by the monarchy were not harmed by wind.
Shmuel: even they would have been healed if not for the wind, which prevents the healing.
Rabbi Hanina: sickness refers to cold, since all things come from Heaven except excess cold and heat, which a person must avoid.
Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina: sickness refers to excrement of the nose and ear, where excess is harmful but a little is beneficial.
Rabbi Elazar: sickness refers to the gall bladder, which causes many illnesses, and morning bread with salt and water negates its effects.
A baraita lists thirteen praises of morning bread, including protection from heat and cold, wisdom, and good marriage, citing that its effects are well attested.
From where is the saying derived that sixty runners could not catch the man who ate in the morning?
The saying is common, and the Sages taught to rise early and eat, in summer for the sun and in winter for the cold, to be strong.
Rava bar Mari derives it from Isaiah: they shall not hunger or thirst, nor shall heat or sun smite them, since they rose early to eat.
Rava derives it from Exodus instead: serving God means Shema and prayer, and blessing bread and water means morning bread with salt and water.
Rav Yehuda advises Rav Adda the surveyor not to treat small land measures lightly, since even small plots can grow valuable saffron.
Rav Yehuda: do not measure the four cubits along a river at all; estimate them within the larger measurement.
Rav Yehuda consistently holds that the four cubits by a channel belong to the nearby houses, while the four cubits by a river belong to everyone.
Rabbi Ami announces that trees along a river must be cut back to the width of the boat-pullers' shoulders so boats can be pulled.
Rav Natan bar Hoshaya ordered sixteen cubits cut on each side, and was beaten by the people of Mashronya for it.
Rav Natan holds a pathway must be as wide as a public domain; but here only enough for the ropes is needed, so shoulder width suffices.
Rabba bar Rav Huna had a forest on a riverbank and refused to cut until others upstream and downstream cut theirs first.
How can he wait for others to act first?
Scripture says gather yourselves and gather, and Reish Lakish says adorn yourself before adorning others, so one must act first.
The forest belonged to a Persian general who would ignore a scholar; Rabba bar Rav Huna cut only if the workers cut, so the cutting would not be pointless.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since otherwise they cannot walk and must cross the river, there is no advantage in cutting down trees that block part of the river.
Rabba bar Rav Naḥman, traveling by boat, saw a forest right on the riverbank whose trees had not been cut to make room for the pullers.
He asked his companions to whom the forest belonged.
They told him it belonged to Rabba bar Rav Huna.
He compared it to the verse in Ezra that the princes and rulers were first in this faithlessness, since a renowned scholar acted improperly.
He told his companions to cut, cut, to clear a path.
Rabba bar Rav Huna arrived and found his forest had been cut down.
He was within his rights not to cut, so he cursed whoever cut it that his branches should be cut down.
The Sages said the curse was fulfilled, so all his remaining years the descendants of Rabba bar Rav Naḥman died during his lifetime.
Rav Yehuda: everyone pays for building the city wall, even orphans, but Torah scholars are exempt, since Torah protects them.
Clarification: this applies only when residents hire workers, but if they go out in a crowd, scholars need not join them.
Rav Yehuda: for dredging a river, lower residents must help upper ones, while for a rainwater ditch the upper residents must help the lower ones.
A baraita on five gardens or courtyards sharing a spring or sewer supports Rav Yehuda: the upper owner repairs with all, and each repairs his own damage.
Shmuel: one who occupies an open riverbank strip to plow is impudent, but he is not removed, since it is ownerless land.
Shmuel adds that nowadays, under Persian rule, the riverbank strip belongs to the adjacent field owner, so such a person is removed.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Nahman debate whether one who seizes land between brothers or partners may be removed, with Rav Nahman requiring removal.
The Sages of Neharde'a hold that even on the basis of neighboring-field law, one is removed.
They support this from Deuteronomy: do what is right and good in the eyes of the Lord, even when legally entitled otherwise.
If a stranger asks an owner whether to buy the field, and the owner says go ahead, must an act of acquisition be made with him?
Ravina says no, the Sages of Neharde'a say yes, and the halakha is that an act of acquisition is required.
Since an act of acquisition is required, if the buyer skipped it, the price change falls on the neighbor who must reimburse the buyer.
If the price was overpaid relative to the market, the neighbor pays the market price; if the seller sold cheaply to a single buyer, the neighbor pays the full value.
If the buyer paid too much, the neighbor says he was sent to help, not to harm, so he pays only the market value.
Mar the Elder, son of Rav Hisda, reports the Neharde'a teaching in Rav Nahman's name: there is no overcharge in real estate, since land has no fixed value.
A sale of an inner beit se'a surrounded by the seller's fields is valid, since it is a distinct plot, and neighbors cannot object.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the middle plot has no distinct quality, the buyer is contriving to become a neighbor, so the other neighbors may block him.
A gift is not subject to the neighbor's right of first refusal.
Ameimar: if the giver guarantees the recipient against seizure, the gift is treated as a sale, so the neighbor may force a sale.
A sale of all of a seller's property, a sale back to the original owners, and a sale to or from a gentile are not subject to the neighbor's right.
Clarification: a buyer who buys from a gentile can say he protects the neighbor, while a sale to a gentile brings a ban until the seller accepts liability.
A field given as mortgage to the creditor is not subject to the neighbor's right, based on Rav Ashi's report from the elders of Mata Mehasya.
What practical difference does it make whether the mortgage resides with the creditor?
Selling a distant field to buy a close one, or selling a bad field to redeem a good one, is not subject to the neighbor's right.
Sales for taxes, sustenance and burial need no proclamation, and sales to a woman, orphans or partners are exempt, per the Sages of Neharde'a.
Among neighbors with equal claims, those whose fields lie on the city side have precedence over those on the far side.
A Torah scholar takes precedence over an ordinary neighbor or relative.
A dilemma: as between a neighbor and a relative, which one takes precedence?
Proverbs says a near neighbor is better than a distant brother, suggesting the neighbor takes precedence over a relative.
If the first buyer offers good dinars and the second weighed dinars, the owner may prefer the better coin, and ready cash prevails.
A neighbor who says he will fetch money is waited for only if he is able to bring it without delay; otherwise he is not waited for.
If the land and the houses or palm trees belong to different owners, the land owner may block the sale of the houses or trees, but not the reverse.
If one buyer wants to build and another to plant, the settling of the land by building takes precedence and no neighbor right applies.
If a rock or palm row separates fields, the neighbor's right applies only if a furrow can be inserted in the open space.
With four neighbors surrounding a plot, the first to buy is valid; if they come together, the plot is divided by diagonal lines.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a cultivator of a field for fewer than seven years may not plant flax, and has no rights to sycamore beams; with seven years he may plant flax in the first year.
Abaye says the cultivator has no rights to the sycamore beams but has rights to the value of the tree's growth; Rava says he has no rights even to that.
Objection from a baraita: the court appraises the value for the cultivator, which seems to mean the sycamore's enhancement, against Rava.
No: the court appraises only the vegetables and beets left standing, and if market day has not arrived he cannot sell them, so he takes money.
Come and hear a proof from baraitot about the Sabbatical and Jubilee years, where the court appraises the field for the cultivator.
But does the Jubilee release a contractor's term, since the Torah says permanently for sold land and not for leased land?
Rather, the baraita must concern a purchaser of a field, for whom the court appraises the field when the Jubilee arrives.
Objection: if so, the appraisal would be for the vegetables, but the Jubilee makes produce ownerless, so it must mean the sycamore enhancement.
Abaye reinterprets the baraita to fit Rava: there it is different, since the sold property returns but the buyer keeps the enhancement.
The verse about a sold house returning in the Jubilee is cited, indicating the enhancement does not return to the seller.
The cases differ: there it is a full sale released by the King's decree, and the buyer was an owner, while a cultivator is not an owner.
Story: Rav Pappa leased land for hay, palm trees sprouted, and he asked the owners to pay him the value of the enhancement.
Rav Sheisha asks: if so, would you also claim payment for a thick palm tree that grew from the planting?
Rav Pappa: there the cultivator did not intend to plant trees, but here I did descend to the field expecting compensation for growth.
In accordance with whose opinion is this? Is it not Abaye's view that the cultivator gets the sycamore enhancement?
It can be Rava's view: there is no loss from the sycamore, but here there is a loss because palm trees took the hay space.
Rav Sheisha objects: what loss have I caused? You lost only a handful of hay, so take it and go.
Rav Pappa claims he grew saffron, but Rav Sheisha replies that he only intended to plant other crops, so he is owed only the wood value.
Story: Rav Beivai bar Abaye leased land, fenced it with earth, trees sprouted, and he asked for the enhancement value.
Rav Pappi objects that such unsound claims come from unfortunate people, and that Abaye's family descended from Eli.
Rav Pappa's view: one is owed the enhancement only if he suffered a loss; here the trees grew where nothing would have been planted, so no compensation is due.
