Story: Rav Yosef's planter died leaving five sons-in-law, so Rav Yosef cancels the arrangement and offers them the value of their enhancement or removal.
Rav Yosef cites Rav Yehuda, or Rav Huna, or Rav Naḥman: heirs of a deceased planter may be removed without payment for the enhancement.
The Gemara rejects that the halakha follows this opinion.
Story: a planter promised that if he ruined the vines he would leave the field.
Rav Yehuda: he leaves without payment for the enhancement; Rav Kahana: he leaves and takes the payment for his work.
Rav Kahana concedes that if he promised to leave without payment for any loss, he leaves with no compensation.
Rava: such a promise made without expecting to fulfill it is an asmakhta, which does not effect acquisition.
According to Rava, how does this differ from the mishna's cultivator who promised to pay the best-quality produce for letting the field lie fallow?
There he pays for his loss; here the loss he caused is deducted from his share, and the remainder is given to him.
Story: Runya, Ravina's planter, caused a loss, and Ravina removed him from the field, and Runya came before Rava.
Rava says Ravina did well, since Runya caused him a loss.
Runya objects that Ravina did not warn him beforehand, so he cannot be forced to leave without warning.
Rava: no warning is necessary in this case.
Rava's principle, following his reasoning: a teacher of children, a planter, a ritual slaughterer and a bloodletter need no warning.

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A town scribe who drafts documents for residents is treated as forewarned; any unrecoverable loss he causes is deducted from his wages without warning.
Story: a planter asked for the enhancement value before going up to Eretz Yisrael, and Rav Pappa bar Shmuel ruled he must be paid it.
Rava objects: did the planter alone improve the field, while the land did not contribute, so he cannot claim all of it?
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel: the planter is owed half the value of the enhancement.
Rava objects: the owner used to take half and the planter half, but now the owner must also pay a sharecropper his share.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel restates: he is owed one-quarter of the enhancement value.
Rav Ashi reads one-quarter as one-sixth of the whole, citing Rav Minyumi's rule that the planter is paid and removed without loss to the owner.
If one-quarter means an actual quarter, the owner loses half a sixth, so the owner suffers a loss; Rav Aha son of Rav Yosef asks why the planter should bear the cost of paying the sharecropper.
Rav Ashi: come raise this difficulty when you reach tractate Zevahim, since it is a good question that calls for complex reasoning.
Rav Minyumi restates the rule for a planter who wants to leave, and adds the rule for an old vine and for trees felled by a river flood.
Story: an orchard was mortgaged for ten years, and after five years was cut for wood; Abaye holds the wood is produce, Rava holds it is principal.
Objection from a baraita: a dried or cut tree is sold for wood and the creditor consumes the produce of the land bought, which supports Rava against Abaye.
No: the cut tree is like a dried one, both out of their proper time, so the wood counts as produce, and the baraita fits Abaye.
Come and hear a proof for Rava from a mishna in Ketubot about a wife's inherited old vines and olive trees.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Such trees are sold as wood and land bought with the proceeds, while the husband consumes the produce of that land.
The text should be emended to say they grew old after inheritance, or else the vines were inherited in a different field, so they count as principal and are sold.
Case: a mortgage document lacks a term; the creditor says three years and the debtor says two, and the creditor consumed the produce in the third year.
Which of them is deemed credible?
Rav Yehuda: land remains with its owner; Rav Kahana: produce remains with whoever consumed it, and the halakha follows Rav Kahana.
But the halakha follows Rav Naḥman, who holds land remains with its owner in the leap-year rental case; these rulings seem to conflict.
The cases differ: the leap-year uncertainty can never be revealed, while the document's terms will eventually be revealed by its witnesses.
Another case: the creditor says five years and the debtor three, and the creditor says he lost the document; Rav Yehuda deems the creditor credible.
Rav Pappa objects that Rav Zevid and Rav Avira disagree: a document ready for collection would not be lost, so the creditor is hiding it.
Ravina objects: under the Sura custom, would the Sages credit a creditor who hides the document, risking loss to the debtor?
Rav Ashi: there the Sages made the owner pay taxes and dig trenches, which secures his ownership; that is the institution.
Ravina asks: what could the debtor do on land that needs no trenches and bears no tax?
He should have protested before the three years of presumptive status passed; if he did not, he caused his own loss.
Sharecropper dispute over the agreed share: Rav Yehuda believes the owner; Rav Naḥman says follow the regional custom.
The two Sages do not really disagree: Rav Naḥman's rule is for a location where the sharecropper takes half, and Rav Yehuda's for one-third.
Rav Mari son of Shmuel's daughter reports Abaye: they disagree even where the sharecropper usually takes half.
Rav Yehuda's reasoning: the owner could claim the other was merely a hired worker or a gleaner, so the owner is believed.
Orphans claim they enhanced an inherited lien field, and the creditor says their father enhanced it; upon whom does the burden of proof fall?

110b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Hanina holds the land stays with the orphans in their possession, so the creditor must bring proof.
An elder reports Rabbi Yohanan: the orphans must bring proof, since land ready for collection counts as already collected by the creditor.
Abaye cites a mishna on a tree planted by a city: if it is uncertain which came first, the tree is cut down and no money is paid.
The analogy: the tree is cut regardless, yet its owner must prove priority, so the lien document counts as collected and the orphans must prove.
The orphans brought proof of their enhancement, and Rabbi Hanina thought they should be removed by a portion of the land.
The Gemara rejects this: they are removed by money, not land, as Rav Naḥman cites Shmuel.
Shmuel's three cases where the enhancement is appraised and paid in money: a firstborn to his brother, a creditor or widow to orphans, and a creditor to buyers.
Ravina asks: does Shmuel hold that a creditor must pay buyers for enhancement, when Shmuel also says a creditor collects the enhancement too?
A suggested resolution, that only enhancement reaching the shoulders is at issue, is rejected because Shmuel collects daily even large enhancements.
Not difficult: where the debt covered the land and enhancement together, the creditor leaves buyers nothing; otherwise he must pay them for the excess.
If the debtor did not owe that sum, can the buyer with money remove the creditor, and why should he not claim a plot equal to his enhancement?
The land was set aside as designated repayment for this creditor alone, so he may claim all of it.
Mishna: a cultivator hired for a seven-year cycle counts the Sabbatical Year in the tally only in the first arrangement; wage collection rules for day, night and hourly laborers follow.
Baraita: from Leviticus, a day laborer's wages may not remain all night, so he collects all night, and from Deuteronomy, a night laborer collects all day.
Why not say the opposite, that a night laborer is paid all night and a day laborer all day?
Baraita: the words until morning teach that the prohibition of delaying wages is violated only until the first morning, not for further delay.
From that point forward, what is the halakha?
Rav: one who delays wages after that point violates the prohibition against delaying, the prohibition of bal tashheh.
Rav Yosef asks: what is the verse from which that prohibition is derived?
Proverbs: do not say to your neighbor, go and come again, and tomorrow I will give, when you have it with you.
Baraita: when one tells another to go hire workers for him, neither violates the prohibition of delaying wages, since the employer did not hire them himself.

111a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The middleman is exempt from the wage-delay prohibition, because the work is not performed for him.
What are the circumstances of this case?
If the middleman said that the workers' wages are on him, then the wages are indeed his responsibility.
Baraita: an employer who mistakenly sends a worker to another's field pays the worker in full and then recovers from the owner the benefit gained.
No: this rule is needed when the middleman said the wages are on the employer, so they share responsibility and neither violates the prohibition.
Yehuda bar Mareimar instructed his attendant to hire workers saying the wages are on the employer, to avoid violating the prohibition on delaying wages.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: the Sura market workers violate only the rabbinic prohibition, since workers know they are paid on market day.
Rav and Shmuel dispute the hourly laborer: Rav limits wages to the same day or night, while Shmuel adds the following day for night work.
The mishna says an hourly laborer collects all night and all day, which appears to refute Rav.
Rav could say the mishna is disjunctive: a day laborer collects all day, a night laborer all night.
The mishna on weekly, monthly and yearly laborers suggests night workers collect throughout the following day, against Rav.
Rav could say it is a dispute between tanna'im: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon differ on hourly laborers.
Baraita: withholding a laborer's wages violates five prohibitions and one positive mitzva, citing verses from Leviticus and Deuteronomy.
These prohibitions take effect at different times of day, so how can one violate them all?
Rav Hisda: the phrase means the general concept of withholding wages includes all these prohibitions and one mitzva.
What is defined as oppression, what as stealing, and how do they differ?
Rav Hisda: oppression is saying he will pay later, while stealing is admitting the money is owed but refusing to pay it.
Rav Sheshet objects from a baraita comparing oppression to denying a deposit, so oppression must be denial; he offers his own distinction.
Abaye objects that stealing must be like denying a deposit, so oppression is claiming never hired, and stealing claiming payment was made.
What is different about oppression that Rav Sheshet objected to, and what is different about stealing that he did not?
Rav Sheshet could say stealing means first taking the money by refusing to pay, and later denying the debt.
If so, oppression could also be first admitting then denying the wage, so why must oppression be a denial of hiring?
The verses differ: stealing is written with admission at the outset, while oppression is written as the actual act of oppressing.
Rava: oppression and stealing are the same, and the Torah split them so the offender violates two prohibitions.
Mishna: wages for a person, an animal or utensils are subject to the same-day and overnight prohibitions, but only once the creditor demands payment.
Mishna: a laborer who requests wages on time takes an oath and collects; if the time has passed, he cannot swear, unless witnesses show a timely demand.
Mishna: hiring a resident alien who keeps the seven Noahide laws violates only the same-day obligation, not the overnight one.
Whose opinion is the mishna, if not the first tanna of the baraita or Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda? Which baraita is meant?

111b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Verse excludes gentiles and a righteous convert; the ger toshav living in the Land is the one meant.
Derives that animal and vessel rentals are covered, using the phrase 'in your land'.
Sages' ruling: hiring people, animals and vessels all carry same-day payment liability and delay liability.
Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda: a ger toshav has only same-day liability; animals and vessels only the oppression prohibition.
Which opinion does the mishna follow, and what difficulty does each possibility create?
Rava: the mishna's tanna belongs to the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
A baraita from Rabbi Yishmael's school lists the same rulings, supporting Rava's claim.
What is the reasoning of the first tanna?
Two 'hired laborer' verbal analogies; Rabbi Yosei does not use the analogy.
Even without that analogy, animals and vessels should still be liable under same-day payment.
Rabbi Chananya's baraita: 'for he is poor' excludes animals and vessels, which cannot become rich or poor.
What does the first tanna do with the verse 'for he is poor'?
It gives a poor person precedence over a rich one; Rabbi Yosei derives that from 'poor and needy'.
Why does the first tanna need a second verse for the same point?
Both verses are needed, since each one alone would leave a case uncovered.
On either derivation, how does the mishna's tanna justify including animals and vessels?
He does not use the analogy; 'his work with you' covers animals and vessels, and 'your neighbor' excludes a ger toshav.
Why include animals and vessels but exclude a ger toshav if 'with you' is the basis?
Animals and vessels are at least part of the neighbor's property, whereas a ger toshav is not.
What does the first tanna do with the verse 'your neighbor'?
It excludes gentiles, as a baraita teaches.
The exclusion of gentiles is already derived from 'your brothers', so no extra verse is needed.
Two verses are needed: one permits oppressing a gentile, the other permits stealing from him, since each case needs its own source.
What does Rabbi Yosei do with the verse 'wages shall not remain with you all night'?
Rav Asi: liability applies even when a laborer is hired for only one cluster of grapes.
The first tanna derives from 'he sets his soul upon it' that liability applies to any work.

112a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What does the second Sage derive from the verse 'he sets his soul upon it'?
Baraita: the verse explains why workers must be paid promptly, since the laborer risked his life for his wages.
Withholding a laborer's wages is as if the employer took the laborer's soul from him.
Rav Huna and Rav Chisda disagree over whose soul is meant: the robber's or the robbed person's.
Supporting the robber's soul reading, a verse in Proverbs says God will plead for the poor and take the robber's soul.
Supporting the robbed person's soul reading, a verse in Proverbs says a greedy person takes the life of its owners.
If the robbed-soul reading holds, how does the other opinion explain the verse that it takes the owners' soul?
That verse uses the 'what is the reason' style, so God spoils the spoilers because they took a soul.
Mishna: the prohibition is violated only when the worker has demanded his wages from the employer.
Baraita: 'with you' limits the violation to wages that were demanded, that are available, and not deposited with an agent.
Mishna: an employer who left his payment with a storekeeper or money changer does not violate the prohibition.
If the agent delays payment, may the laborer return to the employer or not?
Rav Sheshet says the laborer may not return; Rabba says he may return.
Rabba's support: the mishna's wording implies the laborer may return, since the employer is only exempt from the violation.
Rav Sheshet: 'does not transgress' means the employer is not in the category of transgressing at all.
Does the prohibition apply when a laborer is paid as a contractor for a finished job, depending on whether a craftsman acquires the item by enhancing it?
Rav Sheshet: yes, the employer does violate the prohibition.
A baraita says a contractor does not violate it, which seems to contradict Rav Sheshet.
Baraita support: a craftsman's client violates only after the sun sets, when the garment was returned and he delayed payment.
If a craftsman acquires the item through enhancement, why would the owner violate the prohibition at all?
Rav Mari: the baraita concerns laundering thick garments, where there is no enhancement and no acquisition.
Why would the owner give the garment to be softened, if softening is not an enhancement the craftsman acquires?
The baraita concerns treading a garment for a set fee per tread, which is hired labor, so the prohibition applies.

112b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a laborer claiming unpaid wages at the proper time swears the oath and then receives his wages.
Why did the Sages make the plaintiff laborer swear, reversing the usual rule that the defendant takes the oath?
Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel: the Sages taught great halakhot here.
These are not halakhot but ordinances, so the terminology is wrong.
Corrected version: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel that they taught great ordinances here.
Does calling them great imply that there are minor ordinances, and which ones are those?
Rav Nachman reports Shmuel: they taught fixed ordinances necessary for practical life.
The employer's oath was transferred to the laborer so that the laborer's livelihood is protected.
Why should the employer lose out for the laborer's livelihood, when the employer himself would prefer to swear?
Better for the employer that the laborer swears, so laborers will hire out with their wages secured.
Why not argue the reverse: the employer should swear so that he can exempt himself and laborers get hired?
The employer must find laborers to hire, but laborers equally must be willing to be hired out.
Rather, the employer is preoccupied with many laborers, so he may have forgotten and mistakenly thought he paid.
If he may have forgotten, the laborer should be paid without any oath.
The laborer swears to ease the employer's worry that he was cheated.
Why not pay in front of witnesses each time to remove the uncertainty?
Finding witnesses before each payment would be an inconvenience for both sides.
Why not pay the wages upfront, before the work starts, when the employer is less busy?
Both parties prefer payment on credit at the end of the day, for their own convenience.
If so, should the laborer swear even when the wage amount is disputed, as in a fixed-sum case?
Baraita: when a craftsman and employer dispute a fixed wage, the one who claims the change bears the burden of proof.
A fixed wage is something people remember, so the employer would not forget how much he agreed.
If forgetting is a concern, why does the mishna deny the oath once the time for claiming has passed?
Mishna: if the time has passed, the laborer does not swear and collect his wages.
An employer is presumed not to violate the prohibition of delaying wages, so no oath is needed after that time.
But didn't you say the employer is preoccupied with his laborers, which makes forgetting likely?
That concern applies only before the time for payment arrives, since forgetting is possible then.

113a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When the time to pay arrives, the employer focuses and remembers the details so he does not delay wages.
Is the laborer suspected of violating the prohibition of stealing, if his claim is accepted?
The employer has two presumptions in his favor, while the laborer has only one, so the cases differ.
Mishna: if witnesses testify that the laborer claimed his wages, he swears and collects them.
Why is a claim at the proper time not already noted in an earlier passage?
Rav Asi: the witnesses testify to a claim made at the proper time.
Perhaps the employer paid afterward, so the claim at the proper time does not settle the matter.
Abaye: the witnesses testify that the claim was made throughout the whole day, not only at one moment.
Rav Chama bar Ukva: the claim covers the same day of the claim, and the laborer may still press it that day.
Mishna: a creditor may seize collateral only through a court agent and may not enter the debtor's house; he returns items needed for sleep and work.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: collateral needed by the debtor is returned only up to thirty days, after which it is sold in court.
Shmuel: a court agent may seize items in the marketplace but may not enter the debtor's house to take collateral.
The mishna's wording implies that a court agent may enter the house, which contradicts Shmuel.
Shmuel replies: the mishna forbids seizing collateral except through court, and the house clause follows that point.
Who is the tanna referring to in the house clause: the creditor or the court agent?
The reasoning is inconclusive, since the mishna may only be stating a rabbinic decree barring creditors from entering houses.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita: other items may be taken, so the court agent can enter the house, though limits apply.
Who is permitted to enter the house: the creditor, or only the court agent?
Rav Pappa's explanation: the baraita concerns a creditor who violates two prohibitions by taking certain items.
Another baraita: the word 'the man' includes the court agent, so the agent has the status of the debtor.
Does 'the man' include the court agent as if he were the borrower himself?

113b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An agent of the court is treated like the creditor, who must wait outside for the collateral.
Exodus verse about returning a neighbor's garment taken as collateral, read as referring to a court agent.
Or does that verse refer only to a creditor, since Deuteronomy addresses the creditor entering the house?
This is a dispute between tanna'im, so the verse is a conditional case, not a settled rule.
Baraita: a court agent may not enter the house and must stand outside while the debtor brings out the collateral.
Second baraita: a creditor must also stand outside, but the court agent may enter the debtor's house.
The court agent who comes to seize may enter the house and take the collateral himself, but not items for food preparation.
Items needed for sustenance: a rich debtor keeps two beds and a mat, a poor one a bed and mat, for himself only.
The same arrangements apply to valuation obligations owed to the Temple treasury, as the Torah sets them out.
The Master earlier said a rich debtor keeps beds and blankets, and a poor one keeps a bed and a mat.
If the extra bed is not for his wife or children, who is it for, given that they get nothing?
Why does the debtor need two beds at all?
One bed is for eating and one for sleeping, following Shmuel's view on avoiding illness after eating.
Rav Nachman asks whether the debtor's collateral is sold if he may keep it, given the mishna's rule about the pillow and plow.
The baraita follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who sells collateral after thirty days, so the arrangement does not apply.
Does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel mean a full sale, or only sale of items unfit for the debtor after thirty days?
Rejected: for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel nothing is unfit, since all Israel are children of kings.
Mishna example: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits moving raw arum on Shabbat because it is food for ravens.
Mishna example: Rabbi Shimon holds that all Jews are princes, so all may use rose oil on Shabbat.
Baraita: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva hold that every Jew is fit for an expensive cloak, so it is not sold for debt.
If the mishna sells what is unfit, how can a plow be unfit and sellable, since it is not an ornament?
Rava bar Rabba: the plow is silver, an ornament not used for work, so it can be sold.
Rav Chagga objects: why should the creditor make allowances for the debtor's livelihood at all?
Abaye begins his reply to Rav Chagga's objection.

114a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The debtor's needs are indeed placed on the creditor's responsibility.
The verse 'and it shall be righteousness to you' shows the creditor must act with righteousness toward the debtor.
Does a verbal analogy from the word 'poor' in the debtor and valuation laws allow arrangements for the debtor?
Ravin's letter: a question about a vow to give a hundred dinars to the Temple repairs, whether arrangements are made for it.
Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Yirmeya: a fortiori, if no arrangements are made for consecrated property, then none for a debtor.
Rabbi Yochanan: the verse on vows juxtaposes consecrated property with valuations, so arrangements apply to consecration too.
The other Sages read that juxtaposition as teaching that consecrated property is judged by its significance, like valuations.
A fortiori from valuations: if valuations get no return of collateral yet arrangements apply, the debtor should get arrangements.
The verse says 'if he is poor' for valuations, so arrangements apply only to a person who stays poor throughout.
If no arrangements are made for a debtor, why should consecrated property not be returned by a fortiori reasoning?
The verse on returning collateral mentions a blessing, which excludes consecrated property since it needs no blessing.
Is consecrated property really exempt from needing a blessing, given the verse about eating and blessing God?
The verse about tzedaka refers to a needy person, which excludes consecrated property that needs no charity.
Rabba bar Avuh asks Elijah what the halakha is on arrangements for a debtor.
Elijah: derive a verbal analogy from the word 'poor' in the valuation and debtor verses, so arrangements apply.

114b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: From where is it derived that one who is naked may not separate teruma?
The verse 'he sees no unseemly thing in you' shows that holy words may not be spoken in front of a naked person.
Why does a priest stand in a cemetery, given that priests are forbidden contact with the dead?
Elijah asks whether Rabba has studied the order of Teharot, which covers this point.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai: gentile graves do not defile, because only Jews are called man in Ezekiel.
Rabba bar Avuh: he cannot master even the four common orders, let alone all six.
Elijah asks why he is not learned in all of them.
Rabba: a livelihood matter weighs on him, so he cannot study properly.
Elijah takes Rabba into the Garden of Eden and has him gather leaves.
Rabba is rebuked for using his World-to-Come, so he sells the cloak and divides the money among his sons-in-law.
Baraita: for a poor debtor the creditor may not sleep with the collateral, but a wealthy one may.
What is the tanna saying with that baraita?
Rav Sheshet: a poor man's collateral must be returned before sunset, while a rich man's may be kept overnight.
Baraita: a creditor may not take collateral and need not return it, yet he transgresses all these prohibitions.
What is the tanna saying in that baraita?
Rav Sheshet: a creditor may not take collateral, and if he did, he must return it, and the latter clause covers that case.
Rava: the rule applies to collateral taken later, not at the time of the loan, which may be kept.
Rav Shizbi's baraita: a garment worn at night is returned by day, and one worn by day is returned by night.
Rava asks why the garment would be needed at those times, since it is useless then.
Rava explains the baraita concerns a garment taken as collateral at a time it may be held, and it must be returned at the proper time.
Rabbi Yochanan: if the debtor dies after the collateral was returned, the creditor may take it from the heirs.
Rabbi Meir objects: if collateral must be returned, why take it at all, since the Torah requires return?

115a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why does the creditor take the collateral again, if he must return it to the debtor the next day?
So that the Sabbatical Year does not cancel the debt and the item does not become movable property for his sons.
This inference implies that taking collateral only once is not enough, which contradicts Rabbi Yochanan.
Rav Adda bar Mattana: reword the baraita so that it fits Rabbi Yochanan, that one taking collateral once may collect from heirs.
Baraita: the verse permits entering a guarantor's house to take collateral, supported by a verse in Proverbs.
Proverbs 6 warns that a guarantor ensnared by his words should act quickly to free himself from the debt.
Explanation of the Proverbs passage: pay the debt if you have money, or else apologize and seek forgiveness.
The verse is read in another way: a wage debt can be secured by collateral, but a loan cannot be secured against the debtor's will.
Mishna: collateral may not be taken from a widow, whether she is poor or wealthy.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda rules that a widow, whether poor or rich, may not be pledged.
Rabbi Shimon: collateral may be taken from a wealthy widow, but not a poor one, since it must be returned and would harm her reputation.
Does Rabbi Yehuda not interpret the reasons behind verses, while Rabbi Shimon does, given the reverse elsewhere?
Baraita on a king's wives: Rabbi Yehuda permits many wives if they do not turn his heart, while Rabbi Shimon forbids even Abigail-like wives.
Rabbi Yehuda generally does not read reasons into verses, but this verse states its reason explicitly for the king.
Rabbi Shimon: the stated reason is unnecessary, and it widens the prohibition to even one wife who would turn his heart.
Mishna: taking a millstone as collateral is prohibited, and the prohibition extends to any item used to prepare food.
Rav Huna: taking a lower millstone brings two sets of lashes, and taking both millstones brings three.
Rav Yehuda: taking one millstone brings one set of lashes, and taking both brings two sets.

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The phrase 'roasted with fire' comes to teach the prohibition on other food items taken as collateral.
Do Abaye and Rava dispute the same point as Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda, in the Paschal offering case?
Rava: eating raw meat or cooked meat of the Paschal offering each brings its own sets of lashes, and both bring three.
Abaye: one is not flogged for a general prohibition that covers many cases.
Does Abaye hold as Rav Yehuda, and Rava as Rav Huna, given their disagreement on the same point?
Rava: Rav Yehuda limits his view to collateral, since 'for he takes a man's life' is a general statement, not a specific list.
Abaye: Rav Huna also limits his view to the collateral case, since the general statement does not add the millstones.

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since 'roasted with fire' is superfluous in that context, it is applied as a separate prohibition on the millstones.
In the Paschal case the phrase is needed: eating raw meat is forbidden only when one must eat roasted meat that night.
Baraita following Rav Yehuda: a pair of scissors or a pair of cows gives two sets of lashes if taken together, one if taken singly.
Opposing baraita: the verse on millstones teaches that any two-part item doing one task is liable for each part separately.
A man took a slaughtering knife as collateral; Abaye ordered its return, while Rava said he may claim up to its value.
Why does Abaye not accept Rava's reasoning, given the goats that ate barley case where the claim up to value was allowed?
Goats are not usually lent out, so possession gives a presumption of ownership, while a knife that is lent out needs proof.
Does Rava not accept that distinction, given that he removed lent-out items from orphans on possession alone?
Rava: a knife is easily damaged, so people are particular about lending it out and it is not a typical loan item.
End of the chapter marker, which closes the chapter 'The one who receives'.

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: when a collapsed building belonged to two owners, they split the debris, with stones awarded by likely breakage.
The word 'they see' implies that the mode of collapse can be determined from the debris.
If the mode of collapse can be known, why does the first clause divide without considering it?
The case is one where the house fell at night, or the stones were cleared by the public and no one can be asked.
Quoting the mishna: if one of them recognized his stones, he takes them.
What does the other party claim when he says he does not know, and is that a concession?
The case: one says I have a hundred dinars of yours, and the other says I do not know.
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda hold liable, Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan exempt, depending on whether an oath is involved.
Rava reads the mishna's sharing as proportional to the broken stones, since the claimant who says he does not know is worse off.
Abaye objects that the one who recognizes stones is worse off, since his knowledge shows he knows nothing more.
Abaye's reading: the recognized stones are counted against unbroken stones, so the other party takes the rest of the unbroken ones.
If so, what does the first party gain from recognizing his own stones?
He gains bricks from a wider mold, or clay that was processed better.
Mishna: if the upper floor of a rented house collapses and the owner will not repair it, the tenant may live below; Rabbi Yosei divides the repair duties.
To what extent must the upper floor be damaged for the tenant to be unable to live there?
Rav: the damage must be most of the floor, since a person cannot live partly above and partly below.
Shmuel: a break of four handbreadths suffices, since a person cannot live partly above and partly below.
What is the situation where the owner renting an upper story gives the tenant an alternative, and what does the rental term mean?
Rava: the owner rents the upper story with a condition that the tenant moves down when it is no longer usable.
If there is already an explicit condition, what does the mishna add?
Rav Ashi: the upper story is rented as lying above that particular house, so the house is liened to it for that purpose.
Ravin bar Rav Adda's report: a man sold a vine above a peach tree, and the peach tree was uprooted; Rabbi Chiya required replanting it.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel raised a dilemma about that ruling.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When the upper-story tenant moves into the lower story, does the owner leave, or do both live there together?
If both live there, must the tenant enter by the roofs as before, or by the stairs, given what he agreed to?
Two upper stories, one above the other: what if the upper floor or lower floor breaks, and may the tenant claim the lower floor? Left unresolved.
Mishna: Rabbi Yosei says the lower owner provides the ceiling.
What does the word ceiling mean here?
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: mats and beams; Setini, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: wide planks; each follows local custom.
Two residents of one house: the upper floor's plaster broke and water from washing ran down and damaged the lower apartment.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba: the upper resident repairs it; Rabbi Elai, citing Rabbi Chiya son of Rabbi Yosei: the lower resident repairs it.
Do these Sages dispute the same principle as Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis in the mishna, about who must distance himself from damage?
A mishna on trees and pits shows the opposite: the tree owner must distance himself, so the earlier reading is rejected.
Rabbi Yosei holds the one at risk of damage must distance himself, while the Rabbis hold the one causing damage must do so.
If the disagreement is elsewhere, what do Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis disagree about in this mishna?
They dispute the strength of the ceiling: the Rabbis hold the plaster strengthens it, Rabbi Yosei that it levels holes.
Rav Ashi: Rabbi Yosei concedes that one who pours water causing damage from a distance, like an archer, must prevent it.
Mishna: if the upper and house collapsed, the upper owner may build the house and live there until repaid his expenses.
Rabbi Yehuda: the upper owner must pay rent while living in the house, unless he builds the upper story first and then lives in the lower part.

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Yehuda teaches in three places that one may not benefit from another's property without consent; this is the first.
Mishna on the dyer who changed the color of wool: Rabbi Yehuda says the dyer may not keep the dyed wool, as he would benefit from another's property.
Mishna on the debtor who deposited a note with a trustee: Rabbi Yehuda says the trustee may not return the note, illustrating the same principle.
Rabbi Yosei says the trustee should give the note; Rabbi Yehuda says he should not, since the stipulation is void.
Rabbi Yehuda's ruling might apply only to the house case, due to blackened walls, so the dyer example proves nothing general.
The trustee case is an asmakhta, an exaggerated condition that does not effect acquisition, so it is no proof of the general principle.
Rav Acha bar Adda in the name of Ulla begins to set out rules for rebuilding a collapsed house.
Ulla's rules: the court permits changes that strengthen the building and refuses those that weaken it, for both lower and upper owners.
What was taught about the rights of the upper owner to the land when neither can afford to rebuild?
Baraita: if neither can rebuild, the upper owner has no right to the land, which all belongs to the lower owner.
Baraita: Rabbi Natan gives the lower owner two-thirds and the upper one-third; others give three-quarters and one-quarter.
Rabba: follow Rabbi Natan, who reasons that the upper story lowers the house's value by a third.
Mishna: an olive press under a garden and a wall or tree that fell into the public domain, with rules on liability and warnings.

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a wall's stones or a laborer's hay wages cannot be retracted once the other party has accepted them.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether most of the roof must collapse or a four-handbreadth hole suffices.
The dispute is taught for both the press and the house, since each case alone could be read as a different ruling.
Mishna: if the court gave the owner time to remove a dangerous wall or tree, he is exempt only within that time.
How much time does the court usually allot?
Rabbi Yochanan: the standard period is thirty days.
Mishna: the owner of a fallen wall next to a garden may not retract his offer of the stones.
The clause implies the garden owner cleared the stones, so the stones remained the wall owner's until then.
Why do the stones remain with the wall owner, when the garden owner's courtyard should acquire them for him?
That rule applies only when the giver intends to transfer; here the wall owner only wants the garden owner to clear them.
Mishna: an employer cannot force a laborer hired to work with hay to accept hay as wages.
This halakha must be taught separately, since with stones there is no wage owed, but with hay there is one.
The reverse case: with stones the court may allow retraction, while with hay the court does not, so both are taught.
Mishna conclusion: the court does not listen to the employer who offers hay as wages.
But a baraita says the court does listen to the employer, so how do the two conflict?
Rav Nachman: the mishna concerns work on the employer's own property, the baraita work on another's property.
Rabba objects: even on another's property the employer owes the wage, so the distinction fails.
Rav Nachman: the baraita concerns work on ownerless property, where the employer may require hay as wages.
Rava objects: a found item of a laborer belongs to the employer, so he cannot force hay on him as wages.
Rav Nachman: the mishna concerns gathering hay as the employer's agent, the baraita only viewing it, which does not acquire it.
Rabba: whether viewing acquires ownerless property is a dispute between tanna'im.
Mishna on watchmen of the Sabbatical-year growth: Rabbi Yosei says a volunteer watchman acts as a free bailee.
Is it not the same dispute: whether viewing acquires ownerless property?
The first tanna holds viewing acquires it, so a paid watchman acquires for the community; Rabbi Yosei holds it does not.
The Rabbis ask whether a volunteer bailee's view implies the omer and two loaves are not from communal funds.
Rava: all agree viewing acquires ownerless property; they dispute whether to worry the watchman will not hand it over wholeheartedly.
Rabbi Yosei does not worry about that, so the same objection about communal funds applies to his view.
An alternative version: the dispute is about violent people; the first tanna has the Sages pay the watchman to deter them.

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The objection restated: the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei is whether to worry about violent people.
Mishna: one may move manure or building materials into the public domain only briefly, and must pay for damage caused.
Is the mishna not following Rabbi Yehuda, who allows piling manure for thirty days in the public domain?
Rabbi Yehuda may hold the mishna's view: one acting with a mitzva or court permission is exempt, but damage still needs care.
Doesn't a baraita say Rabbi Yehuda exempts from damage caused by permitted public obstacles, so the mishna is not his view?
Abaye: Rabbi Yehuda, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Shimon all exempt when the Sages permitted the act that caused damage.
Mishna on an oven in an upper story: Rabbi Shimon says the measurements only show he is exempt after taking precautions.
Baraita: the stonecutter, chiseler, donkey driver, porter, builder and master builder are each liable once they take delivery.
Another baraita says only the last worker is liable; how is that reconciled?
Hired workers: only the last is liable; contracted workers, who agreed to work together, are all liable.
Mishna on two gardens one above the other: Rabbi Meir gives the vegetables to the upper owner, Rabbi Yehuda to the lower, Rabbi Shimon by reach.
Rava: all agree the root belongs to the upper owner; they dispute the leaves, depending on whether the sprouts follow the root.
Baraita on a tree: Rabbi Meir gives sprouts to the land owner, Rabbi Yehuda splits them between trunk and root owners.

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Parallel baraita on orla: a tree sprouting from trunk or roots of an old tree; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree on which counts as new.
Both halakhot must be taught, since each one alone could be read as limited to money or to a prohibition.
Rabbi Shimon: any vegetables the upper owner can reach by stretching out his hand are his.
Rav Anan asks whether a plant is within reach if its leaves can be reached but not its roots, or the reverse; unresolved.
Efrayim the scribe, citing Reish Lakish: the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, and Shapur praised Rabbi Shimon's view.
Closing colophon: the chapter Ha-Bayit ve-ha-Aliyah concludes and the tractate Bava Metzia ends.
